The Kenya Financial Sector Stability Report 2018 documents that pension industry coverage remained at 20.01 percent of the working population in 2018, with the RBA undertaking reform initiatives to grow pension savings for workers in both formal and informal sectors. The FSR documents that unremitted contributions increased in Defined Contribution schemes due to poor economic performance and insufficient funding of quasi-government schemes, and that the RBA amended the Act to enable direct intervention against sponsors who fail to remit deductions. Pension industry assets stood at KSh 1,166.34 billion with government securities at 39.41 percent, immovable property at 19.71 percent, and quoted equities at 17.28 percent. The FSR notes that pension liabilities are growing faster than assets and that increasing life expectancy is elevating funding risks. The National Social Security Fund has proposed converting itself from a defined contribution scheme into a mandatory defined benefit scheme covering all workers earning above KSh 10,000 monthly, with contribution rates rising from 6 percent to 15 percent of gross salary split equally between employer and employer, arguing that Kenya cannot reach adequate retirement security through voluntary savings and that a defined benefit structure guarantees retirees a predictable income. (Source: Kenya Financial Sector Stability Report, 2018)

The NSSF's proposal to convert to a mandatory defined benefit scheme with 15 percent contribution rates is the most consequential labour market and fiscal policy reform suggested in any of the proposals before us, and its fiscal and macroeconomic implications dwarf its retirement security merits — which are themselves not straightforward.

On the fiscal risk: a defined benefit scheme is only as strong as the sponsor's commitment to fund it when liabilities exceed assets. The FSR documents that even in the existing pension sector, faster growth of pension liabilities relative to assets is already elevating funding risks, and that unremitted contributions in Defined Contribution schemes are increasing. The NSSF — a quasi-government entity — would be operating a defined benefit scheme whose sponsor is ultimately the national government. If actuarial assumptions on investment returns, longevity, or wage growth prove incorrect, the national government inherits the funding shortfall. The FSR already documents the public debt-to-GDP ratio at 59.21 percent. A contingent liability of the scale a large defined benefit scheme can generate — international precedent from the United Kingdom, Brazil, and South Africa shows that public defined benefit pension deficits can reach 20–50 percent of GDP over multi-decade periods — is not a risk the current fiscal position can absorb without explicit prior stress testing and parliamentary approval.

On the labour market impact: a mandatory 15 percent payroll contribution, split 7.5 percent each on employer and employee, raises the effective cost of formal employment. The FSR documents that private sector credit to firms declined, with companies relying more on internal reserves. An immediate 7.5 percentage point increase in employer payroll costs in that environment would accelerate informality — employers would restructure employment relationships to avoid the contribution threshold — and reduce the disposable income of workers earning near the KSh 10,000 minimum threshold, precisely the segment the scheme is intended to benefit. The FSR's own financial inclusion data shows that the proportion of households whose financial health worsened increased to 51 percent in 2018. A lower take-home pay at that level of household financial stress is not a neutral trade-off for a future pension benefit that is 30 years away.

The correct path is incremental: mandatory auto-enrolment in the existing NSSF with an opt-out provision, combined with progressive contribution rate increases linked to wage growth benchmarks, and structural reform of NSSF's investment governance to improve returns on the assets already under management before expanding the liability base.

The Kenya Financial Sector Stability Report 2018 documents that Kenya's domestic debt maturity profile lengthened, with average maturity of government securities rising to 4.6 years in December 2018 from 4.1 years in December 2017. The FSR attributes this to increased uptake of long-term infrastructure bonds and repayment of maturing short-term debt. Treasury bond subscription declined to 76.22 percent in 2018 from 122.36 percent in 2017, with the FSR attributing the decline to lower coupon rates offered to reduce cost of debt. The secondary market for government bonds improved in 2018 relative to 2017 but the bond turnover ratio declined, signifying a less liquid market. Total external public debt was rising faster than domestic debt. The FSR explicitly states it is essential to deepen the local currency bond market to build a strong base for potential shock absorption and create a long-term financing market for the private sector. A coalition of domestic institutional investors including pension funds and insurance companies has formally requested that the National Treasury introduce monthly bond issuances across the full maturity spectrum from 2-year to 25-year tenors, with a pre-announced issuance calendar for the full fiscal year, arguing that predictability of supply will allow them to plan portfolio duration management and will improve secondary market liquidity. (Source: Kenya Financial Sector Stability Report, 2018)

This request from the institutional investor coalition deserves a straightforward and supportive response, because it is technically correct, fiscally responsible, and directly aligned with what the FSR identifies as a structural priority for Kenya's financial system.

A pre-announced annual issuance calendar with monthly auctions across the full maturity spectrum is the single most effective administrative reform available to the Treasury for deepening the local currency bond market, and it costs the government nothing in fiscal terms. The FSR documents that the secondary market for government bonds improved in 2018 but the turnover ratio declined, which is a signal of a market where investors hold bonds to maturity rather than trading them — precisely the illiquidity that makes the LCB market a poor shock absorber. The primary reason investors hold to maturity rather than trade is that they cannot predict when or whether the Treasury will re-open a given tenor, which makes marking their positions to a reliable yield curve difficult and reduces the informational value of secondary market prices. A published issuance calendar resolves this directly: it gives market makers a forward view of supply, enables primary dealers to position inventory, and gives investors the certainty of exit that makes them willing to enter.

The FSR documents that domestic debt grew by 18.12 percent to KSh 2,452.34 billion in 2018, and that the Treasury deliberately offered lower coupon rates on bonds to reduce the cost of debt in line with the debt management strategy. That strategy is correct in direction but it interacts awkwardly with the 76.22 percent subscription rate: under-subscribed auctions force the Treasury to return to the market more frequently at higher cost, which is less efficient than consistent full-subscription at market-clearing rates achieved through supply predictability. The institutional investors making this request are the same pension funds and insurance companies whose combined assets exceed KSh 1.8 trillion — they are the deepest pool of long-duration domestic capital in the economy, and their ability to systematically allocate to the yield curve is the foundation on which the private corporate bond market will eventually be built. I will instruct the Debt Management Office to develop a draft issuance calendar for FY2019/20 for consultation with market participants by the end of the first quarter.

The Kenya Financial Sector Stability Report 2018 documents that non-financial firms listed on the NSE reported improved profitability in the first half of 2018 compared to 2016 and 2017, reflecting better economic activity. However, the FSR notes increased accumulation of short-term debt among listed non-financial firms, implying potential medium-term risks. The FSR also documents that credit to private firms declined as a share of disposable income while credit to households increased slightly, and that the slow growth in disposable income relative to credit accumulation reduces household ability to repay loans. Private sector credit growth was 3.1 percent overall in 2018. The 2019 FinAccess data shows 50.4 percent of credit accessed in 2019 was from shopkeeper credit, with a 45.6 percent default rate on goods-on-credit from shopkeepers. The IMF in its 2019 Article IV consultation has recommended that Kenya accelerate the removal of the interest rate cap, which it identifies as the primary cause of private sector credit rationing. The National Assembly Finance Committee has requested the Treasury's assessment of whether the interest rate cap should be fully repealed, partially reformed, or retained with modifications. (Source: Kenya Financial Sector Stability Report, 2018)

The Treasury's position is unambiguous: the interest rate cap should be fully repealed, and the FSR 2018 provides the empirical foundation for that recommendation across every dimension the Finance Committee needs to consider.

The cap was introduced in September 2016 with two objectives: reducing the cost of credit for borrowers and improving transmission of monetary policy. On both counts, the FSR documents failure. Private sector credit growth fell to 3.1 percent in 2018, a rate that is negative in real terms against nominal GDP growth of approximately 10 percent. Banks responded to the cap not by finding ways to lend more efficiently but by reallocating their portfolios toward government securities — investment in which grew 19.03 percent against 3.07 percent loan growth. This is a textbook credit rationing response: when price controls prevent lenders from pricing risk at market rates, they stop extending credit to risky borrowers rather than accepting below-risk-adjusted returns. The FSR documents that small peer group banks, which are the institutions most dependent on credit spread income and most exposed to the riskier SME and individual borrower segments, recorded negative ROA and negative profit before tax in 2018. These are not banks that lent recklessly before the cap — they are banks that became structurally unviable when their ability to price credit risk was removed.

The distributional consequences the cap was designed to prevent have materialised in their worst possible form. The FinAccess data the FSR cites shows that 50.4 percent of credit accessed in 2019 came from shopkeeper credit — informal trade credit outside any regulatory framework — at a default rate of 45.6 percent on goods-on-credit. The households who were supposed to benefit from cheaper bank credit are instead accessing informal credit at terms that are neither transparent nor regulated, at default rates that are ten to twenty times the bank loan default rates. This is what credit rationing produces: the price-controlled formal sector retreats, and the unregulated informal sector expands to fill the gap at worse terms for the borrowers the regulation was protecting.

On partial reform options: replacing the cap with a floor-above-CBR structure retains the fundamental distortion while creating a new set of boundary effects. Extending the cap to digital lenders, as has been proposed separately, would simply replicate the credit rationing outcome in the mobile credit market. The only modification that removes the distortion is full repeal, paired with a mandatory total cost of credit disclosure requirement that gives borrowers the information they need to make informed choices, and a robust CRB system that enables risk-based pricing across the market. Those are the instruments that protect consumers without rationing credit.

The Kenya Financial Sector Stability Report 2018 documents that EAC regional banking sub-sector assets grew by 11.6 percent by end of December 2018, but that non-performing loans to total gross loans averaged 8.0 percent regionally, driven by delayed government payments to suppliers, reduced real estate occupancy rates, and weak underwriting standards. The FSR warns that if global trade tensions persist and financial conditions tighten abruptly, EAC Partner States would face capital flight to advanced markets, higher funding costs, and increased volatility in domestic capital markets. The FSR notes that the increasing level of government public debt, elevated budget deficits, and reliance on foreign borrowing have reduced governments' ability to respond to adverse shocks. Regional conflicts and slow progress on the EAC Common Market Protocol are identified as additional risks to regional trade and growth. The East African Community Secretariat has proposed that EAC Partner States establish a joint KSh 200 billion Regional Financial Stability Fund, with contributions proportional to GDP, to be deployed as liquidity support to any member state experiencing a financial sector stress event, governed by a joint board of the six central banks, arguing this will reduce contagion risk and signal collective fiscal discipline to international markets. (Source: Kenya Financial Sector Stability Report, 2018)

The Regional Financial Stability Fund concept is institutionally ambitious and addresses a genuine gap in the EAC's financial architecture — the FSR's documentation of shallow domestic capital markets, elevated NPLs across the region, and reduced fiscal buffers makes the case that a regional backstop mechanism has value. However, the proposal as structured raises sovereignty, fiscal, and governance questions that Kenya cannot accept without significant redesign.

On the fiscal commitment: Kenya's proportional contribution to a KSh 200 billion fund, based on our share of EAC GDP, would be approximately KSh 60–70 billion given that Kenya accounts for roughly 30–35 percent of EAC aggregate GDP. The FSR documents Kenya's public debt-to-GDP ratio at 59.21 percent and explicitly flags that fiscal space is narrowing. A KSh 60–70 billion contribution to a regional fund — whether as paid-in capital or callable capital — constitutes a contingent fiscal commitment that must be disclosed under the PFM Act and assessed against Kenya's debt sustainability framework. If callable, it represents an off-balance-sheet liability whose activation would be triggered by another member state's financial stress, which is precisely the moment when Kenya's own fiscal buffers are most likely to be under pressure from contagion effects. The fund's design needs to specify whether contributions are paid-in or callable, and whether the activation mechanism requires unanimous consent or majority voting, before Kenya can assess whether the commitment is fiscally responsible.

On governance: a joint board of six central banks is an unwieldy decision-making structure for a crisis intervention instrument. Speed of deployment is the defining characteristic of an effective lender of last resort — the FSR documents that the NSE's single-day system failure caused a 44 percent equity turnover decline and that the contagion from global financial conditions reached Kenya's bond market within weeks of the 2018 tightening cycle. A governance structure requiring six central banks to reach agreement on deployment terms during an acute stress event is likely to produce the delays that make stabilisation funds ineffective. The IMF's Flexible Credit Line and Precautionary and Liquidity Line operate under clear pre-agreed conditionality frameworks precisely because crisis governance cannot depend on real-time negotiation. The EAC Secretariat should study the ASEAN Chiang Mai Initiative Multilateralisation model, which took nearly a decade to develop workable governance, before committing member state fiscal resources to a fund whose operational architecture has not been designed.

The CBK's Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report of October 2016 documents that the Banking (Amendment) Act, 2016 came into force on September 14, 2016, capping commercial banks' lending rates at no more than 4 percent above the CBR and setting a minimum deposit rate of 70 percent of the CBR. The MPC Report explicitly acknowledges the risks of the cap: possible perverse responses of credit growth to monetary policy in the case of credit rationing by banks, distortion of the market with risk of stifling financial inclusion, and potential increase in bank investment in government securities. Following the cap's introduction, average commercial banks' lending rates declined from 18.0 percent in April to 13.6 percent in October 2016, while the interest rate spread fell from 11.1 percent to 5.8 percent. Private sector credit growth decelerated from 13.5 percent in April to 4.7 percent by October 2016. A Parliamentary caucus is now arguing that the rapid decline in lending rates and spreads documented in the MPC Report proves the interest rate cap is working as intended, and is petitioning for the cap to be tightened to CBR plus 2 percent rather than CBR plus 4 percent. (Source: CBK Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report, October 2016)

The Parliamentary caucus is reading the MPC Report selectively and drawing a conclusion that the data does not support. The decline in the average lending rate from 18.0 percent to 13.6 percent and the compression of the spread from 11.1 percent to 5.8 percent are not evidence that the cap is working as intended — they are evidence that the price control has been imposed. A price ceiling mechanically reduces the measured price within the regulated space. The policy question is what happens to the quantity and distribution of credit as a result, and the MPC Report answers that question in the same document the caucus is citing: private sector credit growth decelerated from 13.5 percent to 4.7 percent during the same period.

The MPC Report is explicit about the transmission mechanism at work. The slowdown in credit reflects structural factors including banks holding high levels of excess reserves, diversifying asset portfolios with a bias toward government securities, interbank market segmentation, and slower deposit growth. These are not coincidental developments — they are the credit rationing responses the MPC Report itself identified in advance as a risk of the cap. A bank that cannot price a small business loan at a rate that compensates for the borrower's credit risk does not price that loan cheaper — it declines to make the loan. The average lending rate in the market has fallen, but the borrowers benefiting from that fall are the large, creditworthy corporates and households whose risk profiles banks can price within the cap. The marginal borrowers — the SMEs, the smallholders, the first-time borrowers without credit history — are exiting the formal credit market.

Tightening the cap to CBR plus 2 percent would accelerate exactly this dynamic. With the CBR at 10.0 percent as of September 2016, a CBR plus 2 percent cap implies a maximum lending rate of 12.0 percent. A bank funding itself at deposit rates of 7.0–7.5 percent — which the minimum deposit floor of 70 percent of CBR has pushed upward — would be left with a gross spread of approximately 4.5–5.0 percentage points before operational costs, provisioning for NPLs, and credit losses. For any loan with meaningful credit risk, this arithmetic does not work. The result would not be cheaper credit for Kenyan businesses — it would be a further contraction of the credit supply toward zero-risk government securities and an effective exit of formal banking from the riskiest but most development-critical lending segments.

The CBK's Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report of October 2016 documents that the MPC reduced the Central Bank Rate by a cumulative 150 basis points during the period — 100 basis points to 10.5 percent in May 2016 and a further 50 basis points to 10.0 percent in September 2016 — citing declining inflation expectations and the need to ease the policy stance to support private sector credit growth. However, the MPC Report documents that despite CBR reductions, private sector credit growth still decelerated from 13.5 percent in April to 4.7 percent in October 2016. The MPC attributes this to structural factors — excess reserves held by banks, interbank market segmentation, slower deposit growth, and the diversion of funds to government securities — rather than the price of credit. The Ministry of Industrialisation has proposed that the MPC be required to reduce the CBR by a further 200 basis points over the next six months to 8.0 percent, arguing that cheaper overnight money will stimulate private sector lending and support the manufacturing pillar of the Big 4 agenda. (Source: CBK Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report, October 2016)

The Ministry of Industrialisation's proposal requires the Treasury to explain why the monetary policy transmission mechanism is currently broken, and why further CBR cuts in that environment would not achieve the stated objective.

The MPC Report is explicit: private sector credit growth decelerated from 13.5 percent to 4.7 percent during a period when the CBR was cut by 150 basis points. The constraint on credit growth was not the price of overnight money — it was structural. The Report identifies three distinct structural blockages: first, banks holding excess reserves and diverting portfolios toward government securities; second, interbank market segmentation preventing efficient liquidity redistribution across bank tiers; and third, slower deposit growth reducing the loanable funds pool. These three factors operate entirely independently of the CBR level. A bank holding excess reserves at CBK is not doing so because overnight money is expensive — it is doing so because lending to the private sector at the capped rate is less attractive than holding risk-free government paper. Reducing the CBR to 8.0 percent does not change that calculation; it reduces the floor on government security yields alongside it, leaving the relative attractiveness of government paper over private lending largely unchanged or potentially worsening it if the deposit floor — set at 70 percent of CBR — falls below the rate required to mobilise deposits from cost-sensitive savers.

There is also a monetary policy credibility dimension here. The MPC held the CBR at 10.5 percent in July 2016 specifically to anchor inflation expectations and maintain market stability. Overall inflation had risen to 6.5 percent in October against a 5 percent target, sitting in the upper bound of the target range. Cutting the CBR by a further 200 basis points to 8.0 percent while inflation is at the upper bound of its target range and global uncertainty — Brexit, U.S. monetary policy tightening, potential OPEC-driven oil price increases — poses upside inflation risks would compromise the MPC's credibility as an inflation-targeting institution. The correct instruments for stimulating manufacturing sector credit are structural: removing the credit-rationing incentive created by the interest rate cap, addressing interbank market segmentation through CBK regulatory interventions, and creating sector-specific credit guarantee schemes that reduce the risk-adjusted cost of manufacturing lending without distorting the overall price of money in the economy.

The CBK's Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report of October 2016 documents that Chase Bank Limited was placed in receivership in April 2016, creating temporary liquidity shortages in segments of the banking market. The CBK used Reverse Repos to supply liquidity to affected market segments, and the quick and successful reopening of Chase Bank was credited with enhancing confidence in the banking sector. The MPC Report notes that the interbank market remained segmented with some banks holding excess liquidity while others had shortages, and that not all banks have credit lines with each other. The banking sector liquidity ratio increased to 43.6 percent in October from 40.5 percent in April 2016, while the capital adequacy ratio rose to 19.1 percent from 18.8 percent. The National Treasury has proposed establishing a mandatory Interbank Liquidity Sharing Facility requiring all commercial banks to make available up to 5 percent of their excess reserves for redistribution to banks in liquidity shortfall via a CBK-administered pool, arguing that this will address the interbank market segmentation identified in the MPC Report and improve monetary policy transmission. (Source: CBK Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report, October 2016)

The interbank market segmentation identified in the MPC Report is a genuine impediment to monetary policy transmission and its resolution is a legitimate priority. However, the mandatory pooling mechanism proposed is the wrong design for the problem, and I want to be clear about why before the Treasury advances this further — including to the CBK, which is the institution with primary authority over the interbank market architecture.

The MPC Report identifies the source of segmentation as bilateral credit line constraints — not all banks have credit lines with each other, which means that when a small or medium bank needs overnight liquidity, it cannot access the interbank market from a large bank that does not recognise it as a counterparty. The mandatory facility as proposed would require large banks to make 5 percent of their excess reserves available through a CBK pool, which effectively compels them to extend unsecured credit to counterparties they have assessed as too risky for bilateral lending. A bank's decision not to extend a credit line is a credit risk assessment, not a market failure in the conventional sense. Overriding that assessment through regulatory compulsion does not eliminate the underlying credit risk — it transfers it to the mandatory facility, and through the pool mechanism, potentially to participating banks that have no visibility into the creditworthiness of the borrowing institution.

The CBK already has the appropriate instruments. Reverse Repos — which the MPC Report documents as having been deployed effectively during the Chase Bank liquidity event — allow the CBK to supply collateralised liquidity to segments of the market facing shortages without compelling bilateral credit exposure between institutions with different risk profiles. Horizontal Repos, documented in the MPC Report's glossary, use government securities as collateral to allow commercial banks without bilateral credit lines to access interbank credit — this is precisely the instrument that addresses the segmentation problem without mandatory exposure. Strengthening the Horizontal Repo market, improving the quality and availability of eligible collateral for smaller banks, and enhancing CBK's real-time liquidity monitoring are the correct sequence of interventions. A mandatory sharing facility is a blunt regulatory tool that creates moral hazard — banks that know their liquidity shortfalls will be met by a compelled pool have a weaker incentive to manage their liquidity conservatively.

The CBK's Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report of October 2016 documents that despite global financial market volatility following Brexit, the foreign exchange market remained stable. The stability was supported by a narrowing current account deficit, improved earnings from tea, coffee, and horticulture, lower petroleum import bills, resilient diaspora remittances averaging USD 143.4 million per month during the six months to October 2016, and improved tourism performance. The report notes that about 40 percent of Kenya's exports were to Africa, contributing to resilience against external shocks. It also notes that the stock of inward FDI from Europe stood at 45 percent of total FDI, with the UK accounting for 23 percent. The current account deficit narrowed to 5.3 percent of GDP in the 12 months to October 2016 from 6.8 percent in the year to December 2015. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has proposed establishing a formal Kenya-UK bilateral trade and investment treaty as a priority in the Brexit negotiations, arguing this should be negotiated independently of the EAC-EU Economic Partnership Agreement, to protect the 23 percent UK share of Kenya's FDI stock and preserve preferential market access for tea and horticulture. (Source: CBK Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report, October 2016)

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs is responding to a genuine economic risk — the MPC Report's documentation of Kenya's 45 percent European FDI concentration and the UK's 23 percent share represents a material exposure to post-Brexit trade policy uncertainty — but the proposed approach of negotiating a standalone Kenya-UK bilateral agreement outside the EAC-EU EPA framework is analytically unsound and operationally complicated.

The EAC-EU Economic Partnership Agreement is a regional instrument. Kenya's decision to pursue a standalone bilateral with the UK would be taken within a regional integration architecture that requires, at minimum, consultation with EAC partner states under the Common Market Protocol. It would also set a precedent that individual EAC members can fragment the region's collective trade negotiating position when it suits their bilateral interests — a precedent that Tanzania, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, and South Sudan would each be free to invoke for their own bilateral priorities. The MPC Report notes that slow progress in implementing the Common Market Protocol is already a risk to regional trade and growth. A unilateral Kenyan trade treaty with the UK would exacerbate, not ameliorate, that risk.

On the substance: the UK's departure from the EU means Kenya will eventually need a trade arrangement with the UK to preserve preferential access. But the timeline for that arrangement is constrained by the UK's own Brexit implementation schedule, which in October 2016 was highly uncertain. Pursuing a priority negotiation against an unclear UK timeline risks consuming diplomatic and trade policy capacity that Kenya needs for the EPA completion and for the AfCFTA negotiations, which represent a larger long-term opportunity than the UK bilateral. The correct instrument is a transitional trade continuity agreement with the UK that rolls over the terms of the existing EPA framework on a temporary basis while longer-term arrangements are negotiated collectively through the EAC. This protects the tea, horticulture, and FDI flows the Ministry is concerned about without fracturing the regional trade architecture or creating a precedent of bilateral fragmentation.

The CBK's Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report of October 2016 documents that overall inflation stood at 6.5 percent in October 2016, up from 5.3 percent in April, sitting in the upper bound of the Government's target range of 5 percent plus or minus 2.5 percent. The CPI category food and non-alcoholic beverages accounted for 4.7 percentage points of the month-on-month inflation in October compared to 2.8 percentage points in May 2016. International sugar price inflation rose from 16.0 percent to 59.8 percent in the period due to reduced production in Brazil and India. The MPC Report also notes that the 3-month annualised non-food-non-fuel inflation remained stable below 5 percent, suggesting no adverse demand pressures. The MPC Report identifies risks including a likely pickup in international oil prices following OPEC's decision to cut production, rising global food prices particularly sugar, and unfavourable weather conditions affecting hydro electricity generation. The Ministry of Agriculture has proposed a price control on domestically produced sugar, capping the retail price at KSh 110 per kilogram, arguing that this will protect consumers from imported food inflation and keep overall inflation within target. (Source: CBK Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report, October 2016)

A domestic retail price cap on sugar will not protect consumers from imported food inflation — it will create a parallel shortage dynamic that makes the consumer welfare outcome worse, not better, and the MPC Report's own analysis explains why.

The MPC Report documents that international sugar price inflation rose from 16.0 percent to 59.8 percent due to supply-side shocks in Brazil and India. Kenya is a net sugar importer — domestic production is insufficient to meet national demand, and the gap is filled by imported sugar that clears at international prices. A KSh 110 per kilogram retail cap set below the market-clearing price — which at current import parity would be substantially higher — creates an immediate incentive for sugar importers and distributors to divert supply out of formal retail channels where the cap is enforceable, into informal or export markets where it is not. Kenyan consumers who shop at formal retailers face empty shelves at the capped price; consumers who can access informal channels pay the market price or higher. The price cap therefore redistributes access to sugar by wealth and market proximity rather than reducing the price of sugar.

The MPC Report also documents that the 3-month annualised non-food-non-fuel inflation remained stable below 5 percent, which is a critical diagnostic: the inflation Kenya is experiencing is a supply-side food price shock, not a demand-driven broad price increase. The correct monetary policy response to a supply-side food shock is exactly what the MPC is doing — holding the CBR steady to anchor inflation expectations and prevent second-round effects — not commodity price controls, which are a microeconomic intervention that monetary policy cannot substitute for and that fiscal policy should not reach for as a first response. If food security policy requires intervention, the instruments are targeted cash transfers to vulnerable households to protect their purchasing power, strategic reserve releases from the National Cereals and Produce Board, and import duty suspensions on sugar — all of which address consumer welfare without distorting the price signal that producers and importers respond to.

The CBK's Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report of October 2016 documents that Kenya's economy grew by 6.2 percent and 5.7 percent in the second and third quarters of 2016 respectively, compared to 5.9 percent and 6.0 percent in the same periods of 2015. Growth was supported by public investment in infrastructure, strong private consumption, and recovery of the tourism sector. Agricultural sector growth slowed in the third quarter due to unfavourable weather. The MPC Report documents that CBK's usable foreign exchange reserves stood at USD 7.7 billion, equivalent to 5.1 months of import cover, supplemented by the IMF Precautionary Arrangements equivalent to USD 1.5 billion. The IMF Precautionary Arrangements are described as providing an adequate buffer against short-term shocks. The National Treasury's Debt Management Office has proposed exiting the IMF Precautionary Arrangements when they mature, arguing that Kenya's current reserve levels of 5.1 months of import cover are adequate without the IMF backstop and that maintaining the arrangements imposes conditionality that constrains fiscal policy space. (Source: CBK Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report, October 2016)

The Debt Management Office's proposal to exit the IMF Precautionary Arrangements upon maturity is a position I understand but do not support at this juncture, and the MPC Report's own characterisation of the arrangements as providing an adequate buffer is the reason why the timing of exit matters more than the exit itself.

The MPC Report describes the combined reserve buffer — USD 7.7 billion in usable foreign exchange reserves plus the USD 1.5 billion IMF Precautionary Arrangements — as adequate against short-term shocks. The word combined is doing important work in that sentence. On its own, 5.1 months of import cover sits above the conventional 3-month floor but it is not generous in the current global context. The MPC Report documents several active risk vectors: global financial market volatility following Brexit, possible resumption of US Federal Reserve tightening, uncertainty about the impact of divergent monetary policies in advanced economies, and the upside risk to international oil prices from OPEC production cuts. Each of these risks, if they materialise simultaneously, would put pressure on Kenya's current account through a stronger dollar reducing the value of remittances, higher oil prices expanding the import bill, and capital outflows from frontier markets reducing the financial account surplus. The USD 1.5 billion IMF backstop is Kenya's second line of defence against exactly that scenario. Its value is not just in the dollars it makes available — it is in the market signal that an IMF engagement sends to international investors and rating agencies that Kenya's macroeconomic framework has external endorsement.

The conditionality argument deserves scrutiny rather than dismissal. The IMF Precautionary Arrangements carry performance criteria on Net International Reserves and Net Domestic Assets, which the MPC Report documents Kenya met for June and September 2016 and was on track to meet for December 2016. These criteria are not constraints on fiscal policy that Kenya would not adopt in its own interest — they are the NIR and NDA targets that the Treasury itself uses as operational anchors. Framing them as constraints that limit fiscal space assumes Kenya would pursue a looser fiscal path absent the arrangements, which is not the position the Treasury should be advocating publicly. The arrangements should be renewed on merit when they mature, not exited because the conditionality is inconvenient.

The CBK's Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report of October 2016 documents sectoral private sector credit growth data showing that mining and quarrying credit contracted sharply from 5.3 percent growth in April 2016 to -36.4 percent in October 2016, building and construction credit fell from 26.2 percent to -4.9 percent, and manufacturing credit declined from 18.3 percent to -4.3 percent. In contrast, consumer durables credit rebounded from 9.1 percent in April to 37.5 percent in October, and transport and communication maintained growth of 14.3 percent. The MPC Report attributes the overall credit deceleration primarily to structural factors rather than the cost of credit. Total private sector credit growth fell from 13.5 percent to 4.7 percent over the period. The Ministry of Mining has proposed a Sector-Specific Credit Guarantee Scheme for the extractives sector, backed by KSh 10 billion in Treasury funds, that would guarantee 80 percent of any commercial bank loan to a licensed mining or quarrying operation, arguing that the -36.4 percent credit contraction in mining represents a critical financing gap that threatens the sector's contribution to Kenya's GDP growth. (Source: CBK Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report, October 2016)

Before the Treasury can evaluate the credit guarantee proposal on its merits, we need to understand what is actually driving the -36.4 percent contraction in mining and quarrying credit, because a guarantee scheme addresses only one possible cause — credit risk perception — and the MPC Report's data suggests other factors may be dominant.

The MPC Report attributes the overall credit deceleration to structural factors: banks diverting to government securities, interbank segmentation, and slower deposit growth. These are sector-neutral factors that would reduce credit across all sectors. But mining and quarrying shows the sharpest contraction by far — from +5.3 percent in April to -36.4 percent in October, an 8-month swing of nearly 42 percentage points. That magnitude is inconsistent with a purely structural explanation. Such a severe sectoral contraction typically reflects one or more of: specific loan defaults or NPL reclassifications in the sector forcing write-downs that turn net credit negative, a collapse in commodity prices reducing the value of collateral and the viability of projects, or regulatory uncertainty in the extractives sector affecting both lender appetite and borrower demand. The MPC Report records that international oil prices rose during the period, so commodity price collapse is not the explanation for mining credit. The NPL reclassification the MPC Report documents for the broader banking sector — the ratio of gross NPLs to gross loans rose from 8.2 percent to 9.3 percent between April and October 2016 — is the more likely explanation for at least part of the mining credit contraction.

If the contraction reflects NPL reclassification of existing mining loans — meaning the credit was extended and has not been repaid — an 80 percent guarantee scheme on new lending to the same sector without resolving the underlying credit quality issues would layer new contingent liabilities onto the Treasury while the existing impaired loans remain unresolved. The KSh 10 billion guarantee fund would need to be held as a provision on the government's books. A cleaner sequence is: first, understand the NPL composition in the mining sector; second, address any regulatory barriers to project development that are causing cash flow shortfalls among existing borrowers; and third, if the sector demonstrates improved credit performance, a guarantee scheme on new lending becomes a rational use of public resources. Not before.

The CBK's Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report of October 2016 documents that diaspora remittances averaged USD 143.4 million per month during the six months to October 2016, up from an average of USD 137.3 million per month in the six months to April 2016. The MPC Report identifies resilient diaspora remittances as one of the key factors supporting foreign exchange market stability and the narrowing of the current account deficit to 5.3 percent of GDP. The MPC also notes that about 40 percent of Kenya's exports were to Africa, and that the proportion of imports financed by exports improved marginally to 60.5 percent. The MPC Report further identifies the potential impact of Brexit as a monitoring risk, since Kenya has significant trade and investment links with Europe. The Kenya Revenue Authority has proposed introducing a 5 percent remittance tax on all inward diaspora transfers above USD 500, to be collected at the point of money transfer operator clearance, arguing this will raise revenue to support the fiscal consolidation programme and that the inelastic nature of family remittances will prevent significant volume reduction. (Source: CBK Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report, October 2016)

The KRA's remittance tax proposal is one of the most counterproductive revenue measures I have seen brought to this table, and the inelasticity argument used to justify it is empirically contested and strategically dangerous.

The MPC Report documents that diaspora remittances averaged USD 143.4 million per month — approximately USD 1.72 billion annually — and identifies them as a pillar of Kenya's foreign exchange stability and current account improvement. The current account deficit narrowed from 6.8 percent of GDP in December 2015 to 5.3 percent in October 2016, and remittances are explicitly credited as one of the supporting factors. A 5 percent tax on transfers above USD 500 would reduce the after-transfer value received by Kenyan families and therefore reduce the incentive to remit through formal money transfer channels relative to informal channels. The KRA's claim that remittances are inelastic is only partially true: the aggregate amount that diaspora Kenyans want to support their families may not change, but the channel through which they transmit it is highly elastic. Hawala networks, hand-carried cash, and cryptocurrency transfers are all substitutes for formal remittance operators. A 5 percent cost wedge is more than sufficient to shift a material share of flows from taxable formal channels to untaxable informal ones — producing lower fiscal revenue than projected, lower foreign exchange reserve accumulation from formally cleared remittances, and reduced CBK visibility into cross-border financial flows that are relevant to both monetary policy and AML/CFT compliance.

At USD 143.4 million per month, the theoretical revenue at 5 percent on flows above USD 500 might appear significant on a spreadsheet. But remittances are not a static pool to be taxed — they are discretionary family transfers made by individuals with banking and mobile money options. The World Bank's own research on remittance taxation consistently finds that formal channel elasticity is high enough that tax-induced channel diversion reduces fiscal yield below the static estimate. The KRA should focus its collection efforts on domestic tax gaps — the informal sector VAT compliance deficit, rental income under-declaration, and transfer pricing by multinationals — before reaching for a tax that directly undermines a stable, growing foreign exchange inflow that the CBK relies upon for current account balance management.

The CBK's Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report of October 2016 documents that broad money supply (M3) growth slowed from 9.2 percent in April 2016 to 6.9 percent in October 2016, below its projected growth path, alongside the deceleration in private sector credit growth from 13.5 percent to 4.7 percent. The MPC Report notes that some banks persistently held high levels of excess reserves throughout the period, diverting asset portfolios toward government securities considered low risk. The Report documents that deposits account for approximately 68 percent of total bank liabilities, and that slower growth in deposits for some banks has reduced the pool of loanable funds. The MPC met its Net Domestic Assets and Net International Reserves targets for June and September 2016. A Senate Finance Committee has proposed that the CBK be required to publish monthly targets for private sector credit growth alongside its bi-monthly CBR announcements, and that failure to achieve those targets for three consecutive months should trigger an automatic review of the CBR regardless of the scheduled meeting cycle, arguing that making credit growth a co-equal target with inflation will improve monetary policy accountability. (Source: CBK Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report, October 2016)

The Senate Finance Committee's proposal to make private sector credit growth a co-equal target for monetary policy reflects a genuine frustration with the decoupling of CBR reductions from credit outcomes, but it fundamentally mischaracterises what monetary policy can and cannot control, and codifying it would undermine the CBK's operational independence in ways that damage Kenya's macroeconomic credibility.

Monetary policy operates through the price of money — the CBR — which transmits through the yield curve and the interbank rate to bank lending rates and ultimately to credit demand. The MPC Report is explicit that the current deceleration in private sector credit growth is not a price-of-money problem. M3 slowed from 9.2 percent to 6.9 percent and private sector credit fell from 13.5 percent to 4.7 percent while the CBK was cutting the CBR. The binding constraints are structural: excess reserves being held rather than deployed, interbank segmentation preventing efficient liquidity distribution, and slower deposit growth reducing loanable funds. A credit growth target does not resolve any of these structural constraints. It creates a target that the CBK does not have the instruments to reliably hit, and the Senate's proposed automatic CBR review trigger would then force rate changes in response to credit shortfalls that the CBR itself cannot remedy.

The deeper problem is the target hierarchy. The CBK Act gives the MPC a price stability mandate. Credit growth is an intermediate variable that should respond to price stability conditions — stable inflation, appropriately priced money — not a primary target that overrides them. If credit growth is weak because inflation is too high and rates need to stay elevated, forcing the CBK to cut in response to a credit target would produce exactly the inflation the price stability mandate is designed to prevent. Kenya's inflation targeting framework, the IMF Precautionary Arrangements, and Kenya's Eurobond credit standing all rest on the credibility of the CBK's commitment to price stability as its primary objective. Publishing mandatory credit growth targets alongside the CBR announcement would signal to markets that the MPC is operating a dual mandate it is not equipped to manage — with the likely consequence of a sovereign credit rating review that raises the cost of Kenya's external borrowing.

The CBK's Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report of October 2016 documents that the overall balance of payments recorded a deficit of USD 957.8 million (1.5 percent of GDP) in the year to October 2016, compared to a surplus of USD 458.2 million (0.7 percent of GDP) in the year to October 2015. The Report attributes this deterioration to a widening of the deficit in the financial account and a reduction in the capital account surplus. Separately, the current account deficit narrowed to 5.3 percent of GDP from 7.1 percent a year earlier, supported by improved merchandise trade. The share of imports of machinery and transport equipment in total imports declined from 35.3 percent to 34.0 percent, partly due to completion of the first phase of the Standard Gauge Railway. The Ministry of Transport has proposed immediately commencing procurement of Phase 2 of the SGR from Naivasha to Kisumu, to be financed through a new Chinese government concessional loan of approximately USD 3.6 billion, arguing that momentum from Phase 1 construction provides optimal conditions for continuation and that the infrastructure investment will stimulate GDP growth. (Source: CBK Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report, October 2016)

The MPC Report's own balance of payments data provides the most relevant context for evaluating this proposal, and it contains a significant caution that the Ministry of Transport has not addressed.

The MPC Report documents a swing in the overall balance of payments from a surplus of USD 458.2 million to a deficit of USD 957.8 million — a deterioration of USD 1.4 billion in one year — driven by a widening financial account deficit and reduced capital account surplus. The completion of SGR Phase 1 is documented as having reduced the share of machinery and transport equipment imports in total imports from 35.3 percent to 34.0 percent. A new USD 3.6 billion Chinese concessional loan for Phase 2 would immediately reverse that improvement, driving a substantial increase in machinery imports for construction, a corresponding widening of the current account, and a matching increase in external public debt. Let me close the fiscal accounting loop on this explicitly: at an exchange rate of approximately KSh 102 per USD at the time of the report, USD 3.6 billion converts to approximately KSh 367 billion. Adding that to the public debt stock would increase the debt-to-GDP ratio by approximately 4.5 percentage points at the 2016 GDP level — before any growth benefit from the infrastructure materialises.

The MPC Report also notes that the CBK and Treasury are monitoring the impact of Brexit, since 45 percent of Kenya's FDI stock comes from Europe. A USD 3.6 billion Chinese government loan deepens Kenya's external debt concentration in a single bilateral creditor beyond what a prudent debt diversification strategy would endorse. The current external debt portfolio already has Eurobond exposure and multilateral debt; adding a large bilateral Chinese concessional loan creates refinancing risk if the terms are renegotiated and reputational risk with multilateral creditors who calibrate their lending on debt sustainability assessments. Phase 2 of the SGR should be evaluated against its economic rate of return — freight volumes on Phase 1, revenue performance, and the trade facilitation case for the Naivasha-Kisumu corridor — before the financing structure is determined. The investment case must precede the financing decision, not follow from it.

The CBK's Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report of October 2016 documents that the NSE index fell from 3,990 in April to 3,229 by October 2016, with listed banking sector stocks registering significant declines after the enactment of the Banking (Amendment) Act, 2016 capping interest rates. The MPC Report notes that the downward trend in banking stock prices had since stabilised. The report also documents that global financial market uncertainties — Brexit, capital outflows from emerging and frontier economies, and divergent monetary policies in advanced economies — contributed to the NSE decline. The MPC notes that Kenya's economy remained relatively resilient due to export and market diversification, with approximately 40 percent of exports going to Africa. The Capital Markets Authority has proposed a Bank Equity Support Programme under which the Government would purchase NSE-listed banking sector shares on the open market up to a total of KSh 15 billion, arguing that the interest rate cap has artificially depressed banking valuations and that government buying will stabilise prices and restore investor confidence. (Source: CBK Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report, October 2016)

The CMA's Bank Equity Support Programme would be fiscally inappropriate, operationally ineffective, and would send precisely the wrong signal to the capital markets it is intended to stabilise.

The decline in banking sector stock prices from April to October 2016 documented in the MPC Report is not a market malfunction — it is a rational market repricing of the expected future earnings of listed banks following the enactment of the interest rate cap. The Banking (Amendment) Act reduced the maximum spread between deposit costs and lending rates from the market rate to a regulated ceiling. Banks' equity valuations are discounted present values of their future earnings. If future earnings are permanently lower because spreads are capped, the market correctly marks equity down. That is the price mechanism working as intended. A government purchase programme that pushes prices back up against that fundamental repricing does not restore confidence — it creates artificial price support that obscures the real earnings impact of the cap and leaves retail investors who buy at the supported price exposed to the correction when the government stops buying.

The fiscal mechanics are also objectionable. KSh 15 billion deployed in open-market equity purchases is KSh 15 billion of public money invested in listed commercial banks at prices that the government's own legislation has depressed. If banking sector profitability continues to decline under the cap — which the FSR 2018 subsequently documents it did, with small bank ROA turning negative by 2018 — the government's equity position would be underwater. This is a contingent liability in the guise of an investment. The correct response to the market's repricing of banking equities is for Parliament to assess whether the interest rate cap legislation is achieving its objectives — which the MPC Report documents in real time it is not, given the credit growth deceleration — and to repeal or amend it accordingly. That is the intervention that would restore banking sector valuations on a sustainable basis because it addresses the fundamental, not the symptom.

The CBK's Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report of October 2016 documents that the MPC continued to coordinate closely with the National Treasury to ensure alignment of monetary and fiscal policies for overall macroeconomic stability. The Report notes that the execution of the Government's domestic borrowing programme continued to support market stability, and that interest rates on government securities remained relatively stable during the period — an indication of this coordination. The flattening and stabilisation of the yield curve is described as having enhanced predictability in the Government securities market. The MPC reduced the CBR by a cumulative 150 basis points during the period while simultaneously meeting its NDA targets. A proposal from the Office of the President has suggested that going forward the MPC should be required to formally consult with the Executive prior to each CBR decision and share the meeting minutes with the President's Economic Advisory Council before publication, arguing that closer executive coordination will improve policy alignment and prevent monetary policy decisions that conflict with the Government's growth agenda. (Source: CBK Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report, October 2016)

This proposal cuts to the heart of what makes a central bank credible, and I will not support it — not because coordination between monetary and fiscal policy is undesirable, but because the mechanism proposed would destroy the operational independence that makes monetary policy effective in the first place.

The MPC Report documents that coordination between the CBK and the Treasury already operates through well-designed institutional channels. The Principal Secretary of the National Treasury sits on the MPC as a non-voting member. This design — representation without a vote — is deliberate: it ensures the fiscal perspective is present in monetary policy deliberations without allowing the executive to outvote the technocrats responsible for price stability. The requirement for formal executive consultation before each CBR decision and presidential access to minutes before publication would transform this carefully balanced architecture into something qualitatively different. A CBK Governor who knows the President's Economic Advisory Council will review draft minutes before publication cannot make genuinely independent assessments of whether the inflation outlook warrants rate action. The formal consultation requirement gives the executive a pre-decisional veto mechanism over monetary policy — not in law, but in practice.

The credibility cost of this would be immediately visible in Kenya's sovereign credit ratings and Eurobond spreads. International investors and rating agencies price Kenya's external debt partly on the basis that CBK monetary policy is insulated from short-term political pressures. The MPC Report documents that the Governor held meetings with potential investors and International Rating Agencies to appraise them on economic developments — those meetings are valuable precisely because the CBK can speak independently of the executive. A formal pre-decision consultation requirement would give those same investors a legitimate reason to reprice Kenya's sovereign risk upward. The existing coordination between monetary and fiscal policy is working: the MPC met its NDA and NIR targets, the yield curve stabilised, and the domestic borrowing programme proceeded without market disruption. The coordination mechanism does not need redesigning — it needs to be protected.

The CBK's Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report of October 2016 documents that growth in credit to the private sector slowed to 4.7 percent in October 2016, and that one contributing factor was the low utilisation of overdraft facilities by some large corporate borrowers. The report also documents that credit to consumer durables rebounded sharply from 9.1 percent growth in April to 37.5 percent in October, while credit to transport and communication maintained growth of 14.3 percent. Credit to agriculture, real estate, and private households also remained positive. The MPC notes that the economy grew at 6.2 percent and 5.7 percent in Q2 and Q3 2016, supported by public investment in infrastructure and strong private consumption. The Kenya Association of Manufacturers has proposed that the National Treasury introduce a Manufacturing Credit Acceleration Fund of KSh 50 billion, financed by redirecting 10 percent of the annual domestic borrowing programme to a ring-fenced fund lending directly to manufacturers at 8 percent per annum, arguing that below-market lending to the productive sector will revive manufacturing credit growth that has fallen to -4.3 percent. (Source: CBK Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report, October 2016)

The Manufacturing Credit Acceleration Fund proposal conflates a supply-side credit rationing problem with a demand-side interest rate problem, and its financing mechanism — redirecting 10 percent of the domestic borrowing programme — creates a secondary fiscal risk that the proposal has not accounted for.

The MPC Report documents manufacturing credit growth at -4.3 percent in October 2016. But it also documents that consumer durables credit grew at 37.5 percent and transport and communication at 14.3 percent in the same period. These are manufacturing-adjacent demand categories. If manufacturing credit were contracting because credit was genuinely unavailable to the sector, we would expect related demand-side credit to also be weak. Instead, the pattern suggests that the manufacturing credit contraction is specific to particular borrowers or loan classes within the sector — consistent with the NPL reclassification the MPC Report documents in the broader banking sector, and consistent with the MPC's attribution of the credit slowdown to structural portfolio diversification rather than the price of credit. A below-market government lending facility at 8 percent does not resolve NPL reclassification, does not improve the creditworthiness of manufacturers whose loans are in distress, and does not address the banks' risk aversion that is driving them toward government securities.

On the financing mechanics: redirecting 10 percent of the domestic borrowing programme to a direct lending fund means the Treasury borrows from the market and on-lends at 8 percent. In October 2016, 91-day Treasury bill rates were approximately 8–9 percent — meaning the proposed on-lending rate is at or below the Treasury's own borrowing cost. The fund would be borrowing at market rates and lending below market, generating a negative carry that the government must absorb from the budget. At KSh 50 billion, even a 2 percentage point negative carry represents KSh 1 billion annually in subsidy cost — a recurrent expenditure not included in the proposal. If the fund is capitalised from the borrowing programme, it also means KSh 50 billion less in Treasury bonds available to the market, reducing the supply of risk-free assets that pension funds and insurance companies need for portfolio management. The correct instrument for manufacturing credit support is a first-loss credit guarantee scheme — not direct government lending — which achieves the same credit risk sharing at a fraction of the fiscal cost.

The CBK's Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report of October 2016 documents that the non-food-non-fuel (NFNF) inflation measure declined from 5.8 percent in April to 5.4 percent in October 2016, while the 3-month annualised NFNF remained stable below 5 percent, indicating no adverse demand pressures in the economy. Overall inflation, however, rose from 5.3 percent to 6.5 percent over the same period, driven by food prices — the food and non-alcoholic beverages CPI category contributed 4.7 percentage points to month-on-month inflation in October compared to 2.8 percentage points in May. Inflation increased sharply in Rwanda, but remained relatively stable in Kenya between July and October. International sugar prices rose 59.8 percent due to supply disruptions in Brazil and India. The KNBS has proposed rebasing the CPI basket to reduce the weight of food and non-alcoholic beverages, which currently dominate the inflation measure, arguing that this will produce a more accurate inflation reading that better reflects the consumption patterns of Kenya's growing middle class and reduce the distortion caused by volatile food prices. (Source: CBK Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report, October 2016)

CPI rebasing is a legitimate and necessary statistical exercise — it is not a political manipulation of the inflation measure, and I want to be careful that this distinction is clearly understood before addressing the specific proposal.

The KNBS is correct that the CPI basket should periodically be updated to reflect actual consumption patterns. If the current basket over-represents food expenditure relative to what Kenyan households actually spend, the measured inflation rate will be systematically biased upward during food price spikes and downward during food price declines. The MPC's monetary policy decisions are calibrated against the government's 5 percent target, which is applied to the current CPI measure. If the basket is genuinely unrepresentative, rebasing it produces a more accurate signal for monetary policy — which is in the CBK's interest, not a convenience for fiscal policy.

However, the framing of the proposal — reducing food weight to better reflect middle-class consumption patterns and reduce distortion from volatile food prices — deserves scrutiny. Kenya's headline CPI is intended to capture the price experience of the median Kenyan household, not the growing middle class. The MPC Report itself documents that lower food prices contributed to declining inflation in Uganda and Tanzania, and that higher food prices pushed Kenyan inflation to 6.5 percent — evidence that food price movements have genuine welfare significance for the majority of Kenyan households who spend a high proportion of income on food. If rebasing reduces food weight primarily because middle-class households spend less on food, the resulting CPI would underweight the inflation experience of lower-income households — a group with no political voice to contest the methodology but the greatest welfare exposure to food price volatility. Any rebasing exercise must be grounded in a nationally representative Household Income and Expenditure Survey that samples across the income distribution, not calibrated to a target consumption profile. The KNBS should also publish the old and new series in parallel for at least 24 months to enable the MPC and the public to assess the impact of the methodological change before the new basket becomes the policy-relevant measure.

The CBK's Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report of October 2016 documents that the CBK was implementing measures to promote innovation in the banking sector leveraging on ICT, and strengthening Credit Reference Bureaus to provide for a credit scoring framework. The MPC Report describes these as part of CBK's broader effort to sustainably reduce the cost of credit. The Report also notes that some large corporate borrowers demonstrated low utilisation of overdraft facilities in the period, contributing to the credit slowdown alongside structural bank-side factors. Credit growth to private households stood at 5.6 percent in October 2016, relatively stable, while consumer durables credit grew 37.5 percent. The Ministry of ICT has proposed that the CBK be required to mandate all licensed banks and digital lenders to share full transaction-level data with a government-owned National Credit Data Repository, with the data accessible to all licensed financial institutions at no cost, arguing that universal credit data access will lower credit risk pricing and expand credit access for unbanked Kenyans. (Source: CBK Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report, October 2016)

The underlying objective of the proposal — expanding credit data infrastructure to improve risk pricing and broaden credit access — is well-aligned with what the MPC Report identifies as a priority reform direction. The CBK's stated commitment to strengthening Credit Reference Bureaus for a credit scoring framework points in the same direction. Where the proposal goes wrong is in the governance model: a government-owned repository with cost-free universal access is not the right institutional design for a credit data infrastructure in Kenya's financial sector context, for reasons that are both technical and structural.

On the technical side: transaction-level data sharing across all licensed banks and digital lenders represents a data privacy challenge of significant scale. Kenya's Data Protection Act creates obligations around the collection, storage, and sharing of personal financial data that a government-owned repository would need to comply with. Transaction-level data is more granular than the credit history data currently held by the three CBK-licensed CRBs — it includes payment behaviour, spending patterns, cash flow timing, and account activity that goes well beyond creditworthiness assessment into territory that is commercially sensitive and personally identifying. A government-owned repository holding this data at transaction level creates a concentration of financial surveillance capability that the Data Protection Act's principles of purpose limitation and data minimisation would constrain, and that would generate legitimate public concern about the boundary between credit infrastructure and financial monitoring.

On the governance model: cost-free universal access removes the commercial incentive for the repository to maintain data quality, resolve disputes, and invest in security infrastructure. The existing CRB framework works because licensed bureaus have commercial skin in the game — their business depends on the reliability of their data. A government repository with free access has no such incentive. The correct model is a shared utility owned jointly by licensed financial institutions, governed by a board with CBK oversight, operating on a cost-recovery fee structure. This achieves universal access to credit data without creating a government-owned financial surveillance instrument or removing the quality incentives that make credit data reliable.

The CBK's Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report of October 2016 documents that Kenya's current account deficit narrowed to 5.3 percent of GDP, supported by improved tea, coffee, and horticulture export earnings and a lower petroleum import bill. The petroleum products share of total imports fell from 15.5 percent to 15.0 percent in the period, reflecting lower international oil prices. The MPC Report identifies OPEC's decision to cut oil production as a risk to Kenya's inflation and import bill going forward, noting that oil prices had already risen from USD 30 per barrel in early 2016 to USD 51.4 per barrel by October 2016. Foreign exchange reserves stood at USD 7.7 billion (5.1 months of import cover). The Energy Regulatory Commission has proposed capping domestic petroleum retail prices at their October 2016 levels and establishing a Petroleum Price Stabilisation Fund, capitalised at KSh 20 billion from the national budget, to absorb any increase in international oil prices for a period of 24 months, arguing this will protect consumers and businesses from oil price volatility and insulate inflation from imported energy shocks. (Source: CBK Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report, October 2016)

The Petroleum Price Stabilisation Fund proposal requires the Treasury to be direct about the fiscal arithmetic before any policy merit is assessed, because the numbers make the proposal unsustainable at the scale of risk it is attempting to absorb.

Oil prices rose from USD 30 to USD 51.4 per barrel between early 2016 and October 2016 — a 71 percent increase in under 12 months. The MPC Report flags OPEC production cuts as a further upside risk. Kenya imports approximately 6–7 million metric tonnes of petroleum products annually. At October 2016 prices, the import bill was running at approximately 15.0 percent of total goods imports, which the MPC Report places at roughly USD 14 billion annually — implying a petroleum import bill of approximately USD 2.1 billion. A further 30 percent increase in oil prices from the October 2016 level — well within the range of historical oil price movements and consistent with the OPEC risk the MPC flags — would increase the annual petroleum import bill by approximately USD 630 million. The proposed KSh 20 billion fund (approximately USD 196 million at October 2016 exchange rates) would be exhausted in under four months at that rate of price increase. It is not a stabilisation fund — it is a one-quarter buffer followed by a cliff.

The deeper structural problem is that price stabilisation funds for globally traded commodities require either very large capitalisation or very short duration to be effective. Kenya's fuel pricing mechanism, including the existing automatic pricing formula administered by the Energy Regulatory Commission, already provides a degree of pass-through smoothing. The correct long-term instrument for protecting Kenya from oil price volatility is reducing the petroleum import intensity of the economy through energy diversification — the geothermal capacity the government has been developing, the solar and wind renewable pipeline, and improved public transport efficiency — not a KSh 20 billion buffer that would be consumed before the next MPC meeting if global oil markets move sharply. The KSh 20 billion would be better deployed as equity capitalisation for the Kenya Electricity Generating Company's geothermal expansion than as a temporary cushion against a commodity price risk that the domestic budget cannot sustainably absorb.

The CBK's Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report of October 2016 documents that the average deposit interest rate for banks rose from 6.9 percent to 7.8 percent following the Banking (Amendment) Act, 2016, which set a minimum deposit rate of 70 percent of the CBR. The Report notes that the rise in deposit interest rates was mainly in large and medium tier banks, while small banks were already paying higher interest rates on deposits prior to the cap. The MPC Report further documents that the deposit rate floor, combined with the lending rate ceiling, compressed the average interest rate spread from 11.1 percent to 5.8 percent. Slower growth in deposits for some banks was identified as a structural constraint on lending capacity, as deposits account for approximately 68 percent of total bank liabilities. The Kenya Bankers Association has petitioned the Treasury to remove the minimum deposit rate floor of 70 percent of CBR, arguing that this component of the Banking Amendment Act is economically counterproductive because it raises the cost of funds for banks and worsens the credit rationing effect of the cap by squeezing net interest margins below the level needed to service small and medium enterprise loans. (Source: CBK Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report, October 2016)

The Kenya Bankers Association has identified a genuine asymmetry in the Banking Amendment Act's design, and their analysis of the mechanism is technically correct — but the recommendation of removing only the deposit floor while retaining the lending cap would produce an outcome that is worse for consumers than either the current regime or full repeal.

The MPC Report documents that small banks were already paying above-70-percent-of-CBR deposit rates before the Act, meaning the deposit floor's principal effect has been on large and medium banks — it has forced them to pay more for deposits from savers who previously received below-market rates. From a financial inclusion and saver welfare perspective, this is one of the few distributive gains from the Act: depositors at large banks received higher rates on their savings. Removing the deposit floor while retaining the lending cap would allow large banks to reduce their deposit rates back toward their pre-Act levels, capturing the margin compression benefit for shareholders rather than passing it to borrowers who remain subject to the lending ceiling. The net interest margin would widen for large banks, credit rationing would not be resolved — because the binding constraint remains the lending ceiling, not the cost of funds — and savers would lose the deposit rate protection they gained. This is a worst-case outcome from a distributive standpoint: no improvement in credit access, reduced saver returns.

The correct policy position remains full repeal of both the lending ceiling and the deposit floor simultaneously. The MPC Report documents that the floor-to-ceiling mechanism as a unit is producing credit contraction. Removing one half of it without the other creates new distortions in the opposite direction. If the political economy of Parliament makes simultaneous full repeal difficult, the sequencing should be ceiling removal first — which addresses the credit rationing that the MPC Report documents as the primary damage — with a transition period for deposit rate deregulation to prevent an abrupt reduction in savings rates. Removing the floor first, as the KBA proposes, inverts that priority.
