The CBK's Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report of October 2016 documents that Kenya's economy grew by 6.2 percent in Q2 2016 and 5.7 percent in Q3 2016, supported by public investment in infrastructure, strong private consumption, and recovery of the tourism sector. Agricultural sector growth slowed in Q3 due to unfavourable weather conditions. The Report documents that diaspora remittances averaged USD 143.4 million per month and that export diversification — with approximately 40 percent of exports going to Africa — provided resilience against external shocks. The current account deficit narrowed from 6.8 percent of GDP to 5.3 percent. However, the overall balance of payments moved from a surplus of USD 458.2 million to a deficit of USD 957.8 million, driven by the financial and capital account deterioration. The Kenya Tourism Board has proposed a Tourism Recovery Bond of KSh 8 billion, to be issued on the NSE with a government guarantee, allowing licensed tourism businesses to access long-term capital at subsidised rates to invest in infrastructure upgrading, arguing that the tourism sector recovery documented in the MPC Report represents an optimal entry point for leveraging capital markets to accelerate sector investment. (Source: CBK Seventeenth Bi-Annual MPC Report, October 2016)

The Tourism Recovery Bond proposal is better constructed than many sector financing proposals the Treasury receives, and I want to engage with it seriously rather than dismiss it, because the MPC Report's documentation of a genuine tourism sector recovery creates a legitimate case for capitalising on that momentum.

The MPC Report identifies tourism recovery as one of the growth drivers in Q2 and Q3 2016. Tourism is a foreign exchange earner, an employment generator, and a sector where Kenya has genuine comparative advantage — the wildlife, coast, and adventure tourism assets are irreplaceable. The case for a capital markets instrument to finance sector upgrading is more credible than many government-backed lending proposals because it connects the sector to market discipline: bondholders who assess the credit quality of tourism businesses are more selective than a government loan facility administered through a ministry.

However, the government guarantee is the element that requires careful design. A guarantee on KSh 8 billion of tourism sector bonds means the national government is the residual payer if the underlying businesses cannot service the bond. Tourism revenue is highly sensitive to security incidents, disease outbreaks, and global travel sentiment — precisely the shocks that are hardest to predict and manage at the individual business level. The 2016 recovery documented in the MPC Report followed the security deterioration that depressed tourism between 2013 and 2015. A government-guaranteed bond issued during a recovery phase creates the risk that the guarantee is called during the next downturn, converting what was marketed as a private sector bond into a public sector bailout. The guarantee structure should instead be a first-loss credit enhancement of no more than 20–25 percent of the issuance, provided through a Development Finance Institution such as the Kenya Development Corporation, with commercial bank credit enhancement covering the residual risk. This preserves market discipline, limits the government's contingent liability, and still achieves the below-market pricing that makes the instrument accessible to mid-sized tourism operators. At that structure, with proper credit assessment of the underlying businesses, I would support the proposal.

CS Infrastructure has just made the following claim in our roundtable debate: 'Building the Naivasha-Malaba SGR extension will boost Kenya's GDP by 10 percent within three years of completion, generating enough additional tax revenue to fully service the construction debt without any net fiscal cost to the Government.' He cites SGR Phase 1 Mombasa-Nairobi as proof. Respond. (Source: Kenya FSR 2018, MPC Report October 2016)

I need to stop the roundtable here because that 10 percent GDP claim is not a projection — it is a number without a model behind it, and we cannot build a financing decision on it.

Let me do the arithmetic publicly. Kenya's nominal GDP in 2018 was KSh 8,904,984 million. A 10 percent GDP increase means generating approximately KSh 890 billion in additional output within three years of completion. For context: Kenya's entire annual real GDP growth in 2018 — the strongest year in recent memory, recovering from drought and election disruption — was 6.3 percent, adding roughly KSh 560 billion in nominal terms from all sources combined: agriculture, manufacturing, services, tourism, construction, and everything else. The CS is claiming a single railway corridor will add more economic output in three years than the entire economy added in its best recent year. That requires a multiplier of extraordinary magnitude and a transmission mechanism that has not been specified.

On Phase 1 as proof: the FSR 2018 documents that SGR completion reduced the share of machinery and transport equipment imports from 35.3 percent to 34.0 percent of total imports — a measurable effect. It does not validate a 10 percent GDP projection. Phase 1 also created a debt obligation that contributed to the public debt-to-GDP ratio rising from 50.4 percent in December 2017 to 59.21 percent in December 2018. The construction debt did not self-service.

The self-financing claim requires freight and passenger revenue to cover both operating costs and debt service. No revenue projection for the Naivasha-Malaba corridor has been tabled. Without passenger and freight volume forecasts, a tariff structure, an operating cost model, and a debt service schedule, the claim is assertion. I will not allow the roundtable to proceed to a financing decision on that basis.

Walk me through Kenya's debt sustainability arithmetic for 2018 and project forward two years under two scenarios. Scenario A: fiscal consolidation holds — nominal GDP grows 10 percent annually, fiscal deficit stays at 5 percent of GDP. Scenario B: consolidation slips — nominal GDP grows 8 percent, deficit widens to 7 percent. Starting point: public debt at 59.21 percent of GDP, nominal GDP at KSh 8,904,984 million, December 2018. (Source: Kenya FSR 2018)

Running both scenarios step by step.

Starting values — December 2018:
GDP₀ = KSh 8,904,984 million
Debt₀ = 59.21% × 8,904,984 = KSh 5,272,540 million

Scenario A — Consolidation holds (10% nominal growth, 5% deficit/GDP)

Year 1 (2019):
GDP₁ = 8,904,984 × 1.10 = KSh 9,795,482 million
Deficit₁ = 5% × 9,795,482 = KSh 489,774 million
Debt₁ = 5,272,540 + 489,774 = KSh 5,762,314 million
Debt/GDP₁ = 5,762,314 / 9,795,482 = 58.8% — ratio falling

Year 2 (2020):
GDP₂ = 9,795,482 × 1.10 = KSh 10,775,030 million
Deficit₂ = 5% × 10,775,030 = KSh 538,752 million
Debt₂ = 5,762,314 + 538,752 = KSh 6,301,066 million
Debt/GDP₂ = 6,301,066 / 10,775,030 = 58.5% — continuing to stabilise

Scenario A verdict: Debt ratio declining gradually. Nominal growth rate (10%) exceeds the deficit-to-GDP contribution. Sustainable.

Scenario B — Consolidation slips (8% nominal growth, 7% deficit/GDP)

Year 1 (2019):
GDP₁ = 8,904,984 × 1.08 = KSh 9,617,383 million
Deficit₁ = 7% × 9,617,383 = KSh 673,217 million
Debt₁ = 5,272,540 + 673,217 = KSh 5,945,757 million
Debt/GDP₁ = 5,945,757 / 9,617,383 = 61.8% — ratio rising

Year 2 (2020):
GDP₂ = 9,617,383 × 1.08 = KSh 10,386,773 million
Deficit₂ = 7% × 10,386,773 = KSh 727,074 million
Debt₂ = 5,945,757 + 727,074 = KSh 6,672,831 million
Debt/GDP₂ = 6,672,831 / 10,386,773 = 64.2% — compounding upward

Scenario B verdict: Two years of slippage pushes the ratio to 64.2 percent. The IMF indicative threshold for market access countries before reclassification risk is approximately 70 percent. At the Scenario B trajectory Kenya reaches that boundary within four to five years. Every percentage point above 60 percent widens Kenya's Eurobond spread — the FSR 2018 already documents Eurobond yields rising as domestic LCB yields fell. Scenario B accelerates that divergence exactly when Kenya needs external financing headroom. The consolidation path must hold.

In our roundtable debate on the interest rate cap, CS ICT argued: 'The cap is essential for digital financial inclusion. Mobile lending is thriving precisely because the cap forced banks out of SME lending, creating space for M-Shwari and Fuliza. Removing the cap will let banks flood back into digital lending, crush the fintechs, and reverse a decade of inclusion progress.' Respond directly. (Source: Kenya FSR 2018, MPC Report October 2016)

CS ICT's argument inverts the causality and I want to challenge it directly.

M-Shwari launched in November 2012. Fuliza launched in January 2019. The interest rate cap came into force September 14, 2016. The cap did not create the market space for mobile digital lending — the market space was created four years earlier by mobile penetration, real-time transaction data as a credit signal, and the structural absence of collateral requirements for low-income borrowers. These are innovations that banks were never positioned to replicate regardless of the interest rate environment. The sequencing alone kills the causal claim.

What the cap actually did to digital credit is documented in the FSR 2018 financial inclusion chapter: mobile banking loan defaults driven by 26 percent of borrowers not understanding their terms, 28.8 percent finding payments higher than expected, and consumer financial health declining from 39.4 percent in 2016 to 21.7 percent by 2019. That is not a thriving market in protected space. That is a market where formal credit price controls pushed borrowers into products whose total cost of credit was never capped and whose disclosure standards were inadequate.

On the competitive threat from bank re-entry: a bank extending a KSh 500,000 working capital loan to a registered SME with audited accounts is not competing with M-Shwari extending KSh 5,000 for seven days via mobile wallet. Different products, different risk profiles, different channels. The FSR 2018 documents private sector credit to firms declining while digital credit expanded simultaneously — they were filling different gaps, not the same market. Removing the cap does not crush fintechs. It restores formal credit for the segment that fintechs structurally cannot serve.

A policy brief submitted for roundtable debate contains these data points to justify a KSh 40 billion social protection budget expansion: 'Kenya's GDP grew by 6.3 percent in 2018. Poverty rate is approximately 36 percent. Total government revenue in 2018 was KSh 1.6 trillion. The public debt-to-GDP ratio improved from 61 percent in 2017 to 57 percent in 2018. The IMF Article IV 2019 rated Kenya's debt as sustainable.' Assess this brief before we debate it. (Source: Kenya FSR 2018)

This brief has data problems that must be resolved before it enters debate. I am flagging three.

Error 1 — Debt ratio: directionally wrong and numerically incorrect.
The FSR 2018 documents public debt at 50.4 percent of GDP in December 2017 rising to 59.21 percent in December 2018. The brief states 61 percent improving to 57 percent. Both figures are wrong. More critically, the direction is inverted — the brief describes improvement when the FSR documents one of the steepest single-year deteriorations in the series, approximately 9 percentage points of worsening. This is not a rounding issue. The fiscal space argument for a KSh 40 billion spending expansion rests on a debt trajectory the brief has described backwards. If the debt ratio is rising, not falling, the headroom argument collapses.

Error 2 — Revenue figure is unsourced.
KSh 1.6 trillion in total government revenue for 2018 is plausible in order of magnitude but cannot be cross-referenced to any document before this roundtable. Cross-checking: the FSR documents public debt-to-tax revenue at 60.61 percent in December 2018. At KSh 5,272 billion in total debt that arithmetic implies tax revenue of roughly KSh 8,700 billion — which is clearly wrong and confirms the FSR ratio uses a different revenue denominator than total tax. The brief needs a specific KRA Annual Report citation with a line reference.

Error 3 — Poverty rate is undated.
Kenya's poverty estimates vary significantly across KIHBS survey years and methodology vintages. '36 percent' without a survey year and source is unanchored and cannot be used in policy debate.

Ruling: Error 1 is disqualifying. The brief cannot proceed to debate until the debt trajectory is corrected with FSR 2018 figures. The entire fiscal space argument is built on a claim that is factually false in both magnitude and direction.

Should Kenya prioritise revenue mobilisation or expenditure rationalisation as the primary path to fiscal consolidation? Give me your position in under 150 words. (Source: Kenya FSR 2018)

Both. But sequencing matters.

Expenditure rationalisation first — because it signals fiscal discipline without requiring new legislation and delivers immediate deficit reduction. The FSR 2018 documents domestic debt service consuming 4.24 percent of tax revenue in December 2018. Every shilling spent on interest is a shilling not available for development. Cut before you collect more.

Revenue mobilisation second — but not through rate increases. Kenya's tax-to-GDP ratio has structural room through base broadening: informal sector compliance, property taxes, VAT gaps. The KRA's own data shows compliance rates well below potential in these categories.

What I will not accept: using optimistic revenue projections to justify spending today. Kenya has a history of budgeting against forecasts that do not materialise. Consolidation means real expenditure discipline now, with revenue upside as buffer — not as permission to spend ahead of collection.

CS Agriculture is arguing: 'Kenya should issue a KSh 120 billion Fertiliser Subsidy Bond, government-guaranteed, to distribute subsidised fertiliser to two million smallholder farmers for five years. Productivity gains will increase agricultural GDP by 15 percent, generating KSh 200 billion in additional tax revenue that pays back the bond within five years.' CS Finance, your response? (Source: Kenya FSR 2018)

The revenue payback claim does not survive arithmetic. Let me show the work.

Step 1 — Check the tax revenue figure.
Agricultural GDP in 2018 was approximately 26 percent of KSh 8,905 billion = roughly KSh 2,315 billion. A 15 percent productivity gain on that base = KSh 347 billion in additional agricultural output. Kenya's effective tax rate on agricultural income is low — the sector is largely informal and smallholder-dominated. In the roundtable debate on domestic borrowing, CS Infrastructure argues: 'Reduce domestic borrowing to zero — fund the entire fiscal deficit through cheaper concessional external borrowing, freeing the bond market for private issuers.' CS Education counters: 'Increase domestic borrowing significantly to fund education infrastructure — accept higher coupon rates as the price of building human capital that grows GDP for decades.' CS Finance, where do you stand? (Source: Kenya FSR 2018)

Neither position as stated is defensible. I want to explain why each fails before giving my own.

Why CS Infrastructure is wrong:
Zero domestic borrowing eliminates the yield curve. The FSR 2018 documents government bonds at 24.36 percent of total banking assets — they are the price benchmark against which all Kenyan fixed income instruments are valued. Remove the government from the domestic bond market and pension funds, insurance companies, and banks lose their risk-free pricing anchor. Full external financing also concentrates all refinancing risk in foreign currency — when the shilling depreciates, every shilling of external debt service costs more in tax revenue. The FSR 2018 documents external debt rising faster than domestic debt. Accelerating that shift in the wrong direction increases exchange rate exposure at the worst time.

Why CS Education is wrong:
Increasing domestic borrowing without an expenditure offset widens the fiscal deficit and adds to the KSh 2,452 billion domestic debt stock the FSR 2018 documents. The same banks that would buy additional government bonds are the ones whose private sector lending grew only 3.1 percent in 2018. More government paper equals less bank capacity for private lending. The crowding-out is not theoretical — it is documented.

My position:
— Maintain domestic borrowing at current trajectory. Do not zero it out and do not expand it.
— Extend average maturity from the FSR-documented 4.6 years toward 7–10 years to reduce rollover risk.
— Use concessional external borrowing selectively for capital projects with clear foreign exchange earnings that can service external debt in the original currency.
— No net increase in total deficit. Composition of financing can be optimised. Quantum cannot expand without a revenue or expenditure offset.

Claim 1 — KSh 30 billion budget surplus in FY2018/19: This is inconsistent with every fiscal document before this roundtable. A Sovereign Wealth Fund seeded from a genuine surplus is conceptually sound — Norway's model proves it. The problem is Kenya is not running a surplus. Seeding a SWF from a deficit budget means borrowing at 11–12 percent domestic bond rates to invest in regional equities returning 8–10 percent. That is negative carry funded by public debt. The idea is worth revisiting when Kenya genuinely runs a sustained surplus. Today is not that day.

Give me your position on Kenya's VAT compliance gap in bullet form. What is the problem, what causes it, and what are the three highest-leverage interventions — each with a rough revenue estimate. Be direct. (Source: Kenya FSR 2018, KRA data)

The problem:
- Kenya's tax-to-GDP ratio sits around 17–18 percent against a peer group target of 20+ percent
- The gap is not primarily a rate problem — VAT is 16 percent, comparable to regional peers
- It is a compliance and base problem: large portions of economic activity are unregistered, under-declared, or structurally exempt

Root causes:
- Informal sector accounts for a significant share of GDP but contributes a fraction of VAT receipts — mobile money transaction volumes documented in FSR 2018 (KSh 3,984 billion annually) dwarf formal VAT-registered turnover in comparable segments
- Refund abuse and backlog: legitimate exporters claim VAT refunds slowly; the backlog becomes a cost of doing business for formal firms, pushing them toward informal workarounds
- Threshold gaming: businesses fragment deliberately to stay below the KSh 5 million VAT registration threshold

Three highest-leverage interventions:

1. Electronic Tax Invoice Management System full rollout — estimated additional yield KSh 40–60 billion annually. Real-time invoice matching eliminates ghost invoices and under-reporting. Rwanda and South Africa saw 15–20 percent VAT compliance improvements within three years of similar systems.

2. VAT refund automation tied to eTIMS — not a direct revenue gain but removes the refund backlog driving formal firms into informal workarounds. Net effect: positive through improved voluntary filing rates and reduced incentive for threshold gaming.

3. Presumptive tax expansion for informal sector using mobile money transaction data — link M-Pesa and mobile banking volumes to tax assessment for traders above a transaction threshold. Estimated yield: KSh 15–25 billion annually at scale, subject to CBK data-sharing framework and Data Protection Act compliance.

Bottom line: the compliance gap is solvable without touching rates. The data infrastructure exists — mobile money alone provides better transaction visibility than most tax authorities dream of. The binding constraint is political will to enforce against the informal sector, not technical capacity.

CS Infrastructure opens the debate: 'We must build the Naivasha-Malaba SGR extension immediately. The corridor serves Uganda, Rwanda, and DRC trade flows. Every year we delay costs Kenya approximately KSh 15 billion in foregone transit revenue. The project pays for itself. CS Finance, your objection?' (Source: Kenya FSR 2018)

My objection is the payback claim, not the strategic logic. Let me be precise about the distinction.

The strategic case for the Naivasha-Malaba corridor is real. Kenya's value as a regional hub depends on completing the logistics chain to the landlocked hinterland. I am not disputing that.

What I am disputing is 'the project pays for itself.' That claim requires three things to be true simultaneously: freight and passenger volumes sufficient to generate revenue above operating costs, a tariff structure that is competitive with road transport so those volumes actually materialise on the railway rather than staying on trucks, and a debt service schedule that the net operating surplus can cover. None of those three figures have been tabled in this debate. The KSh 15 billion in foregone transit revenue is an opportunity cost estimate — it is not the same as a revenue projection for the railway itself. SGR Phase 1 revenue performance should anchor any Phase 2 projection. What were Phase 1 freight volumes versus the feasibility study forecast? Until CS Infrastructure answers that question, I cannot accept 'pays for itself' as a working assumption for a financing decision.

CS Infrastructure rebuts: 'CS Finance is hiding behind process. Phase 1 projections were conservative — actual freight volumes exceeded targets in Year 2. The corridor will handle 5 million tonnes annually within five years, generating KSh 25 billion in annual revenue against KSh 18 billion in annual debt service. That is a net positive of KSh 7 billion per year. The numbers work. We are losing time.' (Source: Kenya FSR 2018)

Now we are having a real conversation. Those are actual numbers and I will engage with them directly.

Five million tonnes annually at KSh 25 billion in revenue implies an average revenue of KSh 5,000 per tonne. I need to know whether that is a freight-only figure or blended with passenger revenue, and what the tariff assumption is relative to current road haulage rates on the Mombasa-Kampala corridor. If the railway tariff is materially above road transport cost, shippers will not shift — freight volume projections built on optimistic modal shift assumptions consistently disappoint. CS Infrastructure said Phase 1 volumes exceeded targets in Year 2. I want that data in front of this roundtable before we proceed, because if Phase 1 outperformed, it strengthens the case considerably and I am willing to move.

I am not hiding behind process. I am asking for the three numbers that determine whether this project is financeable on its own merits: net operating surplus after full operating costs, debt service coverage ratio, and the Phase 1 volume performance data CS Infrastructure just cited. Bring those to the next session and I will give a substantive answer on financing.

CS ICT opens: 'The interest rate cap must stay. It reduced lending rates from 18 percent to 13.6 percent in six months — proof it works. Kenyan borrowers deserve protection from bank exploitation.' (Source: MPC Report October 2016)

The lending rate fell because a price ceiling was imposed, not because credit conditions improved. A price control mechanically reduces the measured price in the regulated space — that is not proof the policy works, it is proof the law was enforced.

The MPC Report documents the same six-month period CS ICT is citing: yes, lending rates fell to 13.6 percent. Also in that same period: private sector credit growth fell from 13.5 percent to 4.7 percent. Both facts are in the same document. The question is not whether the price of credit fell for borrowers who retained access — it is whether the total amount of credit available to the economy increased or decreased. It decreased sharply. The borrowers who benefit from a lower rate are the creditworthy large corporates and salaried households banks were already willing to serve. The borrowers who lost access entirely are the SMEs and smallholders who needed risk-priced credit and are now either unserved or pushed into digital lending at uncapped rates.

CS ICT pushes back: 'CS Finance always argues for the banks. Those high spreads — 11.1 percent — were pure profit extraction. Banks ROE was 22.5 percent in 2018. They can afford lower margins. The people come first.' (Source: Kenya FSR 2018)

I argue for the data, not for the banks. Let me answer both points directly.

On the spread: 11.1 percent spread in a market with NPLs at 9.3 percent and rising, an interbank market with structural segmentation, and high operational costs for branch and agency banking is not pure profit extraction — it is risk pricing. The FSR 2018 documents that by 2018 the NPL ratio had risen to 12.7 percent. Banks were provisioning heavily. The spread was not excess margin; it was partly covering credit losses that the cap then prevented them from pricing into new loans.

On ROE of 22.5 percent: that figure is the large peer group. The FSR 2018 Table 8 documents small peer group banks with ROE of negative 0.58 percent and negative profit before tax. The banking sector is not one homogeneous entity with 22.5 percent ROE across the board. The cap's distributional effect was to protect the profitability of large banks — who could divert to government securities — while making small banks unviable. If CS ICT wants to protect people, the banks that serve lower-income markets are the small ones. The cap is destroying them.

The people coming first is not a value I dispute. The mechanism for achieving that matters. A policy that reduces the price of credit for those who already had access while eliminating it for those who did not is not a pro-people policy. It is a pro-existing-borrower policy. Those are not the same group.
CS ICT final push: 'Fine. Then what is your alternative? Just repeal and let banks do whatever they want?' (Source: Kenya FSR 2018, MPC Report October 2016)

No. Repeal plus mandatory total cost of credit disclosure. Those two things together.

Repeal removes the price ceiling that is causing credit rationing. It restores the risk pricing mechanism that allows banks to lend to SMEs at rates that cover their actual risk — which means those borrowers get credit again instead of being turned away.

Mandatory total cost of credit disclosure means every loan product — bank, SACCO, digital lender — must state the annualised percentage rate inclusive of all fees before the borrower signs. The FSR 2018 documents that 26 percent of mobile banking borrowers did not understand their loan terms and 28.8 percent found payments higher than expected. That is a disclosure failure, not a price problem. You fix a disclosure failure with disclosure requirements, not price controls.

Combined: market-rate credit available to more borrowers, with full transparency about what that credit costs. That is the pro-people policy. The cap as currently designed gives cheap credit to fewer people with no disclosure requirements on the digital alternatives they are pushed into when banks decline them. I will take the first option every time.

Design a medium-term revenue mobilisation plan for Kenya that raises the tax-to-GDP ratio from approximately 17.5 percent to 20 percent within five years, without increasing any existing tax rate. Constraints: no new taxes on agriculture or informal MSEs below KSh 1 million annual turnover. Show your reasoning. (Source: Kenya FSR 2018, MPC Report October 2016)

Step 1 — Quantify the target.
At 2018 nominal GDP of KSh 8,905 billion, 17.5 percent tax-to-GDP = KSh 1,558 billion in current revenue. Moving to 20 percent = KSh 1,781 billion. The gap to close: KSh 223 billion annually within five years. GDP will grow, so the absolute target rises — but so does the base available to tax. Working at 2018 GDP levels for clarity.

Step 2 — Identify the structural gaps.
Three categories with the largest compliance upside, consistent with the constraints:
(a) VAT compliance — eTIMS rollout and refund automation. Estimated yield: KSh 40–60 billion annually based on regional comparators at similar rollout stages.
(b) Rental income — severely under-assessed in urban areas. Estimated yield: KSh 15–25 billion annually through a simplified presumptive rental tax linked to county land registry data.
(c) Digital economy and large informal traders — mobile money transaction data enables income estimation for traders above a threshold. Estimated yield: KSh 20–35 billion annually, subject to Data Protection Act framework and CBK data-sharing protocol.

Step 3 — Sequence the interventions.
Year 1–2: eTIMS full rollout. Highest certainty yield, lowest political friction, builds KRA digital infrastructure for subsequent measures.
Year 2–3: Rental income campaign using Nairobi, Mombasa, Kisumu county records. Visible enforcement signal.
Year 3–4: Mobile money presumptive tax for traders above KSh 5 million annual transaction volume — above the agriculture/MSE exemption threshold.
Year 4–5: Digitise the customs valuation system to address import under-invoicing, estimated at 15–20 percent of dutiable imports.

Step 4 — Stress-test against the constraint.
All four measures target the formal urban economy, large traders, and digital platforms. None touch agriculture, and the mobile money threshold is set above the KSh 1 million MSE floor. The constraint holds.

Step 5 — Realistic yield range.
Conservative aggregate: KSh 90–145 billion annually at full implementation. That closes approximately 40–65 percent of the KSh 223 billion gap. Closing the remainder requires either institutional capacity improvements that take longer than five years, or — and I am being honest — some rate adjustment in the outer years. The 20 percent target is achievable but requires flawless execution on eTIMS and political will on rental enforcement. Both are uncertain. I would rather plan to this target and miss slightly upward than plan to 18.5 percent and hit it comfortably.

Kenya's fiscal multiplier for recurrent health spending is almost certainly at the lower end of that range based on available evidence — the Abuja studies producing high multipliers are typically capital health infrastructure, not recurrent programme delivery. Bottom line: the informal sector can be taxed more effectively. The mechanism matters enormously. 'Somehow' is not a mechanism.

Step 2 — Run the fiscal arithmetic.
The government borrows at approximately 11–12 percent on domestic 5-year bonds (FSR 2018 yield curve data). Lending at 7 percent creates a negative carry of 4–5 percentage points. On KSh 60 billion fully deployed: annual subsidy cost = 4.5% × KSh 60 billion = KSh 2.7 billion per year. That is a recurrent budget commitment, not a one-time capitalisation cost. Over 20 years at constant rates: KSh 54 billion in cumulative subsidy outflows, approaching the original capitalisation. This is material but not prohibitive if the programme is well-targeted.

Step 3 — Evaluate the targeting mechanism.
KSh 100,000 monthly income = KSh 1.2 million annually. In Nairobi's current market a mortgage for a modest apartment starts at approximately KSh 3.5–5 million, requiring monthly mortgage payments above KSh 30,000 on a 7 percent 20-year term — approximately 30–35 percent of gross income for the target segment. This is at the boundary of affordability. The programme will serve lower-middle-income formal workers effectively. It will not serve informal workers or the rural poor — that segment requires rental housing investment, not mortgage subsidies.

Step 4 — Assess the crowding-out risk.
The FSR 2018 documents real estate credit growing at 2.49 percent from commercial banks in 2018. A KSh 60 billion government mortgage facility does not directly crowd out bank lending in the premium segment — banks do not compete for KSh 3–5 million mortgages at 7 percent. The crowding-out risk is in the domestic bond market: KSh 60 billion in government borrowing to capitalise the fund reduces the private sector credit capacity of the banks that absorb that paper.

Step 5 — Overall assessment.
Programme is justifiable on housing market failure grounds and the annual subsidy cost of KSh 2.7 billion is fiscally manageable if ring-fenced within the housing budget line. Key conditions: (a) the KSh 60 billion must be raised over multiple years rather than in a single bond issuance to avoid a crowding-out spike; (b) the interest rate subsidy must be reviewed every three years as market rates evolve; (c) the programme should not be extended above the income threshold without separate budget justification. Conditional support, subject to those three governance conditions.

The roundtable has a message from a county governor: 'My county needs money urgently. We have a hospital half-built, a water project stalled, and 200 teachers unpaid for three months. The CRA allocation was delayed by six weeks. I need an emergency KSh 800 million advance from the National Treasury immediately. Approve it or explain why you won't.' (Source: Kenya FSR 2018)

I hear the urgency and I am not dismissing it. Three things quickly.

First — the unpaid teachers. That is a cash flow crisis, not a funding gap. If the CRA allocation was delayed six weeks, the arrears are a timing mismatch between the county's obligations and the national transfer schedule. Treasury can and should accelerate the release of the delayed allocation. That resolves the teacher arrears without creating a new advance facility.

Second — the stalled water project and the half-built hospital. These are capital items. A KSh 800 million emergency advance for capital projects sets a precedent under which every county with a stalled project can claim emergency status. The Public Finance Management Act provides for conditional grants and development allocations precisely to avoid this. What is the specific blockage? If it is a pending government contractor payment from the national government's side, that is a payables issue Treasury needs to resolve. If it is a county procurement failure, the advance does not fix the underlying problem.

Third — the advance itself. The FSR 2018 documents that delayed government payments to contractors and suppliers is a primary driver of elevated NPLs across the banking sector. The national government's pending bills problem is already systemic. Adding a KSh 800 million county advance with unclear repayment terms adds to the quasi-fiscal obligations the Treasury is managing.

My answer: Yes to accelerating the delayed CRA transfer — that should happen today. No to a discretionary KSh 800 million advance outside the PFM Act framework. Bring the capital project funding request through the supplementary budget or the conditional grant application process. I will prioritise its review.

The MPC Report October 2016 documents that Chase Bank was placed in receivership in April 2016 and successfully reopened. Imperial Bank had been placed in receivership in October 2015. Both events are described as having had significant negative impact on the growth of deposits and loans. The banking sector's NPL ratio rose from 8.2 percent in April 2016 to 9.3 percent in October 2016. A proposal has been submitted to establish a Standing Bank Resolution Fund, permanently capitalised at KSh 50 billion from the national budget, to be deployed within 72 hours of any future bank failure to protect depositors and prevent contagion. The fund would be replenished through a 0.1 percent annual levy on total banking sector assets. Assess. (Source: MPC Report October 2016, Kenya FSR 2018)

Step 1 — Validate the problem being solved.
The Chase Bank and Imperial Bank receiverships created genuine market-wide confidence shocks — the MPC Report documents that Reverse Repos had to be deployed to address temporary liquidity shortages following Chase Bank's placement in receivership. The FSR 2018 documents that both failures contributed to the significant negative impact on deposit and loan growth through 2016 and into 2017. A resolution mechanism that acts faster than the current receivership process has legitimate financial stability value. The problem is real.

Step 2 — Assess the capitalisation structure.
KSh 50 billion funded from the national budget. At December 2018 GDP of KSh 8,905 billion that is 0.56 percent of GDP as an upfront budget commitment. At the time of the proposal the public debt ratio was already at 59.21 percent. Funding a KSh 50 billion resolution facility through the budget means either an expenditure offset or additional domestic borrowing — neither of which the proposal specifies. This is the same structural gap as every other un-financed proposal before this roundtable.

Step 3 — Assess the levy replenishment mechanism.
The FSR 2018 documents total banking sector net assets at KSh 4,408.59 billion in December 2018. A 0.1 percent annual levy on that base generates KSh 4.4 billion per year. At that replenishment rate, rebuilding a KSh 50 billion fund after full deployment takes over 11 years — too slow to be meaningful as a resolution backstop for a second event within a decade. The levy rate is underspecified.

Step 4 — Compare to existing architecture.
The KDIC deposit protection fund stood at KSh 100.15 billion in 2018 with Effective Cover of 33.28 percent. The KDIC already exists, already collects premiums from member institutions, and already provides deposit protection. The proposal duplicates a mechanism that exists rather than strengthening the one that doesn't. The correct instrument is increasing the KDIC's risk-based premium schedule and expanding its resolution mandate — not creating a parallel fund with a budget-financed capitalisation and a levy rate too low to sustain it.

Verdict: reject the structure, support the objective. Strengthen KDIC instead.

The FSR 2018 documents that EAPS processed 18,307 transactions worth USD 681.48 million in 2018, up from 15,303 transactions worth USD 504.85 million in 2017 — a 35 percent increase in value. REPSS processed 620 transactions worth USD 42.92 million in 2018, up from 262 transactions worth USD 13.38 million in 2017 — a 220.84 percent increase. The FSR notes this reflects increased trade in the EAC and COMESA regions and confidence in the payment system. Kenya's current account deficit narrowed to 5.3 percent of GDP. The EAC Secretariat is proposing that Kenya champion a full East African Monetary Union by 2030, with a single currency replacing the Kenya Shilling, arguing that currency union will eliminate transaction costs, deepen intra-regional trade, and accelerate Kenya's integration into the regional economy. What is the Treasury's position? (Source: Kenya FSR 2018, MPC Report October 2016)

The EAPS and REPSS growth data the FSR documents is the most relevant evidence for evaluating this proposal — and it argues against a monetary union, not for one.

The 35 percent increase in EAPS transaction value and the 220 percent surge in REPSS represent regional payment deepening within the existing multi-currency architecture. These systems are working. Transaction costs between EAC partner states are declining not because currencies are unified but because payment infrastructure is improving. The EAC Payments System achieves the trade facilitation benefit the monetary union proposal promises, without requiring Kenya to surrender monetary policy sovereignty.

On the monetary union itself: the fundamental precondition for an optimal currency area is business cycle synchronisation — member economies need to respond to external shocks in the same direction and magnitude so that a single interest rate serves all of them appropriately. The MPC Report October 2016 documents Kenya growing at 6.2 percent and 5.7 percent in Q2 and Q3 2016 while SSA regional growth was estimated at 1.4 percent, weighed down by Nigeria, South Africa, and Angola. These are not synchronised cycles. Kenya running on a shared East African monetary policy set to accommodate commodity-exporting economies in structural slowdown would mean inappropriately loose monetary policy for Kenya's inflation environment — or inappropriately tight policy for Uganda and Tanzania's growth needs. There is no single rate that serves all six EAC Partner States well simultaneously.

The FSR 2018 also documents Kenya's monetary policy actively managing a specific inflation target of 5 percent with CBR decisions calibrated to domestic conditions. Surrendering the CBR to a regional central bank removes the primary tool the MPC Report documents as successfully anchoring inflation expectations. The existing EAPS and REPSS architecture achieves real trade benefits. A monetary union by 2030 is premature, and I would not champion it.

The MPC Report October 2016 flags unfavourable weather conditions as a risk to both food production and hydro-electricity generation. Kenya's agricultural sector growth slowed in Q3 2016. Food prices drove overall inflation to the upper bound of the target range at 6.5 percent. The food and non-alcoholic beverages CPI category contributed 4.7 percentage points of the month-on-month inflation in October 2016. The Ministry of Energy proposes a KSh 35 billion emergency diesel generation procurement programme to maintain electricity supply during low dam levels, funded through a supplementary budget allocation. Is this a sound fiscal response to the risk? (Source: MPC Report October 2016)

No. And I want to be direct about why the framing of this as an emergency procurement is itself a fiscal governance problem.

Kenya's hydro-electricity vulnerability to drought is not a new risk — it is a structural feature of an electricity generation mix that has historically been over-reliant on hydro capacity. The MPC Report flags it as a risk in October 2016. The same risk appeared in previous drought cycles. An emergency procurement programme funded through supplementary estimates is the most expensive possible response to a known, recurring, foreseeable risk — both in unit cost terms and in fiscal terms. Emergency procurement bypasses competitive tendering, pays premium prices, and creates recurrent expenditure obligations on fuel that the budget absorbs in perpetuity as long as the diesel generators remain the swing capacity.

The fiscal arithmetic: KSh 35 billion in diesel generator procurement. Diesel generation in Kenya costs approximately KSh 25–30 per kilowatt-hour in fuel alone against geothermal at KSh 8–10 per unit. Every kilowatt-hour generated by the emergency diesel fleet rather than by geothermal or solar capacity is a recurring fiscal cost that compounds for the life of the equipment. The KSh 35 billion capital outlay is the smaller part of the long-term commitment.

The right fiscal response to the hydro vulnerability is accelerating geothermal development — KenGen's Olkaria capacity pipeline — and utility-scale solar procurement, both of which provide weather-independent baseload. These have higher upfront capital cost but zero fuel cost and eliminate the recurring weather-driven emergency. The supplementary budget allocation should go to accelerating that transition, not to locking in diesel dependency.

Rank these three reforms in order of priority for Kenya's fiscal health, and give one sentence of justification for each ranking. One: repeal the interest rate cap. Two: implement eTIMS for VAT compliance. Three: extend domestic debt average maturity from 4.6 years to 8 years. (Source: Kenya FSR 2018, MPC Report October 2016)

First: repeal the interest rate cap — because private sector credit at 3.1 percent growth in a 6.3 percent GDP economy is the single most direct drag on productive investment, employment, and the tax base, and no other reform generates more growth per unit of political capital spent.

Second: eTIMS VAT compliance — because estimated additional yield of KSh 40–60 billion annually is the largest revenue gain available without touching rates, it directly narrows the fiscal deficit, and it builds the digital tax infrastructure that makes every subsequent compliance reform cheaper to run.

Third: extend debt maturity — because reducing rollover risk and moving from 4.6 years to 8 years average maturity is fiscally important but it is an interest rate environment reform that requires market conditions to be favourable, whereas the first two are within the government's direct policy control today.

Do not let the fiscal deficit expand while calling it investment.

Every proposal in this roundtable has arrived with a growth story attached — infrastructure multipliers, agricultural productivity gains, human capital returns, digital economy spillovers. Some of those stories are true. The problem is that 'investment' has become the word that makes debt accumulation feel responsible. The FSR 2018 documents the debt-to-GDP ratio rising from 50.4 percent to 59.21 percent in a single year. The FSR also documents that the fiscal consolidation adopted in 2017 was working — the deficit-to-GDP ratio was declining. The risk for the next three years is not that Kenya lacks ambition. It is that ambition will be used to justify borrowing faster than the economy can grow into the debt.

Upper-middle income status by 2030 requires sustained GDP growth above 7 percent annually. That growth comes from private investment, which requires credit, which requires banks to lend rather than hold government paper, which requires removing the interest rate cap. It comes from productivity, which requires reliable power, which means solving the hydro vulnerability through geothermal investment rather than diesel emergency procurement. It comes from an expanding tax base, which requires the informal sector compliance measures we have discussed.

None of those require the government to borrow dramatically more. They require the government to govern better with what it has. The single thing Kenya must not do is mistake higher debt for higher investment.

The National Government Budget Implementation Review Report for FY 2019/20, prepared by the Office of the Controller of Budget, documents that overall development budget absorption was 86.2 percent — an improvement from 79.2 percent in FY 2018/19 — while recurrent absorption declined to 89.8 percent from 95.2 percent. However, the third Supplementary Budget was assented to on 30th June 2020 — the last day of the financial year — giving implementing entities zero time to act on the revised allocations. Additionally, 10 MDAs including the National Treasury itself, the State Department of Infrastructure, and the National Assembly failed to submit pending bills data by the time the report was finalised, meaning the reported KSh 53.49 billion pending bills figure is an undercount of unknown magnitude. The National Treasury has proposed that development absorption rates be used as the primary KPI for evaluating MDA Accounting Officers in annual performance appraisals. Assess. (Source: National Government BIRR FY 2019/20)

The proposal to use development absorption rates as the primary KPI for Accounting Officers has the right instinct — budget execution discipline matters — but it will produce perverse outcomes if applied without addressing the two structural failures the BIRR documents with precision.

The first failure: a Supplementary Budget assented to on 30th June 2020 — the final day of the financial year — is not a budget revision. It is a retroactive accounting adjustment. Accounting Officers evaluated against absorption of allocations they had zero operational time to spend will either over-commit expenditure at year-end without adequate procurement processes, or report low absorption on revised estimates that they had no realistic opportunity to execute. The BIRR documents this explicitly as a key issue: some MDA budget provisions were reduced below expenditure already incurred, meaning the Supplementary Budget in some cases made the absorption rate worse, not better, through no fault of the Accounting Officer. Any absorption KPI that does not exclude this effect will punish the wrong people.

The second failure: ten MDAs — including the National Treasury itself — did not submit pending bills data. The National Treasury is the institution that sets the KPI, manages the IFMIS system, and appraises Accounting Officers. If the National Treasury cannot demonstrate timely submission of its own financial data to the Controller of Budget, it has no standing to impose absorption-based appraisals on other MDAs. The BIRR's warning that the actual quantum of pending bills could be higher than KSh 53.49 billion means we are evaluating Accounting Officers against a fiscal baseline we know is incomplete.

The correct KPI structure is: absorption rate weighted by procurement compliance rate — an MDA that absorbs 95 percent of its budget through emergency single-sourcing has not performed well. Pending bills clearance should be a prerequisite KPI — no new project approvals and no positive appraisal for any MDA carrying pending bills above a defined threshold as the first charge on the following year's budget, which is exactly what the BIRR recommends.

The National Government BIRR FY 2019/20 documents that public debt stood at KSh 6.69 trillion at 30th June 2020, growing 15.3 percent from KSh 5.80 trillion at 30th June 2019. Debt service expenditure was KSh 717.65 billion, representing 92.1 percent of the revised gross estimates and 45.6 percent of ordinary revenue for the year. Ordinary revenue for FY 2019/20 is therefore implied at approximately KSh 1.573 trillion. The BIRR also documents that the Government continued paying commitment and management fees on external loans that had not yet been disbursed, which the OCOB explicitly flags as not meeting value for money considerations. Close the accounting loop and assess the debt trajectory. (Source: National Government BIRR FY 2019/20)

Let me close the accounting loop before the qualitative assessment.

Verifying the ordinary revenue implied figure: KSh 717.65 billion ÷ 0.456 = KSh 1,573.8 billion. Cross-checking against the BIRR's consolidated fund receipts: tax revenue of KSh 1,453.5 billion plus non-tax revenue of KSh 121.7 billion = KSh 1,575.2 billion. The arithmetic is consistent to within KSh 1.4 billion — the BIRR's figures are internally coherent.

Now the debt arithmetic:
Debt at 30 June 2019: KSh 5,800 billion
Debt at 30 June 2020: KSh 6,690 billion
Single-year increase: KSh 890 billion = 15.3 percent growth

GDP for FY 2019/20: The BIRR is a budget execution document and does not cite GDP directly. Using the FSR 2018 baseline of KSh 8,905 billion for 2018 and projecting forward at approximately 6 percent nominal growth for 2019 and approximately 3 percent for 2020 (reflecting COVID impact on growth) gives approximate GDP of KSh 9,750 billion for June 2020. At that denominator: Debt/GDP ≈ KSh 6,690 ÷ 9,750 = 68.6 percent. That is a 9 percentage point increase in the debt ratio in a single year — well above the FSR 2018's documented 59.21 percent as at December 2018.

Debt service at 45.6 percent of ordinary revenue is the more alarming figure. It means nearly half of every shilling collected in taxes and fees goes to servicing existing debt before a single road is built, a teacher is paid, or a drug is procured. The IMF's indicative threshold for debt service sustainability is typically 22–25 percent of revenue for market access countries. Kenya is running at double that rate.

On the commitment fees for undisbursed loans: the OCOB's finding is correct and the fiscal cost is compounding. A government paying annual commitment fees of 0.5–1.5 percent on undisbursed loan tranches is paying for capital it is not deploying. If even 10 percent of the KSh 299.7 billion external loans portfolio has undisbursed tranches incurring fees, that is KSh 30 billion in committed but undeployed capital generating annual fee costs of KSh 150–450 million for no productive return. The National Treasury must publish a complete register of undisbursed external loan tranches and their fee obligations before the next budget cycle.

The National Government BIRR FY 2019/20 documents that the State Department for Information Communications and Technology received only 48.9 percent of its revised net development exchequer estimates — the lowest proportion across all MDAs — while the State Department for Vocational and Technical Training received only 36.5 percent. The State Department for Early Learning and Basic Education received 57.2 percent of development exchequer and recorded an absorption rate of just 47.9 percent of its revised gross development estimates. CS ICT argues in the roundtable: 'These figures prove that Silicon Savannah cannot happen without Treasury releasing the ICT budget in full. You are strangling digital transformation by withholding funds.' CS Finance, respond. (Source: National Government BIRR FY 2019/20)

CS ICT is pointing at the right symptom but misidentifying the cause, and the distinction matters for what the fix is.

The BIRR documents ICT development exchequer at 48.9 percent of revised net estimates. But the BIRR also documents ICT development absorption — what was actually spent — at 90.4 percent of gross revised estimates. Wait: those two numbers are in apparent contradiction. If ICT received 48.9 percent of its exchequer entitlement but spent 90.4 percent of its gross revised estimate, where did the additional spending come from? The answer is in the BIRR's own framework: Appropriations-in-Aid. ICT's gross development expenditure was KSh 17.08 billion against a net exchequer release of only KSh 3.4 billion — meaning KSh 10.65 billion was spent through A-I-A, funded directly by donors and development partners outside the Consolidated Fund. The BIRR flags this as a potential constitutional breach under Article 206(1) which requires all government revenues to be received in the Consolidated Fund before expenditure.

So the correct diagnosis is: the Silicon Savannah is being partly funded outside constitutional channels, not that Treasury is withholding funds. CS ICT cannot simultaneously argue that digital transformation requires full Treasury releases and that donor-funded ICT spending at KSh 10.65 billion is proceeding normally. The two are inconsistent.

On the Vocational Training figure of 36.5 percent exchequer release: that is genuinely concerning and requires explanation. A 36.5 percent exchequer release combined with a 98.7 percent absorption rate implies the same A-I-A mechanism — KSh 5.96 billion spent against KSh 0.89 billion exchequer, with KSh 2.53 billion in A-I-A from donors. Again, spending proceeding outside the Consolidated Fund. The policy question is not why Treasury is withholding — it is why Kenya's education and ICT sectors are being substantially financed by donors in ways that bypass Parliamentary appropriation and constitutional safeguards.

The National Government BIRR FY 2019/20 documents that tax revenue collected was KSh 1,453.5 billion against a revised target of KSh 1,466.2 billion — a performance rate of 99.1 percent. However, the original tax revenue estimate was KSh 1,807.6 billion. The revised target was therefore KSh 341 billion lower than the original estimate — a downward revision of 18.9 percent. Domestic borrowing came in at KSh 558.9 billion against an original estimate of KSh 429.4 billion — a 30.2 percent overrun on the original borrowing plan. A proposal has been tabled to use the near-100-percent performance against the revised tax target as evidence of KRA's strong revenue performance, justifying a performance bonus for the KRA Commissioner General and senior leadership. Assess. (Source: National Government BIRR FY 2019/20)

This proposal rewards the revision, not the performance, and the arithmetic exposes why.

KRA collected KSh 1,453.5 billion against an original target of KSh 1,807.6 billion. That is a shortfall of KSh 354.1 billion against the plan that Parliament approved at the start of the year — a miss of 19.6 percent on the budget that the government committed to when it presented its fiscal framework. The revised target was adjusted downward by KSh 341.4 billion to account for COVID-19's economic impact and the government's deliberate tax relief measures — VAT reduction and PAYE relief documented in the BIRR's conclusion. Against the original plan, KRA underperformed by KSh 354 billion. The near-100-percent performance against the revised target is mathematically equivalent to saying KRA hit the number after the number was moved to where KRA was going to land anyway.

More critically, the domestic borrowing overrun tells the financing side of the same story. Domestic borrowing came in at KSh 558.9 billion against an original estimate of KSh 429.4 billion — KSh 129.5 billion more than planned, a 30.2 percent overrun. That overrun is the direct fiscal consequence of the revenue shortfall: when tax revenue falls KSh 354 billion below plan, the government must either cut spending or borrow more. Kenya borrowed more. The KSh 558.9 billion in domestic borrowing crowded private sector credit in exactly the environment where COVID-19 was already contracting economic activity.

Performance bonuses against revised targets where the revision moved the target to match actual performance are not performance incentives — they are retention bonuses masquerading as accountability. If the Treasury wants to incentivise KRA leadership, the metric should be collection performance against the original budget plan, adjusted only for legislated tax relief measures that were outside KRA's operational control. On that basis, FY 2019/20 was not a bonus year.

The National Government BIRR FY 2019/20 documents that equitable share transfers to counties totalled KSh 286.8 billion in FY 2019/20, but the June 2020 equitable share instalment was not disbursed and was carried forward to FY 2020/21. CARA 2019 had provided for KSh 316.5 billion in equitable share to counties. County governments therefore received KSh 29.7 billion less than their constitutional entitlement for the year. The Council of Governors has formally demanded that the National Treasury release the withheld June 2020 equitable share with interest, arguing that the withholding was unconstitutional under Article 202 of the Constitution and Section 17(6) of the PFM Act 2012, and that counties incurred borrowing costs and service delivery failures as a direct result. How does the Treasury respond? (Source: National Government BIRR FY 2019/20)

The Council of Governors is correct on the law and I am not going to argue otherwise. Section 17(6) of the PFM Act requires disbursement within fifteen days of the commencement of each quarter. The BIRR documents that the June 2020 equitable share — which was the fourth quarter Q4 disbursement — was not released by 30th June 2020. That is a statutory breach, and it sits alongside the OCOB's own finding that this was attributable to fiscal pressure at the national government level, not any administrative processing failure.

On the constitutional dimension: Article 202 of the Constitution provides that revenue raised nationally shall be shared equitably between the national and county governments. Article 203 sets the equitable share floor at not less than 15 percent of the most recent audited national government revenue. Withholding an entire monthly tranche of equitable share to manage the national government's own cash flow position is not a permissible mechanism under those provisions. The counties' constitutionally guaranteed share is not a discretionary transfer that the National Treasury can time to suit its liquidity position.

On the interest claim: this is where I need to be precise. The PFM Act does not provide an explicit statutory interest mechanism for late equitable share disbursements. The Council of Governors would need to establish actual damages — borrowing costs incurred at specific rates on specific facilities taken out because of the shortfall, supported by county financial statements. A blanket interest claim without that documentation cannot be processed. What I can commit to: the withheld June 2020 amount was released in FY 2020/21 per the BIRR's own disclosure. For counties that can demonstrate specific borrowing costs directly attributable to the shortfall, Treasury will review those claims through the Intergovernmental Budget and Economic Council framework. That is the correct process. It is not a blank cheque but it is a genuine commitment to engage.

The National Government BIRR FY 2019/20 documents that the Teachers Service Commission spent KSh 255.8 billion on recurrent expenditure — the single largest recurrent spender — achieving a 99.9 percent absorption rate, with compensation to employees at KSh 254.6 billion representing 23 percent of total MDA gross recurrent expenditure. The Education sector's total budget was KSh 500.6 billion, 15.5 percent of the revised gross national budget. Meanwhile, the State Department for Vocational and Technical Training received only 36.5 percent of its development exchequer — the lowest of any MDA — and recorded development expenditure of KSh 6.86 billion, largely from A-I-A. CS Education argues: 'The TSC wage bill dominates the education budget and crowds out development expenditure for TVET and early learning. We need a separate TVET development fund outside the education budget envelope.' Assess the proposal. (Source: National Government BIRR FY 2019/20)

CS Education has correctly diagnosed the structural problem but the proposed solution creates a new fiscal control problem while solving the allocation one.

The diagnosis is accurate. TSC's KSh 254.6 billion compensation bill consumes 50.9 percent of the KSh 500.6 billion Education sector budget before a single school is built, a TVET laboratory is equipped, or an early childhood centre is constructed. The BIRR documents that TVET development received only 36.5 percent of its exchequer entitlement — meaning even the modest allocation it received was not fully released. This is a classic wage-dominated sector where the recurrent commitments are constitutionally and contractually rigid, leaving development expenditure as the residual that gets squeezed when fiscal space narrows.

On the proposed TVET development fund outside the education envelope: the governance concern is sequencing and accountability. The BIRR already documents that multiple MDAs are spending donor A-I-A outside the Consolidated Fund in ways the OCOB flags as constitutionally problematic. A separate TVET development fund — unless established by an Act of Parliament as a specific public fund under Article 206(1) — would create another off-budget spending vehicle with reduced Parliamentary visibility. The history of sector development funds in Kenya is not reassuring: the Road Maintenance Levy Fund, the Local Authorities Transfer Fund, and various parastatal development funds have all experienced governance challenges when ring-fenced outside the main budget framework.

The correct instrument is not a separate fund — it is a protected development budget line within the Education sector with a statutory floor as a percentage of the sector allocation, enforced through the PFM Act. That achieves the protection CS Education wants without removing the expenditure from Parliamentary appropriation, IFMIS tracking, and Auditor General oversight. The protection has to be statutory, not discretionary, or the wage bill will continue to crowd it out in every fiscal consolidation year.

A summary brief prepared for the roundtable on FY 2019/20 budget performance states: 'Kenya's national budget absorption rate was 91.2 percent in FY 2019/20, above the 88.9 percent recorded in FY 2018/19 — demonstrating improving budget execution. Tax revenue hit 99.1 percent of target. Development expenditure absorption improved to 86.2 percent from 71.3 percent the prior year. The government successfully managed COVID-19 impacts while maintaining fiscal discipline.' Identify every factual error in this brief before the roundtable debates it. (Source: National Government BIRR FY 2019/20)

Four errors. Each one corrected with the BIRR source figure.

Error 1 — Absorption rate comparison is inverted.
The brief states 91.2 percent in FY 2019/20 above 88.9 percent in FY 2018/19. The BIRR documents the opposite: overall national government budget absorption was 88.9 percent in FY 2019/20, a decline compared to 91.2 percent recorded in FY 2018/19. The brief has switched the two years. The direction of change is wrong — absorption deteriorated, it did not improve.

Error 2 — Development absorption prior-year comparator is wrong.
The brief states development absorption improved from 71.3 percent. The BIRR documents FY 2018/19 development absorption at 79.2 percent, not 71.3 percent. The 71.3 percent figure is the FY 2017/18 development absorption rate from the trend chart — the brief has used a figure from two years prior as if it were the immediate comparator. The actual improvement was from 79.2 percent to 86.2 percent, which is still a genuine improvement, but less dramatic than the brief implies.

Error 3 — Recurrent absorption is omitted and would contradict the narrative.
The brief selectively highlights development absorption improvement while omitting that recurrent absorption declined from 95.2 percent in FY 2018/19 to 89.8 percent in FY 2019/20. A complete picture of budget execution includes both. Omitting the recurrent decline while leading with overall absorption numbers creates a misleading summary.

Error 4 — 'Maintaining fiscal discipline' is inconsistent with documented findings.
The BIRR documents: a Supplementary Budget signed into law on the last day of the financial year; ten MDAs including the National Treasury itself not submitting pending bills data; KSh 53.49 billion in disclosed pending bills that are acknowledged to be an undercount; expenditure above exchequer releases through off-Consolidated Fund donor channels that OCOB flags as potentially unconstitutional; and the June 2020 county equitable share not disbursed. None of those are consistent with 'maintaining fiscal discipline' as an unqualified assertion.

Ruling: the brief cannot enter debate as a factual summary. Errors 1 and 2 require direct correction before any absorption-based argument can proceed.

The National Government BIRR FY 2019/20 documents that Capital Transfers to Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies (SAGAs) accounted for KSh 346.3 billion — 56.4 percent of total gross development expenditure of KSh 614.3 billion. The second-largest development category was Construction and Civil Works at KSh 92.5 billion (15.1 percent). The BIRR notes that the State Department for Infrastructure alone transferred KSh 117 billion to SAGAs — 33.7 percent of total capital transfers — and the Ministry of Water and Sanitation transferred KSh 45.1 billion. Meanwhile, the BIRR also documents that some SAGAs did not report Appropriations-in-Aid received during the year, 'resulting in understating of the actual A-I-A received.' The PS for Planning has proposed that all SAGA transfers above KSh 5 billion should require pre-disbursement Treasury approval, arguing this will improve accountability for the largest spending channel in Kenya's development budget. Assess. (Source: National Government BIRR FY 2019/20)

The PS for Planning is responding to a real accountability gap — 56.4 percent of development expenditure flowing through entities that then under-report their A-I-A is a significant oversight failure — but the pre-disbursement approval mechanism as designed will create a budget execution bottleneck without solving the underlying transparency problem.

The fundamental issue is not that SAGA transfers are approved — they are already approved through Parliamentary appropriation in the annual estimates. The issue is that once the money reaches a SAGA, it enters a reporting environment with lower transparency than direct MDA expenditure. SAGAs operate under their own governance frameworks, have separate boards, and submit financial statements to their parent ministries rather than directly to IFMIS. When a SAGA also receives A-I-A from donors or user fees and does not report it, the consolidated government fiscal position is unknowable.

Pre-disbursement Treasury approval of individual transfers above KSh 5 billion is administratively unworkable. The State Department of Infrastructure transferred KSh 117 billion across multiple SAGAs in a single year. Requiring Treasury sign-off on each tranche would add weeks to an already-constrained budget execution calendar — the BIRR documents third Supplementary Budget signed on 30 June 2020, compressing the implementation window to zero. Adding another approval layer in that environment produces pending bills, not accountability.

The correct intervention is post-disbursement, not pre-disbursement: mandatory quarterly financial reporting by all SAGAs receiving above KSh 1 billion in annual transfers, with reports submitted directly to both OCOB and the parent ministry simultaneously; automatic IFMIS integration for SAGA expenditure above that threshold; and a published annual SAGA fiscal transparency index that names and ranks compliance. Accountability through transparency and enforcement works better than approval bottlenecks. The PS knows this — Treasury itself is one of the ten MDAs that did not submit pending bills data to OCOB.

I will take responses from CS Infrastructure and CS Education first, since their sectors account for the largest development expenditure lines.

CS Finance, open the roundtable discussion on Kenya's private sector credit problem. (Source: Kenya FSR 2018, MPC Report October 2016)

The private sector credit problem in Kenya has one proximate cause and the MPC Report documents it precisely: the interest rate cap introduced on September 14, 2016.

Here is the sequence. In April 2016, private sector credit was growing at 13.5 percent. By October 2016 — six months after the cap — it had fallen to 4.7 percent. By 2018, the FSR documents growth at 3.1 percent against GDP growth of 6.3 percent. Credit to the private sector was contracting in real terms while the economy grew. Banks responded rationally: they shifted portfolios toward government securities, which by December 2018 represented 24.36 percent of total banking assets and generated 16 percent of total income. The same capital that should have been financing manufacturing, agriculture, and SMEs was instead financing government recurrent expenditure.

I want CS ICT and CS Agriculture to address one question each before we go further. CS ICT: the FSR documents that digital credit borrowers have an 18.1 percent default rate on mobile banking loans. If the cap is removed and formal bank credit expands to the SME segment, does that reduce or increase the digital credit default problem? CS Agriculture: of the two million smallholder farmers the sector regularly cites as the target for credit interventions, what proportion currently have any form of formal credit access — bank, SACCO, or MFI — and what is the average loan size? I need those figures on the table before we debate any credit expansion programme, because the design of the instrument depends entirely on what the actual credit gap looks like.

A proposal has been submitted to establish a KSh 40 billion Youth Enterprise Development Fund, lending to youth-owned businesses at 3 percent per annum, to be capitalised over three years from the budget. The proposal states it will create 500,000 jobs and generate KSh 120 billion in GDP within five years. Before you assess it, what specific information do you need that is not in this proposal? (Source: Kenya FSR 2018)

I will not assess this proposal yet. Here is what is missing.

First: the financing source. KSh 40 billion over three years is approximately KSh 13.3 billion annually. Which budget line does this come from — new borrowing, expenditure reallocation, or a dedicated revenue stream? If it is new borrowing, at December 2018 domestic bond rates of approximately 11–12 percent, the government borrows at 11–12 percent to lend at 3 percent. That negative carry of 8–9 percentage points on KSh 40 billion is KSh 3.2–3.6 billion annually in subsidy cost that must appear somewhere in the budget. The proposal has not disclosed it.

Second: the default rate assumption. The FSR 2018 documents mobile banking loan defaults at 18.1 percent and digital app loan defaults at 9.4 percent — those are the closest comparable products for the youth borrower segment. What default rate does the fund's financial model assume, and what is the loss provision?

Third: the 500,000 jobs and KSh 120 billion GDP figure. What model produced those numbers? What is the assumed loan-to-job multiplier, what sectors, and over what time horizon? KSh 120 billion in GDP from a KSh 40 billion fund implies a 3x output multiplier, which is high for a lending programme. I need the underlying assumptions before I can tell the President whether this is a credible projection or an advocacy number.

Bring those three things back and I will give a substantive answer.

The BIRR FY 2019/20 documents the State Department for Irrigation achieving 95.1 percent exchequer release and 99.5 percent development absorption — strong performance. That actually works in the proposal's favour. But I need to know whether that performance was on a small base or whether it reflects genuine implementation capacity at scale. What was the total irrigation development budget in FY 2019/20 and what was delivered?

Two: supplementary budget timing. The BIRR documents three supplementary budgets in FY 2019/20, the third of which was signed on 30th June 2020 — the last day of the year — giving implementing entities zero time to act. When in the fiscal year would this supplementary be submitted, and is there enough calendar time for procurement and disbursement before year-end?

Three: what is the source of the KSh 25 billion? Domestic borrowing, reallocation from another vote, or donor funding? If it is domestic borrowing, it adds to the KSh 558.9 billion overrun already recorded in FY 2019/20 against the original domestic borrowing estimate of KSh 429.4 billion.

Four: which specific irrigation schemes, and what is the cost-per-hectare assumption? Without scheme-level detail I cannot verify whether KSh 25 billion is appropriately sized for the coverage CS Agriculture is claiming.

If CS Agriculture can answer questions one and four today, I can give a provisional position before the session ends.

Three things before I can assess this.

First: the revenue cost estimate. What is the current corporate tax yield from entities that would qualify as MSMEs under the proposed definition, and what is the annual revenue forgone? Without that figure I cannot tell whether this is a KSh 5 billion or a KSh 50 billion fiscal commitment, and those are categorically different decisions given that debt service already consumes 45.6 percent of ordinary revenue per the BIRR FY 2019/20.

Second: the MSME definition. Kenya's MSME boundaries have shifted across different policy documents. The proposal needs to specify the turnover threshold, whether it applies to registered companies only or also to sole traders, and whether there is a minimum employee count. Each of those parameters can swing the revenue cost estimate by billions and determines whether the exemption primarily benefits genuine micro-enterprises or is structured in a way that allows larger businesses to restructure through subsidiaries.

Third: the compliance counterfactual. What proportion of businesses that would qualify under this exemption currently pay corporate tax at all? If the effective compliance rate in the MSME segment is low — which KRA's own data suggests — then the revenue cost of formalising the exemption is much smaller than the statutory cost, but so is the growth benefit. The proposal's job creation and formalisation claims depend entirely on this number.

Get me those three inputs and I will have a position within the session.

CS Finance, you earlier argued that the interest rate cap should be repealed because private sector credit growth fell from 13.5 to 4.7 percent after its introduction. CS ICT has made a genuinely valid point and I want to acknowledge it directly before explaining why it does not change my conclusion, only the strength of the attribution.

The point is correct: the MPC Report documents that Chase Bank's placement in receivership in April 2016 created temporary liquidity shortages that required Reverse Repo interventions, and the placement of Imperial Bank in receivership in October 2015 had already begun affecting deposit growth before the cap was introduced. Both events would have suppressed credit growth independently. I overstated the cap's isolated contribution when I attributed the entire decline from 13.5 to 4.7 percent to the cap alone. That was imprecise.

However, the FSR 2018 provides the test that CS ICT's argument needs to survive: by December 2018 — two full years after Chase Bank had been successfully reopened and confidence in the banking sector restored — private sector credit growth was still only 3.1 percent, and banks held 24.36 percent of total assets in government securities. If the credit contraction were primarily a confidence shock from the bank failures, it should have recovered as confidence recovered. The FSR documents confidence recovering — deposit growth of 12.4 percent in 2018, liquidity ratio rising to 48.6 percent — but credit to the private sector did not recover with it. So: CS ICT is right that I should not attribute the full 2016 decline solely to the cap. But the persistence of subdued credit into 2018 — after the confidence shock had passed — is still best explained by the cap's ongoing distortion of bank lending incentives. My conclusion stands; my attribution in the earlier argument was too clean.
