You argued earlier that pension funds should not be directed to invest in below-market infrastructure bonds. CS Infrastructure has now tabled the RBA's own amended investment guidelines from 2018, which explicitly allow pension schemes to invest in infrastructure projects under the PPP framework. Does that undermine your position? (Source: Kenya FSR 2018)

No — and this is an important distinction that I want to draw clearly.

The RBA's amended guidelines allowing PPP infrastructure investment are correct policy and I support them. What I opposed was the specific proposal to mandate a minimum 25 percent allocation of new contributions at a prescribed below-market coupon of 2 percentage points below the prevailing 10-year bond rate. The RBA guidelines CS Infrastructure has now tabled do not mandate an allocation percentage and do not prescribe a below-market yield. They expand the permissible universe of investments — they do not compel trustees to accept sub-market returns on a defined share of their portfolio.

The difference is material. A trustee operating under the RBA's amended guidelines can choose to invest in a PPP infrastructure project if the risk-adjusted return is competitive with alternatives. A trustee operating under the mandatory allocation proposal cannot decline the instrument regardless of the return, because the allocation is statutory. The former preserves fiduciary duty. The latter overrides it.

So: the RBA guidelines strengthen the case for a well-structured, market-rate infrastructure bond that pension funds can choose to hold on its merits. They do not strengthen the case for the mandatory below-market allocation, which I continue to oppose. CS Infrastructure should table an infrastructure bond at a market-clearing yield and let pension trustees decide whether to allocate — that is the approach the RBA guidelines enable.

A CS has just stated in the roundtable: 'Kenya's mobile money sector handled KSh 3,984 billion in transactions in 2018 — that is more than double our total tax revenue, which proves the informal economy is massive and taxation would be easy.' Is that reasoning valid? (Source: Kenya FSR 2018)

The data point is correct; the reasoning has two errors.

First, transaction volume is not income. KSh 3,984 billion in mobile money transfers includes the same shilling moving multiple times — a farmer receives payment, pays a supplier, who pays a wholesaler. Each hop is recorded as a transaction. Total income generated is a fraction of transaction volume, not equal to it.

Second, 'transactions are large, therefore taxation is easy' inverts the actual compliance problem. Identifying that transactions exist is not the same as being able to attribute taxable income to specific individuals and assess it correctly. The FSR 2018 documents 1.74 billion individual transactions averaging KSh 2,290 each — mostly small, numerous, and made by people whose total annual income may fall below any reasonable tax threshold. Taxing the channel rather than the income — which is what a transaction levy does — is regressive and erodes financial inclusion. The informal economy is large; that makes taxation hard, not easy.

What does it mean that Kenya's domestic debt average maturity rose from 4.1 to 4.6 years between December 2017 and December 2018? Is that good? (Source: Kenya FSR 2018)

Good direction, insufficient pace. Longer average maturity reduces rollover risk — the risk that a large tranche of debt matures at a moment when market conditions are unfavourable and refinancing is expensive. Moving from 4.1 to 4.6 years is movement in the right direction. But at 4.6 years Kenya is still refinancing its entire domestic debt stock roughly every five years, which is a relatively short cycle for a country running persistent deficits. The target should be 8–10 years, which most investment-grade emerging markets sustain. The FSR is right to describe the lengthening as positive; it is wrong to treat it as sufficient.

Kenya's gross public debt was 53.2 percent of GDP at end-2016 and is projected to reach 60.7 percent by June 2018. Close the accounting loop mechanically and tell me whether this trajectory is manageable or whether we have a structural problem. (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

Let me run the numbers first. Nominal GDP in FY2017/18 is projected at KSh 8,305 billion. The overall fiscal deficit target is 7.5 percent of GDP, equivalent to a cash deficit of approximately KSh 623 billion. Applying the debt accumulation identity: gross nominal public debt rises from KSh 3,998 billion at end-FY2015/16 to a projected KSh 5,042 billion by end-FY2017/18 — an increase of approximately KSh 1,044 billion over two fiscal years. GDP_FY2018 = GDP_FY2017 × (1 + 5.3% real + 5.1% deflator) ≈ KSh 8,305 billion, which reconciles with the IMF tables. Debt-to-GDP therefore reaches 60.7 percent, which checks mechanically.

The trajectory is manageable only conditionally. Under the IMF baseline adjustment scenario — primary deficit narrowing from 5.6 percent of GDP in FY2016/17 toward near zero by FY2020/21 — debt peaks at 60.7 percent this fiscal year and declines to 54.5 percent by FY2021/22. That is the path I am committed to holding. Under the IMF's unchanged-policy alternative scenario — no fiscal consolidation, no removal of interest rate controls — debt rises to 67.4 percent of GDP by 2022 and continues upward with no turning point in sight. That scenario is not acceptable.

The structural problem is real and must be named. Interest payments have already reached nearly one-fifth of revenue, placing Kenya in the top quartile among frontier economies. The share of non-concessional commercial debt has risen sharply since the 2014 inaugural Eurobond issuances — multilateral creditors now account for just over 40 percent of external credit compared to a higher share in prior years, while commercial creditors have grown to 22.7 percent. The margin for error has narrowed materially since 2013, and any slippage on revenue or growth — as 2017 demonstrated — translates directly into a higher debt ratio with no automatic stabiliser available while interest rate controls constrain monetary policy.

Private sector credit growth collapsed from 16 percent at end-2015 to 2 percent year-on-year by March 2018. The IMF attributes this significantly to interest rate controls introduced in September 2016. What is your assessment and what action are you committing to? (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

The data are unambiguous and the causal chain is direct. Before the controls were introduced, the CBK was adjusting the Central Bank Rate in response to inflation and growth conditions — the standard signaling function of a central bank policy rate. Since September 2016, the CBR was effectively frozen at 10.0 percent for eighteen months because any reduction would mechanically lower the lending rate ceiling, rationing out high-risk borrowers and tightening rather than loosening credit conditions. The perverse result is that an instrument designed to reduce borrowing costs has simultaneously constrained credit volume, disabled monetary policy transmission, and compressed bank profitability — particularly for smaller tier 3 institutions.

The fiscal cost to this Ministry is direct and material. SME credit has contracted sharply, particularly in trade and agriculture. Lower private sector credit growth means weaker corporate profitability, reduced PAYE receipts from the SME sector, and lower VAT flows from trade activity. The IMF's analysis estimates that interest rate controls reduced GDP growth in 2017 by between one-quarter and three-quarter percentage points. At Kenya's nominal GDP of approximately KSh 7,556 billion, each percentage point of lost growth costs KRA roughly KSh 15-20 billion in forgone tax revenue at current tax-to-GDP ratios. This is a self-inflicted revenue wound.

My commitment, consistent with the structural benchmark under the SBA for end-August 2018, is to submit a proposal with the Finance Bill 2018 that significantly modifies the controls. The minimum acceptable modification contains three non-negotiable elements: delinking the lending rate cap from the CBR, substantially raising the cap to protect consumers from predatory lending while restoring credit flow, and abolishing the floor on time deposit rates. Outright repeal remains the first-best option. Following modification, the CBK will establish a formal interest rate corridor two to three months thereafter, restoring the CBR's signaling role and enabling Kenya to use monetary policy to respond to external shocks — a capacity we currently do not have.

Kenya's fiscal deficit in 2016/17 came in at 9.2 percent of GDP against a program target of 6.9 percent — a miss of 2.3 percentage points. Break down what went wrong and tell me what changes you are making to prevent a repeat in 2017/18 and 2018/19. (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

The 2016/17 outturn was a failure of both revenue forecasting and expenditure discipline and I will not minimise it. Let me disaggregate the 2.3 percentage point miss against the 6.9 percent target. Three factors account for the bulk of the slippage. First, higher-than-programmed foreign-financed capital investment — primarily SGR Phase 1 spending — contributed to expenditure overruns that were not offset by domestically-financed cuts in time. Second, income tax revenues significantly underperformed the budget, driven by the upward revision of PAYE tax bands, delays in implementing planned revenue administration measures, and reduced financial sector profitability following the introduction of interest rate controls — the last of which depressed corporate income tax receipts directly and was not anticipated in the budget baseline. Third, drought-related emergency spending and extended election-cycle expenditures added current outlays that could not be absorbed within the existing expenditure envelope without generating arrears.

The core architectural failure is chronic revenue overestimation. Budgets have not provided a transparent indication of what the government will actually spend. Ad hoc freeze circulars issued late in the fiscal year create arrears, disrupt capital project cycles, and produce a worse fiscal outcome than a more conservative budget prepared upfront would have achieved.

For 2017/18, I have issued a May 2018 expenditure control circular targeting lower-priority domestically-financed capital projects, with a hard nominal deficit ceiling of KSh 623 billion. If the April revenue outturn disappoints, spending freezes will be implemented without generating new pending bills. For 2018/19, the target narrows to 5.7 percent of GDP — requiring a primary balance adjustment of over 3 percentage points of GDP cumulatively relative to the 2016/17 outturn. The revenue measures embedded in the draft Finance Bill 2018, including petroleum VAT reinstatement and betting tax expansion, are expected to yield 1.1 percent of GDP. The IMF correctly projects an additional 0.6 percent of GDP gap that will require further expenditure compression or additional revenue rationalisation to close.

These three sum to 0.92 percent of GDP, and the authorities project additional administrative and compliance measures to bring the total to 1.1 percent of GDP.

Through end-March 2018, revenues were already 0.5 percent of GDP short of the revised supplemental budget target, driven by weaker income tax, excise, and VAT performance. The underlying weakness in income tax collection is partly structural — interest rate controls have depressed financial sector profitability and therefore corporate income tax receipts, and this channel does not reverse immediately even if the controls are modified. The IMF projects that these underlying weaknesses will partially offset the new measures, implying a residual gap of approximately 0.6 percent of GDP that will need expenditure compression to close.

The larger opportunity that is not yet being captured is the stock of VAT exemptions, estimated by the IMF at 2.5 to 3.0 percent of GDP annually. The tax expenditure study completed in January 2017 documents their scale. A multi-year programme of systematic exemption rationalisation — sequenced, communicated to stakeholders, and phased to avoid disrupting legitimate productive activity — represents the single largest medium-term revenue lever available without touching headline tax rates. That programme needs to begin in earnest in FY2019/20.

Kenya's current account deficit widened to 6.8 percent of GDP in 2017, and the IMF's EBA-lite methodology suggests the real effective exchange rate is overvalued by 17.5 to 18 percent. How does this feed into your debt management and fiscal strategy? (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

The 2017 widening from 5.2 to 6.8 percent of GDP was largely attributable to identifiable one-off factors — drought-driven food and fuel import surges, with oil products alone rising to 3.6 percent of GDP — and is not a permanent structural deterioration of the full magnitude the headline implies. However, the IMF's EBA-lite assessment is more troubling than the flow figure. Both the current account approach and the REER approach independently point to an overvaluation of 17.5 to 18 percent, driven by continued real effective exchange rate appreciation even as the nominal rate has remained relatively stable. That is not a rounding error.

The fiscal transmission channel is direct and material. Kenya's public external debt stood at approximately 31.2 percent of GDP in FY2017/18, denominated predominantly in US dollars and euros. The IMF's extreme stress scenario applies a one-time 30 percent nominal depreciation — under that scenario the PV of public debt to GDP rises from approximately 58 percent to around 73 percent, uncomfortably close to the 74 percent LIC benchmark for strong-policy countries. This is why the debt management strategy for the next three years must prioritise three things explicitly: lengthening the maturity of non-concessional commercial borrowing to reduce bullet repayment exposure — the February 2018 Eurobond at 10 and 30 year maturities and the extension of the 2015 syndicated loan to seven years are steps in this direction — increasing the share of concessional borrowing where project pipelines permit, and actively avoiding new short-duration commercial instruments.

The CBK's reserve position provides a near-term buffer — gross international reserves reached US$9.1 billion at end-April 2018, equivalent to 6.1 months of import cover, above the 4.8 month optimum level modelled by the Fund. That buffer should not be treated as a reason to relax borrowing discipline; it should be treated as the shock absorber available if the exchange rate requires adjustment, and it is most effective if fiscal consolidation is proceeding simultaneously.

Non-performing loans in Kenya's banking sector have risen from 5.7 percent of gross loans in 2014 to 12.4 percent in April 2018, and three banks were intervened in 2015 and 2016. What is the contingent fiscal liability and how is the National Treasury managing it? (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

The rise in NPLs from 5.7 percent in 2014 to 12.4 percent in April 2018 is a serious supervisory signal but not yet a systemic fiscal threat under current IMF stress test results. The banking sector's regulatory capital to risk-weighted assets ratio remained at 18.5 percent in December 2017, well above the statutory minimum, and the IMF's corporate sector vulnerability analysis indicates that even under extreme shock scenarios banks would experience NPL increases without severe capital deterioration across the system. The more concentrated risk sits in tier 3 and smaller tier 2 banks, where the income impact of interest rate controls — which have compressed net interest margins and forced staff reductions to protect earnings — has been proportionally largest.

The bounded direct contingent fiscal exposure is the two government-owned banks currently non-compliant with capital ratios, which together represent approximately 3 percent of system assets or about 0.3 percent of GDP. These are not systemic institutions and their recapitalisation cost is manageable. The three banks intervened in 2015 and 2016 — Chase Bank, Dubai Bank, and Imperial Bank — are in various stages of resolution and do not represent open-ended Treasury commitments under the current KDI Act framework.

Two specific structural weaknesses concern me as fiscal risks beyond the immediate NPL numbers. First, the treatment of repurchase agreements in the resolution framework places repo counterparties alongside senior creditors under the KDI Act — this creates legal uncertainty that suppresses the horizontal repo market, fragments interbank liquidity, and increases systemic vulnerability without any direct benefit to depositors. Amending the KDI Act to allow netting of repo agreements is a zero-cost fiscal reform that would reduce systemic fragility and should be progressed as part of the Finance Bill 2018. Second, the accumulation of liquidity support from the CBK to small banks — while down from peak levels — remains significant and visible in the CBK's net position vis-à-vis banks. If this support is sustained for years rather than months, it becomes a quasi-fiscal transfer that should be disclosed and budgeted transparently.

The IMF says Kenya's chronically optimistic revenue projections have forced repeated ad hoc spending cuts that generate arrears and undermine investment quality. What specific PFM reforms are you committing to and what is the timeline? (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

The IMF's diagnosis is correct and I will not defend the status quo on budget realism. The pattern has been consistent over multiple fiscal years: ambitious revenue projections are embedded in the budget, revenues disappoint through the year, and this Ministry issues expenditure freeze circulars in the final quarter to defend the headline deficit number. The result is that the budget document does not transparently communicate what the government will actually spend, domestically-financed capital projects are stopped mid-cycle creating contractor disputes and implementation losses, and pending bills accumulate against the exchequer account as commitments exceed cash releases.

Four structural benchmarks committed under the SBA for end-August 2018 address specific gaps. First, automating the release of funds through the exchequer account — within the existing MDA account structure — will impose a hard constraint on spending commitments relative to available revenue releases, making it mechanically impossible for ministries to incur commitments they cannot pay within the exchequer cycle. Legal issues around digital signature validity have delayed this; they will be resolved. Second, operationalising the Centralised Payment System will improve real-time expenditure control at the payment stage and provide this Ministry with live visibility on committed versus released expenditure across all votes. Third, Cabinet adoption of standardised guidelines for project appraisal and selection will impose an economic rate-of-return discipline on public investment allocation, reducing the discretionary channelling of capital budget to politically motivated but low-productivity projects. Fourth, submitting draft legislation to Parliament clarifying counties' powers to set own-source taxes and user fees will reduce the unbudgeted pressure on national transfers to counties — transfers to counties consumed 4.0 percent of GDP in FY2017/18, and any expansion in county own-source revenue reduces that call on the consolidated fund.

The deeper reform is building a medium-term expenditure framework from conservative, independently validated revenue baselines rather than KRA aspirational targets. The IMF's 2018 technical assistance on strengthening the medium-term approach to budgeting provides the analytical framework. What is required now is the political commitment from Cabinet to present budgets that are honest about fiscal space, even when that makes expenditure envelopes look tighter than ministries want.

Kenya has missed the primary balance performance criteria for end-December 2016, end-June 2017, and appears at risk for end-June 2018. Only three of eight structural benchmarks have been met under the SBA. Is this program still worth maintaining and what is its strategic value to Kenya at this point? (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

The program record is poor and I will not pretend otherwise. Missing the primary balance performance criteria for three consecutive test dates is a consequence of revenue shortfalls compounded by the drought, election-related expenditures, and the structural drag from interest rate controls on corporate tax receipts. The extended electoral cycle in 2017 — two presidential elections, a Supreme Court annulment, and an opposition boycott extending into November — created an eight-month window in which reform momentum stalled and the corrective policy dialogue with Fund staff that would normally have occurred could not proceed. Only three of eight structural benchmarks have been met: the tax expenditure study was completed, consolidated financial statements for the budgetary central government were published, and the Public Investment Management unit was established with a head appointed. Five benchmarks involving PFM automation, county fiscal legislation, and centralised payment systems remain unmet. That record demands accountability.

The strategic case for maintaining the SBA as a precautionary arrangement nonetheless remains strong on three grounds and I will make it plainly. First, market credibility. The existence of a Fund arrangement with agreed performance criteria lowers Kenya's sovereign risk premium at a time when public debt has risen to 60.7 percent of GDP. The February 2018 Eurobond — US$2 billion in two tranches at 7.25 percent for 10 years and 8.25 percent for 30 years — was successfully placed in part because the SBA provides an external adjustment anchor that private creditors price. A program lapse at this point in the debt trajectory would be read by bond markets as a signal that fiscal consolidation commitments are not credible, with direct implications for the cost of Kenya's next commercial borrowing. Second, the new end-June 2018 performance criteria — a floor on the primary balance consistent with a 7.5 percent overall deficit, a floor on net international reserves at US$7,710 million, and a ceiling on new public debt contracting — provide operational discipline that Kenya's domestic budget process has demonstrably failed to self-impose. Third, the Fund's technical assistance under the program has generated institutional value — the PIM unit, the TSA expansion work, the revenue administration gap analysis — that outlasts any single review cycle. Losing the program forfeits all three of these.

The Big Four agenda envisages approximately US$2.1 billion in government spending in FY2018/19, plus potential tax incentives for developers and SEZ operators. The IMF is asking for careful costing of these benefits. What is your fiscal risk framework for managing the Big Four without derailing consolidation? (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

The Big Four objectives — raising manufacturing's share of GDP from 9 to 15 percent by 2022, affordable housing, universal health coverage, and food security — are precisely the structural transformation priorities that move Kenya toward upper-middle income status. My role is not to oppose them but to ensure the fiscal architecture does not embed hidden liabilities that undermine the consolidation path Kenya has committed to with the IMF at a time when gross public debt is at 60.7 percent of GDP.

Three fiscal risk categories require explicit management. First, tax incentives. A reduced corporate tax rate for housing developers above a construction threshold, SEZ incentives for manufacturing firms, and off-peak power subsidies for heavy industry all carry revenue costs. Every Big Four tax benefit must be scored against the KRA medium-term revenue baseline before the Finance Bill is finalised — the tax expenditure study completed in January 2017 provides the methodology for doing this. The standard that applies is the same one the IMF applies: policies geared at boosting the manufacturing sector should correct market failures or negative externalities and apply to industries as a whole, not pick winners. Incentives that cannot survive a cost-benefit analysis against direct employment subsidies or logistics investment do not belong in the tax code.

Second, PPP contingent liabilities. The road sector PPP pipeline under the Big Four is large and proposed structures include revenue guarantees and minimum traffic guarantees. The SBA indicative target on the stock of government guarantees is KSh 50 billion. I will not allow PPP guarantees to circumvent this through off-balance-sheet structuring — every guarantee will be scored, disclosed in the Fiscal Risk Statement appended to the budget, and counted against the total fiscal risk register. Third, the housing development fund proposes to use publicly-owned land as equity in a financing vehicle and issue bonds through a refinancing company. Before the fund's capitalisation structure is approved, its financial model must be stress-tested against a scenario where mortgage market uptake is 40 percent below the base projection. If the downside scenario creates a contingent government liability exceeding 0.5 percent of GDP, the structure needs redesign.

The IMF has reclassified Kenya's risk of external debt distress from low to moderate, citing breaches in three PPG external debt indicators under stress tests. What triggered this reclassification and what does it mean operationally for how the National Treasury manages the borrowing programme? (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

The reclassification from low to moderate external debt distress is a material change in Kenya's fiscal risk profile and must change our borrowing behaviour, not merely our disclosure language. Let me be precise about what triggered it. Under the most extreme stress scenarios, three PPG external debt indicators breach their indicative thresholds: the present value of external debt-to-exports ratio breaches the 200 percent threshold for ten years by an average of over 53 percentage points; the debt service-to-exports ratio breaches the 25 percent threshold; and the debt service-to-revenue ratio approaches or exceeds the 22 percent threshold. Even under the baseline scenario — not the stress case — the debt service-to-exports ratio temporarily and marginally breaches its threshold. That baseline breach is related to bullet Eurobond repayments: the structure of Kenya's commercial debt portfolio, heavily weighted toward sovereign bonds with bullet principal repayments, creates discrete refinancing peaks that show up as liquidity stress even when the solvency trajectory is manageable.

Three operational changes follow from this reclassification and I am implementing them. First, new non-concessional external borrowing is limited to projects with demonstrably high social and economic returns — the SGR Phase 2 extension and major energy infrastructure meet this test; commercial borrowing to cover recurrent deficits does not. The SBA ceiling on new public debt contracted or guaranteed — KSh 1,220 billion cumulative through end-June 2018 — is a binding constraint I will respect, not a ceiling to approach as closely as possible. Second, the maturity profile of non-concessional debt must be actively extended. The 2015 US$750 million syndicated loan at LIBOR plus 570 basis points was costly short-duration commercial paper; its extension to seven years in February 2018, alongside the new Eurobond in 10 and 30 year tranches at 7.25 and 8.25 percent respectively, moves in the right direction. The domestic debt average maturity profile of approximately five years as at end-December 2016 also needs to be extended to reduce rollover risk. Third, the composition between domestic and external financing must be managed simultaneously — with net domestic borrowing at 4.1 percent of GDP in FY2017/18, the domestic banking sector is being crowded toward government securities and away from private sector credit. Reducing net domestic borrowing to 1.8 percent of GDP in FY2018/19 is not optional; it is the mechanism by which fiscal consolidation unlocks credit space for private investment and GDP growth.

The Ministry of Sports has proposed that betting tax revenue, which is collected as development Appropriation-in-Aid, should be reclassified as recurrent AIA and used to fund county sports infrastructure grants on an annual discretionary basis. KSh 15 billion in betting tax is currently coded as development revenue precisely because it funds capital expenditure with multi-year productive returns — roads, stadia, infrastructure. Converting it to recurrent discretionary grants means Kenya permanently consumes a revenue stream that should be building assets.

- Betting tax revenue is among the most volatile in the portfolio. The 2019/20 actual was KSh 9.3 billion; the 2021/22 estimate jumps to KSh 15 billion — a 61 percent increase premised on continued gaming sector growth. Building recurrent expenditure commitments on top of a volatile and socially contested tax base is how you create a structural deficit when the revenue disappoints.

- 'County sports infrastructure grants on an annual discretionary basis' is a spending description that has no accountability framework attached to it. Before I approve any reclassification, I need a disbursement formula, absorption history from counties on comparable conditional grants, and an audit trail mechanism. The BIRR FY 2019/20 documented systemic development fund underabsorption across sectors — I will not add another poorly governed grant channel.

- I reject the reclassification. If Sports wants to expand county grants, it should make that case in the budget estimates under the development vote with a proper programme structure. The revenue classification exists for fiscal discipline reasons, not administrative convenience.

Walk me through the arithmetic of Kenya's VAT revenue growth trajectory. Actual net VAT to the Exchequer was KSh 383.7 billion in 2019/20. The 2021/22 estimate is KSh 472.9 billion and the 2023/24 projection is KSh 691.6 billion. Is the growth path credible, and what assumptions does it require? (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

Let me close the arithmetic before assessing credibility.

Base: KSh 383.7bn actual 2019/20.
To 2021/22 estimate: 472.9 / 383.7 = 23.3% cumulative growth over two years, implying roughly 11 percent per annum compound.
To 2023/24 projection: 691.6 / 383.7 = 80.3% cumulative growth over four years, implying roughly 15.9 percent per annum compound from the 2019/20 base, or about 10 percent per annum from the 2021/22 estimate.

Assessment: The near-term path to KSh 472.9 billion by 2021/22 requires VAT to recover from the COVID-19 suppression of 2020/21 and grow at roughly 11 percent annually. That is achievable if nominal GDP grows at 8 to 9 percent and VAT buoyancy holds above 1.2 — consistent with historical performance before the 2017 to 2019 credit crunch. The breakdown matters: domestic VAT in 2021/22 is estimated at KSh 269.0 billion against KSh 239.4 billion actual in 2019/20, a 12.3 percent recovery, which is plausible given COVID base effects. Import VAT at KSh 223.9 billion against KSh 169.8 billion actual implies a 31.9 percent increase, which requires sustained import volume growth and exchange rate stability — this is the more fragile assumption.

The 2023/24 projection of KSh 691.6 billion is aggressive. It requires that eTIMS or equivalent compliance investment materially closes the VAT gap — without that structural improvement, the projection is a budget aspiration, not a forecast. I will not endorse the outer-year numbers until KRA provides a compliance roadmap with milestones.

A policy brief argues: 'Kenya should abolish the Railway Development Levy because it is a tax on imports that raises the cost of doing business. The RDL collected KSh 23 billion in 2019/20 and is projected at KSh 30.6 billion in 2021/22. Removing it would stimulate trade and reduce inflation.' Assess. (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

The brief is correct on the numbers but wrong on the policy conclusion, and the framing ignores the fiscal constraint entirely.

The RDL at KSh 30.6 billion in 2021/22 is classified as development Appropriation-in-Aid under the State Department for Transport — it is a hypothecated levy that funds SGR debt service and railway infrastructure. Abolishing it does not simply reduce the cost of imports by the levy margin; it eliminates a dedicated infrastructure financing stream and transfers the SGR liability to the Consolidated Fund, where it competes with health, education, and social protection for general revenue. That substitution is not mentioned in the brief and it is the central fiscal issue.

On the trade and inflation argument: the RDL is a percentage of customs value, so it is pro-cyclical with import volumes. Its effect on consumer prices depends entirely on pass-through rates by sector. The brief does not quantify the inflation reduction it claims — without a sectoral pass-through analysis I cannot assess the consumer benefit side of the trade-off.

My position: I will not support abolition of the RDL without a fully costed alternative financing plan for SGR obligations. If the policy intent is to reduce the burden on specific import categories — such as capital goods or agricultural inputs — I am open to a targeted exemption with a compensating revenue measure. A blanket abolition that creates a KSh 30.6 billion hole in infrastructure financing is not a trade policy; it is a fiscal problem dressed as one.

CS Infrastructure argues: 'The Road Maintenance Levy collected KSh 62 billion in 2019/20. We need an additional KSh 20 billion annually for county road rehabilitation. I propose increasing the RML rate by 30 percent to generate the required funds.' CS Finance, your response? (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

CS Infrastructure, I have three problems with this proposal and I want to be precise about each.

First, the arithmetic. A 30 percent rate increase on the 2019/20 base of KSh 62 billion implies an additional KSh 18.6 billion — you have not reached your KSh 20 billion target and you have already priced in full volume retention. Fuel levies are not volume-neutral when you raise rates; demand elasticity and the smuggling response mean the real yield increase will be below the nominal rate increase. The 2021/22 RML estimate is already KSh 63.2 billion — the projection assumes modest growth at current rates. Give me KRA's elasticity estimate before I can validate the KSh 20 billion claim.

Second, the RML is already the single largest recurrent AIA line in the budget at KSh 63 to 67 billion annually. It sits inside the fuel levy structure, which also carries the Petroleum Development Levy and excise duties. The cumulative levy burden on petroleum products affects transport costs, food prices, and the cost of production across every sector. A 30 percent RML increase is not a neutral infrastructure financing decision — it is an inflationary measure.

Third, I want to see the absorption data for existing KeRRA and KeNHA county road allocations before I authorise a levy increase to expand those budgets. If the current funds are not being spent efficiently, more money solves nothing.

Bring me the elasticity analysis and the absorption history. I will engage on a targeted rate adjustment if the data supports it.

CS Infrastructure responds: 'Fair point on absorption — KeRRA's 2019/20 county roads absorption was 71 percent. But I'd argue the low absorption is partly because the budget is too small to attract competent contractors. A larger pot will improve absorption rates.' (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

That argument inverts the causality and I am not persuaded by it. Low absorption driven by contractor capacity constraints is a procurement and market development problem — it is not solved by increasing the budget envelope. If the pool of competent contractors is thin at KSh X, doubling X does not create more contractors; it creates more competition for the same thin contractor base, which drives up contract prices and worsens value for money.

The 71 percent absorption figure means roughly KSh 18 billion of the existing KeRRA county road budget went unspent or was spent late in 2019/20. Before I authorise a levy increase that adds KSh 18 to 20 billion more, I need a specific plan to raise absorption to at least 90 percent on the current budget. That plan should cover procurement pipeline management, contractor pre-qualification, and supervision capacity at county level. Those are institutional reforms, not revenue reforms.

I will hold the RML rate at current levels. I am open to a phased rate increase linked to demonstrated absorption improvement — if KeRRA hits 85 percent absorption in FY 2021/22, we can discuss a rate review in the 2022/23 budget cycle. That is the only framework under which I will support this.

A brief claims: 'Kenya's corporate income tax collected KSh 344.6 billion in the 2020/21 Revised Estimate I, making it the single largest tax head. The 2021/22 corporate tax estimate of KSh 398.9 billion represents a modest 15.7 percent increase and is therefore conservative and easily achievable.' Identify any errors and assess the claim. (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

There are two factual errors and one analytical error in this brief.

Error 1: Corporate income tax is not the single largest tax head. The 2020/21 Revised Estimate I for corporate tax is KSh 344.3 billion — close to what the brief states — but PAYE from individuals is estimated at KSh 388.7 billion in the same column, making PAYE the larger head. The brief has the ranking wrong.

Error 2: The corporate figure of KSh 344.6 billion cited in the brief corresponds to the gross line before refunds in the detailed table, not the net figure used in the summary. The net Revised Estimate I for corporate tax after refunds is KSh 344.3 billion. This is a small difference but a brief that claims precision while using gross figures for a net comparison is methodologically inconsistent.

Analytical error: The claim that 15.7 percent growth is 'conservative and easily achievable' ignores the base year context. The 2020/21 revised estimates reflect COVID-19 suppression of corporate profits. A recovery estimate that looks modest as a percentage increase from a depressed base may actually require a substantial absolute recovery in profitability across the corporate sector. The correct benchmark is growth from the pre-COVID 2019/20 actual of KSh 307.7 billion — the 2021/22 estimate of KSh 398.9 billion represents a 29.6 percent increase from that base, which is ambitious, not conservative.

Ruling: The brief overstates its case on all three counts. Reject and resubmit with corrected figures and a base-year-adjusted growth analysis.

Kenya's 2021/22 budget estimates total domestic borrowing via debt securities at KSh 661.6 billion, up from KSh 410.5 billion actual in 2019/20 — a 61 percent increase in two years. Revenue exclusive of grants: KSh 1,775.6bn
Domestic debt securities issuance: KSh 661.6bn
Domestic borrowing as share of revenue: 661.6 / 1,775.6 = 37.3 percent
Domestic borrowing as share of GDP: 661.6 / 11,000 = 6.0 percent of GDP

For context, the 2019/20 actual was 410.5 / 1,573.7 = 26.1 percent of revenue, or approximately 4.0 percent of GDP. In Kenya's 2021/22 revenue estimates, PAYE from individuals is projected at KSh 435.9 billion while corporate income tax is projected at KSh 398.9 billion. An opposition economist argues this proves the tax system is unfair to workers and that the corporate rate should be raised by 5 percentage points to rebalance the burden. Give your assessment. (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

The observation is correct but the diagnosis and prescription are both wrong.

PAYE exceeding corporate tax does not in itself demonstrate unfairness — it reflects the structure of the Kenyan economy, where the formal wage bill is large, PAYE withholding is near-automatic and highly compliant, and corporate profits are subject to legitimate deductions, depreciation allowances, and loss carry-forwards that reduce taxable income. The comparison of gross collection figures between a withholding tax and a net profits tax is not a valid equity analysis.

The more revealing question is the effective corporate tax rate — what corporations actually pay as a share of pre-tax profit — compared to the effective marginal rate on wage income above the top PAYE band. If the effective corporate rate is significantly below the statutory 30 percent due to incentives, exemptions, and transfer pricing, that is a legitimate equity concern. But the remedy is base broadening and compliance enforcement, not a statutory rate increase.

A 5 percentage point corporate rate increase to 35 percent would make Kenya an outlier in the East African region — Uganda and Tanzania both sit at 30 percent — and would create an investment location disadvantage at precisely the moment we need to attract manufacturing FDI. The revenue yield from a rate increase is also uncertain: higher rates increase the incentive for profit shifting, and KRA's transfer pricing enforcement capacity is limited.

I reject the rate increase. If CS Finance is asked to address the equity concern, the answer is expanding the corporate tax base through tighter exemption governance and eTIMS-driven compliance, not raising the headline rate.

Walk me through the external borrowing cliff in Kenya's 2021/22 estimates. Total external borrowing is projected at KSh 884.3 billion in 2021/22 but drops to KSh 605.5 billion in 2022/23 and KSh 517.8 billion in 2023/24. Let me decompose the cliff before assessing credibility.

2021/22 external borrowing: KSh 884.3bn
2022/23: KSh 605.5bn — decline of KSh 278.8bn, or 31.5 percent
2023/24: KSh 517.8bn — further decline of KSh 87.7bn, or 14.5 percent
Cumulative two-year reduction: KSh 366.5bn, or 41.4 percent from the 2021/22 peak

Now look at the composition driving the cliff. Commercial loans — classified as borrowing from foreign financial corporations — are estimated at KSh 475.3 billion in 2021/22 and then drop to zero in both 2022/23 and 2023/24. That single line accounts for virtually the entire decline. Everything else — multilateral borrowing, bilateral concessional loans, direct payment loans — is relatively stable across the three years.

This tells me the KSh 475.3 billion commercial loan figure in 2021/22 is almost certainly a Eurobond or syndicated loan refinancing event, not a recurring annual borrowing programme. The 2022/23 and 2023/24 projections assume that commercial borrowing is not repeated at that scale, which is the correct fiscal consolidation assumption — but it requires that the refinancing need in 2021/22 is genuinely one-off and that the domestic market can absorb the residual financing gap.

Is it credible? Conditionally yes, but only if two things hold: the commercial loan in 2021/22 retires an existing liability rather than adding net new debt, and the domestic borrowing programme in 2022/23 and 2023/24 is sustainable at the projected levels. The domestic securities issuance drops from KSh 661.6bn in 2021/22 to KSh 445.6bn in 2022/23, which is a meaningful consolidation. If both paths hold, the overall borrowing reduction is real. If the commercial loan slips or is partially rolled over, the cliff becomes a plateau and the debt dynamics deteriorate materially.

Analytical error: The brief conflates the level of grant receipts with aid dependence. Dependence is measured as grants as a share of total revenue, not as an absolute figure. CS Tourism, I understand the sector's frustration but I cannot endorse a revenue estimate that is more than double the conservative projection on the basis of optimism about vaccine rollout.

Let me be precise about what is in the 2019/20 figure. The KSh 14.7 billion actual included KSh 10.4 billion in Air Passenger Service Charge — a levy that depends on international arrivals and is entirely COVID-sensitive. The 2021/22 estimate for APSC is KSh 0.64 billion, reflecting continued suppression of international travel. For tourism AIA to reach KSh 8 billion in 2021/22, you would need APSC and related levies to recover to roughly 50 percent of pre-COVID levels within a single budget year. That is not a budget estimate — that is a best-case scenario.

The budget process requires conservative revenue estimates precisely to avoid creating expenditure commitments against receipts that may not materialise. If I budget KSh 8 billion and the sector recovers to only KSh 4 billion, CS Tourism has either underspent its programmes — wasting implementation capacity — or overspent against revenue, adding to the deficit. That is a more reasonable ask, and I am partially open to it — but the ring-fencing mechanism needs to meet specific conditions before I will approve it.

What I will not accept is an off-budget account that accumulates receipts outside the normal appropriation cycle — that is how contingent liabilities and governance gaps are created.

If CS Tourism submits a programme design by end of Q1 that specifies the eligible expenditure categories, the procurement framework, and the audit arrangements, I will consider allocating upside tourism AIA receipts above KSh 3.8 billion to a dedicated tourism recovery programme line in the first supplementary budget. The money stays on-budget, it is appropriated by Parliament, and it is audited by the Auditor General. Those are non-negotiable conditions. Bring me the programme design and we can move forward.

Work permit fees collected KSh 8.33 billion actual in 2018/19 but only KSh 3.69 billion in 2019/20 — a 55.7 percent single-year drop. The 2021/22 estimate is KSh 4.99 billion. Second, the 2021/22 estimate of KSh 4.99 billion assumes recovery to roughly 60 percent of the 2018/19 level. Given COVID suppression of international mobility in 2020/21, that is a reasonable short-term target. But the medium-term trajectory matters: work permit revenue is a direct function of Kenya's attractiveness as a destination for skilled foreign workers. If our permit processing times are long, our fee structure is arbitrary, or our investor confidence is low, the revenue will stay suppressed regardless of the estimate.

I want a permit issuance volume breakdown by sector alongside the revenue figure so I can assess whether the composition of incoming skilled workers aligns with the sectors where we have the largest productivity gaps.

Kenya's domestic debt is 29.5 percent of GDP at end-2017, with commercial banks holding 54 percent and the average maturity profile at approximately 5 years. What are the rollover and crowding-out risks and what is your strategy to manage them? (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

The domestic debt structure carries two intersecting risks that I want to name precisely. The first is rollover risk. With KSh 2,210 billion in gross domestic public debt at end-2017 and an average maturity of approximately five years, a significant portion of this stock requires refinancing within a relatively compressed window. Treasury bonds account for 67 percent of domestic debt and Treasury bills for 32 percent — meaning nearly a third of domestic debt is short-duration, subject to repricing at each auction. If domestic interest rates rise, driven by tighter global monetary conditions or by a crowding dynamic I will describe in a moment, the refinancing cost on this rolling stock rises immediately and feeds through to a higher interest bill. Interest payments on public debt already reached nearly one-fifth of revenue in 2017, placing Kenya in the top quartile among frontier economies. That ratio worsens quickly if rollover rates rise.

The second risk is crowding out. Commercial banks hold 54 percent of Kenya's domestic debt, and in the period since interest rate controls were introduced in September 2016, banks have actively shifted their portfolios away from private sector lending and toward government securities. This is a rational response by banks to the controls — government paper carries no credit risk and is not subject to the lending rate ceiling, while SME and agricultural lending carries high credit risk and is now capped in yield. Net domestic borrowing at 4.1 percent of GDP in FY2017/18 is therefore not a neutral fiscal financing choice; it is actively crowding private credit out of the banking system at the exact moment the economy needs credit growth to recover.

The medium-term strategy on both fronts is the same: reduce the fiscal deficit so that net domestic borrowing falls from 4.1 percent of GDP in FY2017/18 to 1.8 percent in FY2018/19, as committed under the SBA. That contraction in domestic market issuance simultaneously reduces rollover frequency and frees bank balance sheet capacity for private sector lending. In parallel, the Debt Management Office should extend the average maturity of new domestic issuance toward eight years or beyond, accepting a modest premium on longer bonds in exchange for a lower rollover risk profile over the medium term.

Kenya's interbank market saw overnight rates fluctuate between 3 and 10 percent during 2017 and early 2018, a range that signals severe market dysfunction. What does this mean for the CBK's monetary policy and what is this Ministry's role in resolving it? (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

An overnight interbank rate range of 3 to 10 percent within a single year is not normal volatility — it signals that the interbank market is not functioning as a unified market. The IMF identifies three drivers: a small number of large banks dominating the market and rationing liquidity selectively; inefficiencies in the processing of large government transactions through the National Treasury that create unpredictable intraday and intraweek liquidity swings; and unsterilised CBK foreign exchange interventions that inject or absorb shilling liquidity without a corresponding open market operation to neutralise the monetary impact. The closure of three banks in 2015 and 2016 compounded this by triggering a substantial increase in counterparty risk aversion among small banks, who now face borrowing rates significantly above the weighted average. This segmentation is visible in the CBK's net position data — the CBK has maintained significant net liquidity support to isolated small banks who cannot access the interbank market on normal terms.

The CBK's policy rate has lost its signaling role as a direct consequence. Before interest rate controls, movements in the CBR transmitted through to lending and deposit rates with reasonable speed. Since September 2016, the CBR is simultaneously the ceiling from which the lending rate cap is mechanically derived — so reducing the CBR to signal accommodation would tighten credit conditions rather than loosen them, the opposite of the intended transmission. The CBK's March 2018 cut of 50 basis points was a signal of intent but explicitly acknowledged the potential for perverse outcomes.

This Ministry's role is specific and actionable on one of the three drivers. Large government transactions — exchequer releases, tax receipt processing, external debt service payments — are a significant and partially predictable source of intraday liquidity shocks. Improving the National Treasury's liquidity forecasting and the timeliness and transparency of its cash flow projections shared with the CBK would allow the central bank to sterilise these flows proactively rather than reactively. Operationalising the Centralised Payment System is a PFM reform that simultaneously improves expenditure control and reduces the liquidity volatility caused by lumpy, unpredictable government cash flows. These are within my remit and I am committed to delivering them by August 2018.

County governments received transfers of 4.0 percent of GDP in FY2017/18. The IMF is pressing Kenya to clarify counties' own-source tax powers and reduce pressure on national transfers. How serious is the devolution fiscal risk and what is the reform path? (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

Devolution is constitutionally embedded and the fiscal transfer to counties is not discretionary — the Constitution mandates a minimum equitable share. At 4.0 percent of GDP in FY2017/18, transfers to counties represent the third largest line in the recurrent expenditure budget, behind wages and interest payments. This is a structural pressure on the fiscal envelope that does not compress easily in a consolidation exercise, because the equitable share formula is determined by the Commission on Revenue Allocation using a population-weighted formula and any reduction requires a legal process that takes years.

The more pressing risk is county-level debt accumulation. The 2015 amendments to PFM regulations cap county gross debt at 20 percent of last audited revenues and debt service at 15 percent of last audited revenues — these are important guardrails but their enforcement depends on the quality and timeliness of county financial reporting, which remains inconsistent. Two specific structural fault lines concern me: pending bills accumulated at the county level, which are not consolidated into the national public debt figures but represent real contingent liabilities to suppliers and service providers who will ultimately seek national redress; and off-budget county borrowing through supplier credit arrangements that may not be captured within the statutory debt ceilings.

The reform path has two tracks that I am pursuing simultaneously. The first is submitting to Parliament the draft legislation clarifying counties' constitutional powers to set their own taxes and user fees — this is an SBA structural benchmark for August 2018. Expanding county own-source revenue reduces dependence on national transfers and gives county governments a fiscal stake in their own economic development rather than treating the equitable share as an entitlement independent of local revenue effort. The second track is strengthening the reporting and audit requirements on county fiscal accounts, extending GFS coverage to county governments, and publishing consolidated general government fiscal data that includes both national and county fiscal positions. You cannot manage fiscal risk you cannot measure.

The IMF notes that Kenya's VAT exemptions could be worth 2.5 to 3 percent of GDP annually and that property tax is largely unexploited. These are described as major untapped revenue levers. What is blocking their exploitation and what is your plan? (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

These are the two most significant structural revenue opportunities available to Kenya and the obstacles to exploiting them are political, not technical. Let me address them separately.

On VAT exemptions: the stock of exemptions is estimated at 2.5 to 3.0 percent of GDP annually — at FY2017/18 nominal GDP of KSh 8,305 billion, this represents KSh 208 to 249 billion per year in forgone revenue. To put this in context, KRA's total VAT collection in FY2016/17 was KSh 339 billion. Kenya is therefore exempting roughly two-thirds of its actual VAT yield every year through the exemption regime. The tax expenditure study completed in January 2017 documents their scale and composition. The blocking factor is that every exemption has a constituency — petroleum products exemptions were put in place under inflationary pressure, agricultural inputs exemptions are defended by agribusiness lobbies, financial services exemptions are embedded in longstanding practice. The 2018/19 Finance Bill begins to address this at the margin, removing specific VAT and CIT exemptions projected to yield 0.15 percent of GDP. This is a beginning, not a programme. A credible three-year exemption rationalisation plan, published with the 2019/20 budget, phased to protect genuinely vulnerable beneficiaries while removing rent-protecting exemptions, would be the most important medium-term revenue measure available to this Ministry.

On property tax: this is a county-government revenue instrument, not a national tax, which makes it politically easier in one sense — counties that develop effective property tax collection reduce their dependence on national transfers — and technically harder in another, because cadastral data, property valuation systems, and collection infrastructure are underdeveloped across most county governments outside Nairobi. The reform is a medium-term investment: IMF technical assistance to build property valuation frameworks at the county level, combined with the own-source revenue legislation I am submitting to Parliament, creates the legal and capacity foundation. Revenue yield within five years could realistically reduce transfer pressure by 0.5 to 1.0 percent of GDP if implemented seriously by the ten largest counties.

The IMF's Box 3 identifies specific weaknesses in Kenya's international corporate taxation regime — treaty shopping, thin capitalisation, transfer pricing enforcement gaps, and indirect offshore transfers. How large is the revenue leakage and what specific reforms are you prioritising? (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

International tax leakage is a growing fiscal risk as Kenya's cross-border inbound investment increases and the treaty network widens. Let me be specific about the four channels the IMF identifies and my assessment of each.

Treaty shopping is the most immediate risk. Kenya's bilateral investment treaties and double taxation treaties have historically not included limitation-of-benefits provisions — meaning a third-country investor can route investment through a treaty partner to access reduced withholding tax rates on dividends, interest, and royalties that Kenya has agreed to in treaty but did not intend to extend to unrelated investors. The fix is clear: future treaties must include LOB provisions and, where Kenya adopts the Multilateral Legal Instrument, these provisions should be added to the existing treaty network retrospectively. The Seychelles Treaty Article 13 model for technical services is the benchmark for structuring these provisions.

Thin capitalisation and interest stripping are the second channel. The current thin capitalisation rule is debt-ratio based, which creates avoidance opportunities through definitional manipulation. Replacing it with or augmenting it through a fixed-ratio earnings-stripping rule — limiting net interest deductions to 30 percent of EBITDA, the OECD base standard — would be both more robust and more consistent with international practice. The draft Income Tax Bill should incorporate this.

Transfer pricing enforcement is the most resource-intensive gap. The IMF recommends risk-based case selection — identifying the highest-risk related-party transactions by sector and introducing the profit split method, which the draft Income Tax Bill begins to address through the Eighth Schedule. The KRA needs dedicated transfer pricing audit capacity; the 2018 technical assistance on revenue administration integrity is building this.

On indirect offshore transfers — where a foreign investor sells a holding company whose primary asset is Kenyan land or resources — the relatively recent ITA amendments designed to permit taxation of such transfers are not yet effective under several of Kenya's existing treaties. This is a revenue protection issue, not a revenue generation measure, but the scale of real estate and resource-sector transactions means the amount at stake is material. Treaty renegotiation or adoption of the MLI is the mechanism.

Kenya improved its World Bank Doing Business ranking by 33 places to 80 between 2016 and 2018 and moved to 91 out of 137 on the WEF Global Competitiveness Index. Does this progress change the fiscal calculus for public investment — can Kenya now attract more private capital and reduce government capital expenditure? (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

The ranking improvements are real and I will not dismiss them. Moving 33 places on the Doing Business Index — with documented gains on starting a business, protecting minority investors, and resolving insolvency — and moving from 106 out of 144 to 91 out of 137 on the WEF competitiveness rankings over six years reflects genuine institutional progress. These are the preconditions for attracting private investment at lower fiscal cost. However, the leap from better rankings to meaningfully lower government capital expenditure is not automatic and I want to be precise about the sequencing.

Public capital expenditure was 8.4 percent of GDP in FY2014/15 and remains at 6.6 percent in the FY2018/19 projections — the compression already underway partly reflects the completion of SGR Phase 1. The question is whether the business environment improvement is sufficient to crowd in private capital at the pace and in the sectors where infrastructure gaps are most binding. The IMF's external stability assessment and the competitiveness data both suggest that logistics, power reliability, and trade facilitation remain constraining — the WEF subcategory on infrastructure and the Doing Business subcategory on trading across borders both show room for improvement against Sub-Saharan African peers. Private capital will not substitute for public investment in these areas spontaneously; it will co-invest where the regulatory environment is de-risked and where anchor public investment has reduced first-mover risk.

The fiscal calculus therefore changes in a specific and bounded way: PPPs become more viable as investor confidence in contract enforceability and dispute resolution improves — the insolvency resolution improvement is directly relevant here. For road infrastructure and energy generation specifically, carefully structured PPPs with well-scoped risk allocation can reduce direct government capital outlay without creating contingent guarantee liabilities that exceed the savings. But corruption indicators, as measured by Transparency International and World Bank governance scores, remain a challenge — and governance risk is the primary factor that raises the private capital hurdle rate above the level at which PPPs become cost-effective. Good rankings on contract enforcement mean little if the procurement process that selects contractors is not transparent.

Kenya's poverty rate fell from 46.8 percent in 2005/06 to 36.1 percent in 2015/16, but the top income quintile still accounts for 59.4 percent of consumption and youth employment is only 27.6 percent. What does this mean for how the National Treasury allocates the budget between growth and redistribution? (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

A 10 percentage point reduction in the poverty headcount over a decade is significant progress and it is driven primarily by rural areas, where two-thirds of Kenya's population lives and where the poverty rate fell from 52.5 to 40.1 percent. This is partly the return on public investment in rural infrastructure, agricultural support, and expanded financial inclusion — M-Pesa penetration and mobile savings have meaningfully expanded access to financial services in rural Kenya in a way that the standard banking sector did not deliver. I take this as evidence that well-targeted public investment has distributional returns, not just growth returns.

But the inequality and youth employment numbers are a fiscal warning as much as a social one. A Gini consumption share of 59.4 percent for the top quintile means that economic growth that is concentrated in the urban formal sector and in capital-intensive industries has very weak poverty transmission to the bottom three quintiles. Youth employment at 27.6 percent among 15 to 24 year olds, against an overall employment ratio of 71.6 percent, means Kenya is producing a growing cohort of working-age people who are not absorbed into productive employment — this is a fiscal time bomb in terms of future social spending pressures and a lost growth dividend.

The allocation implication for this budget is not to choose between growth and redistribution as if they are alternatives, but to prioritise the specific growth expenditures that have demonstrated distributional return. Free secondary education — preserved in the consolidation programme and ring-fenced as priority social spending under the SBA indicative target — is the single highest-return investment in human capital available within the budget envelope, with the longest lead time before it affects the labour market. The IMF's Big Four health care expansion, if designed with an explicit benefit incidence weighted toward the bottom three quintiles rather than a flat universal entitlement, maximises distributional impact per shilling of public spending. The fiscal constraint is real — I cannot expand the expenditure envelope beyond what consolidation permits — but within that envelope I will protect education and targeted transfers to orphans, vulnerable children, and the elderly, which together represent the floor of the safety net.

The IMF Risk Assessment Matrix flags tighter global financial conditions as a high-likelihood risk with medium impact on Kenya. Kenya has significant Eurobond exposure — a 2014 inaugural issuance and a February 2018 issuance of US$2 billion. How would a 200 basis point rise in global yields affect Kenya's fiscal position? (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

Let me work through the exposure channels precisely. Kenya's commercial external debt stock includes the inaugural 2014 Eurobond — a five-year $500 million tranche at 5.875 percent and a ten-year $1.5 billion tranche at 6.875 percent, with a December 2014 tap adding $250 million and $500 million to each tranche respectively — plus a 2015 syndicated loan originally at LIBOR plus 570 basis points, extended to seven years in February 2018. The February 2018 Eurobond added $2 billion in two equal tranches: $1 billion at 7.25 percent for 10 years and $1 billion at 8.25 percent for 30 years. These instruments are fixed-rate sovereign bonds — a 200 basis point rise in global yields does not reprice the coupon on outstanding bonds. The direct cash flow impact on existing debt service is therefore zero on the fixed-rate Eurobond stock.

The fiscal impact materialises in two channels, both of which are material. First, refinancing cost. The 2014 five-year tranche and related instruments mature within the near-term horizon. When Kenya returns to the Eurobond market to refinance these maturities — as it must, given the bullet repayment structure — it does so at the prevailing spread over US Treasuries. The IMF's extreme stress test applies a 200 basis point shock to the effective interest rate on new external borrowing. At Kenya's current PPG external debt stock of approximately US$25.8 billion in PV terms, a 200 basis point increase in the marginal refinancing rate on the commercial component — roughly $8 billion — generates an additional annual interest cost of approximately US$160 million or about 0.2 percent of GDP. This is manageable in isolation but compounds if accompanied by exchange rate depreciation.

Second, capital outflow pressure. Tighter global financial conditions are not just a refinancing cost story — they trigger a repricing of emerging and frontier market risk assets globally. Portfolio investors holding Kenyan government securities and equities will face redemption pressure and will sell, creating exchange rate depreciation pressure simultaneously. This is the scenario where Kenya's limited monetary policy space — constrained by interest rate controls — is most dangerous. The first line of defence is exchange rate flexibility combined with CBK reserve use. But with gross reserves at US$9.1 billion in April 2018, there is meaningful buffer. The second line is that fiscal consolidation — lower borrowing needs — reduces Kenya's exposure to refinancing risk in exactly the scenarios when external conditions are tightest.

The EAC Monetary Union convergence criteria require Kenya to achieve a fiscal deficit of 3 percent of GDP and gross public debt below 50 percent of GDP in present value terms by 2021. On current IMF projections, is Kenya on track and what would it take to meet these targets? (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

On current IMF baseline projections, Kenya is not on track to meet either EAC convergence criterion by 2021 and the numbers make this plain. The IMF projects the overall fiscal deficit at 5.7 percent of GDP in FY2018/19, declining to 4.0 percent in FY2019/20 and 3.5 percent in FY2020/21 — which is the end of the period the EAC deadline covers. The 3 percent ceiling is not reached in the baseline by 2021; it remains at 3.5 percent. That is a gap of 0.5 percentage points of GDP, equivalent to approximately KSh 55 billion in additional fiscal adjustment relative to the IMF baseline that would need to be identified and implemented within two years.

On the debt criterion, the picture is more challenging. The EAC ceiling is 50 percent of GDP in present value terms. The IMF projects the PV of public sector debt at 60.6 percent of GDP in FY2018/19, declining to 58.4 percent in FY2019/20 and 55.6 percent in FY2020/21. Even under the adjustment scenario, Kenya's PV debt ratio is still 5.6 percentage points above the 50 percent ceiling by 2021. Reaching 50 percent by 2021 would require either a significantly faster primary balance improvement than currently programmed, unexpectedly high nominal GDP growth driven by a real GDP overshoot, or a combination of both. Under the IMF's unchanged-policy alternative scenario the PV debt ratio is still rising in 2021, making the criterion breach even larger.

Meeting both criteria by 2021 is arithmetically possible only if Kenya delivers approximately 1.0 to 1.5 percentage points of GDP in additional fiscal adjustment per year above the IMF baseline from FY2019/20 onward. That means either the VAT exemption rationalisation programme — which I have described as the largest available structural revenue lever at 2.5 to 3.0 percent of GDP — is accelerated, or further capital expenditure compression beyond what the Big Four programme already assumes, or both. These are hard choices but the EAC convergence criteria are not aspirational decorations; they are the macroeconomic framework within which Kenya intends to operate as monetary union deepens. Missing them consistently while treating the SBA primary balance targets as the operational constraint sends an inconsistent signal to regional partners and bond markets about which fiscal commitment is actually binding.

The Standard Gauge Railway Phase 1 from Mombasa to Nairobi cost KSh 111.4 billion in foreign-financed capital expenditure in FY2016/17 alone, mostly funded by semi-concessional Chinese loans. Phase 2 is planned. How do you assess the SGR's fiscal and economic returns and what standard should future large infrastructure borrowing meet? (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

The SGR is the largest single capital project in Kenya's postindependence history and its fiscal footprint is substantial enough that the IMF tracks SGR-related spending separately in the program performance tables and reports the fiscal deficit on both an including-SGR and excluding-SGR basis. In FY2016/17, SGR Phase 1 foreign-financed spending of KSh 111.4 billion — approximately 1.5 percent of GDP — accounts for a significant portion of the gap between the overall deficit and the ex-SGR deficit. The exclusion from the primary balance performance criterion of SGR Phase 1 spending during the SBA was an accommodation recognising that this was a discrete infrastructure investment with a defined completion date, not recurrent structural spending.

Phase 1 is now complete and the economic return case rests on two legs: reduction in freight costs on the Mombasa-Nairobi corridor, which directly affects the competitiveness of Kenya's exports and the landed cost of imported inputs for manufacturing; and logistics time savings that reduce inventory costs for businesses using the corridor. The IMF's medium-term growth projections explicitly embed SGR supply-side effects in the projected recovery to 6.0 to 6.5 percent real growth over 2018 to 2022. Whether those returns materialise at the projected scale will be visible in freight volume data and manufacturing output over the next three years.

For Phase 2 and all future large non-concessional infrastructure borrowing, the standard I am establishing operationally is this: every project must pass a standardised economic appraisal using the guidelines that are an SBA structural benchmark for August 2018 — internal rate of return above the government's cost of capital adjusted for project risk, with a conservative traffic or utilisation scenario. Projects that clear this bar in the pipeline should be sequenced against the debt ceiling — the SBA performance criterion caps new public debt contracting including Phase 2 SGR borrowing within the KSh 1,220 billion ceiling for FY2017/18. The shift in Kenya's debt distress rating from low to moderate means the bar for new non-concessional borrowing is now higher than it was when SGR Phase 1 was contracted. That is the new fiscal reality.

The State Department for Infrastructure dominates Kenya's Appropriation-in-Aid budget. Its total AIA in 2021/22 is estimated at KSh 88.3 billion — more than a third of all recurrent and development AIA combined. The Road Maintenance Levy alone accounts for KSh 63.2 billion of that. An opposition economist argues this concentration creates a single-point-of-failure risk in Kenya's budget. Assess in four bullet points. (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

- The concentration observation is factually correct and the fiscal risk is real. KSh 88.3 billion from a single state department — driven overwhelmingly by one levy on one commodity, petroleum — means that a sustained fuel price shock, a smuggling surge, or a policy decision to reduce pump prices by cutting the levy would create an immediate and large budget hole with no automatic compensating mechanism elsewhere in the AIA portfolio.

- However, the opposition economist is mischaracterising the nature of the risk. The RML is not discretionary spending funded from general revenue — it is a hypothecated levy collected at the pump and ring-fenced for road maintenance and infrastructure. The concentration risk is therefore primarily a programme delivery risk for infrastructure, not a general fiscal solvency risk. If RML receipts fall short, road maintenance contracts are delayed; the Consolidated Fund is not directly exposed.

- The more serious concentration risk sits in the development AIA channel, where KSh 25.7 billion of infrastructure development AIA includes KSh 15.0 billion in annuity fund Road Maintenance Levy and KSh 8.0 billion in Petroleum Development Levy. These levies fund SGR and road annuity contract payments that have fixed legal obligations — if the levy underperforms, the government faces a contractual liability it must honour from the Consolidated Fund regardless. That is a genuine contingent liability.

- My recommendation is not to diversify the levy base artificially — that would be revenue policy driven by portfolio theory rather than economic logic. The correct mitigation is to maintain a rolling three-month cash buffer in the Road Annuity Fund and to ensure all annuity contracts contain revenue-shortfall clauses that allow for rescheduling without penalty. Structural concentration in infrastructure AIA is manageable if the contingent liability framework is properly governed.

A brief states: 'Kenya collected KSh 29.99 billion in Import Declaration and Inspection Fees in 2019/20. The 2021/22 estimate is KSh 31.88 billion, a modest 6.3 percent increase. Given import volumes are expected to recover strongly post-COVID, Treasury is leaving money on the table by not raising the IDF rate.' Is this analysis correct? Should the rate be raised? (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

The arithmetic in the brief is correct — KSh 29.99 billion actual in 2019/20, KSh 31.88 billion estimated for 2021/22, a 6.3 percent increase. But the policy conclusion requires much more careful scrutiny before I can endorse it.

The IDF is levied as a percentage of customs value on all imports. It is currently one of several levies stacked on top of customs duties — the total import levy burden already includes customs duties at KSh 119.0 billion, RDL at KSh 30.6 billion, and the IDF at KSh 31.9 billion. Before raising the IDF rate, I need a total effective levy rate analysis by import category showing what importers are already paying as a combined percentage of CIF value. If the cumulative burden on capital goods, raw materials, or food items is already distortionary, adding to it in the name of revenue optimisation is counterproductive.

The brief also conflates volume recovery with rate adequacy. If import volumes recover post-COVID, IDF receipts will grow at the current rate without any policy change — that is what the KSh 31.88 billion estimate already captures. The question is whether volume recovery is fully reflected in the estimate or whether there is upside. I would want the customs clearance volume forecast from KRA before concluding the estimate is conservative.

My position: I will not raise the IDF rate in 2021/22 without a full import levy burden analysis and a KRA volume forecast. If that analysis shows the current rate is below the regional average and the burden on productive imports is manageable, I am open to a rate review in the 2022/23 cycle. Raise it blindly now and we risk suppressing import volumes that generate VAT, excise, and corporate tax downstream.
