Project forward Kenya's total Exchequer revenue exclusive of grants from the 2019/20 actual of KSh 1,573.7 billion to the 2023/24 projection of KSh 2,516.3 billion. What annual compound growth rate does this imply, and is it consistent with Kenya's nominal GDP growth assumptions? Assume nominal GDP grows at 10 percent per annum from a 2019/20 base of KSh 9,800 billion. (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

Let me build this out mechanically.

Revenue CAGR calculation:
Base: KSh 1,573.7bn (2019/20 actual)
Target: KSh 2,516.3bn (2023/24 projection)
Years: 4
CAGR = (2,516.3 / 1,573.7)^(1/4) - 1 = (1.5990)^(0.25) - 1 = 1.1245 - 1 = 12.45% per annum

GDP path at 10% nominal growth:
2019/20: KSh 9,800bn
2020/21: 9,800 × 1.10 = KSh 10,780bn
2021/22: 10,780 × 1.10 = KSh 11,858bn
2022/23: 11,858 × 1.10 = KSh 13,044bn
2023/24: 13,044 × 1.10 = KSh 14,348bn

Revenue-to-GDP ratios:
2019/20: 1,573.7 / 9,800 = 16.1%
2021/22 estimate: 1,775.6 / 11,858 = 15.0%
2023/24 projection: 2,516.3 / 14,348 = 17.5%

Assessment: The revenue CAGR of 12.45 percent exceeds the assumed nominal GDP growth of 10 percent, implying a rising revenue-to-GDP ratio from 16.1 percent in 2019/20 to 17.5 percent in 2023/24. This requires tax buoyancy consistently above 1.2 across the projection period — meaning revenue must grow 20 percent faster than the economy every year. That is achievable only if structural compliance reforms materialise, particularly on VAT and corporate tax. The dip to 15.0 percent in 2021/22 reflects the COVID revenue suppression base effect; the subsequent recovery to 17.5 percent by 2023/24 is the ambitious part. I treat the outer-year projections as targets, not forecasts, until KRA demonstrates the compliance improvement trajectory to support them.

But KSh 8.99 billion of that is from sales of medical inventories and commodities — essentially donor-procured medicines routed through our vote. CS Health is raising a legitimate accounting issue but arriving at the wrong conclusion.

The argument that donor-procured commodities routed through the Health vote should be excluded from AIA performance assessment has merit from a cost recovery analysis perspective — you are correct that KSh 8.99 billion in medical commodity sales does not represent the Ministry's own revenue generation capacity; it is essentially a pass-through of donor-financed goods. However, I will not reclassify it out of AIA for budget management purposes, and here is why: once you remove a revenue line from the AIA framework, you reduce the transparency and accountability attached to it. Donor commodity flows routed through government systems must remain on-budget and within the appropriation framework precisely to ensure they are subject to procurement rules, audit scrutiny, and the Controller of Budget's oversight. Off-budget donor commodities are a governance risk that Kenya has spent years trying to eliminate.

That gives CS Health the analytical clarity they need without weakening the budget governance framework. Bring me a proposed reporting template and I will review it before the next budget cycle.

A brief claims: 'Kenya's stamp duty revenue has been inconsistent — KSh 10.1 billion in 2018/19, dropping to KSh 9.1 billion in 2019/20, then estimated at only KSh 6.2 billion in the 2021/22 budget. There is one significant analytical error and one factual imprecision.

Factual imprecision: The 2021/22 stamp duty estimate of KSh 6.2 billion cited in the brief corresponds to the net figure after the KSh 3 million refund allowance. The gross estimate is KSh 6.778 billion. This is minor but a brief making a precise decline argument should use consistent gross or net figures throughout.

Analytical error — this is the serious one: the brief treats a single revenue estimate in a post-COVID budget year as evidence of structural market decline. The 2020/21 Revised Estimate II for stamp duty was KSh 12.0 billion — higher than the 2018/19 actual — before being revised down. The 2021/22 estimate of KSh 6.2 billion reflects suppressed property transaction activity during COVID-19 restrictions, not a structural decline in the property market. Using a trough estimate as a baseline for a policy recommendation to cut the rate is analytically indefensible.

I will not cut stamp duty rates based on this brief. Resubmit with transaction volume data and an elasticity estimate.

CS Energy proposes: 'The Petroleum Development Levy collected across all budget lines totals roughly KSh 12 billion in 2021/22. We want to consolidate all PDL receipts under a single Energy Development Fund administered by our Ministry, outside the normal AIA framework, to give us flexibility in financing upstream oil and gas projects.' CS Finance, your response? (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

No. I will not support the creation of an off-budget fund for PDL receipts and I want to be direct about why.

The PDL is currently distributed across multiple budget lines — Ministry of Energy development AIA at KSh 2.33 billion, State Department for Petroleum at KSh 1.66 billion, and State Department for Infrastructure at KSh 8.0 billion — precisely because different PDL streams are hypothecated to different infrastructure financing obligations. The Infrastructure share funds road annuity contracts with fixed legal payment schedules. Moving that revenue into a discretionary Energy Development Fund would break the contractual financing chain for road annuities and create an immediate contingent liability on the Consolidated Fund.

Beyond the contractual issue, CS Energy's proposal to administer KSh 12 billion outside the normal AIA framework is a governance regression. AIA funds are subject to appropriation by Parliament, oversight by the Controller of Budget, and audit by the Auditor General. A Ministry-administered fund outside that framework is exactly the structure that creates the pending bills, procurement irregularities, and value-for-money failures that the Auditor General documents year after year.

If CS Energy needs greater flexibility in financing upstream oil and gas projects, the correct mechanism is to make that case in the development estimates with a clearly scoped programme, a procurement plan, and absorption projections. I will engage on a budget increase for upstream financing through proper channels. I will not create a parallel fiscal system to achieve it.

CS Energy pushes back: 'Other countries have national oil funds administered outside the treasury framework — Norway's Government Pension Fund is the obvious example. Why is Kenya different?' (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

Because Norway's Government Pension Fund was established after decades of institutional development, under a legal framework with independent governance, mandatory parliamentary reporting, an independent investment board, and a clear rule prohibiting drawdowns beyond the 4 percent real return threshold. It took Norway thirty years to build the governance architecture that makes that fund credible. Kenya's institutional context is not comparable and CS Energy knows that.

More fundamentally, Norway's fund accumulates surplus oil revenues after all government obligations are met — it is a savings vehicle for a country running a fiscal surplus. Kenya is running a deficit and borrowing KSh 884.3 billion externally in 2021/22. We are not in a position to accumulate sovereign wealth; we are in a position to manage fiscal consolidation responsibly. Invoking Norway as a model for a discretionary ministerial fund with no governance framework is not a serious policy argument.

The comparison also misses that Kenya has less than 1 billion barrels of proven oil reserves, has not yet reached commercial production scale, and has no sustainable oil revenue stream to pool. The PDL is a levy on petroleum products consumed domestically — it is not oil export revenue. These are categorically different revenue sources and they warrant categorically different governance frameworks. My position does not change.

Kenya's direct payment external borrowing — loans disbursed directly to project accounts rather than through the Exchequer — is estimated at KSh 109.7 billion in 2021/22 from bilateral governments and KSh 59.1 billion from international organizations, totalling KSh 168.8 billion. What are the fiscal governance risks of this structure and what should Treasury do about them? (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

Direct payment loans are the most governance-opaque item in Kenya's external borrowing portfolio and they deserve more scrutiny than they typically receive.

The core risk is that KSh 168.8 billion in project-tied loans disbursed directly to implementing agencies bypasses the Exchequer receipt and payment cycle. These funds do not appear in the Consolidated Fund receipts, they are not subject to the same cash management controls as Exchequer-routed funds, and their expenditure is often governed by the creditor's own procurement rules rather than Kenya's PPDA framework. The result is a significant portion of public investment spending that is only partially visible to the Controller of Budget in real time.

The debt liability, however, is fully on Kenya's balance sheet. When a direct payment loan matures, the obligation falls on the Consolidated Fund regardless of whether the project delivered value for money or even whether the funds were fully absorbed. This creates a systematic disconnect between spending control and debt liability — Kenya bears the full credit risk while ceding significant expenditure governance.

A second risk is absorption opacity. The BIRR FY 2019/20 documented development fund underabsorption across sectors, but direct payment loans often show 100 percent disbursement on paper because the creditor controls the drawdown schedule. Physical project completion and financial disbursement can diverge significantly without Treasury visibility.

What Treasury must do: first, require quarterly reporting from all implementing agencies receiving direct payment loans, reconciled against physical progress benchmarks. Second, negotiate with creditors to route future disbursements through the Exchequer single account wherever the creditor's fiduciary requirements permit. Third, ensure the medium-term debt strategy explicitly accounts for direct payment loan service obligations in the outer years — KSh 155.4 billion in bilateral direct payments projected for 2023/24 is a large and growing liability that must be in the fiscal framework transparently.

CS Wildlife reports that their AIA collapsed from KSh 4.07 billion actual in 2018/19 to KSh 0.82 billion in the 2020/21 Revised Estimate I — an 80 percent drop — before recovering to KSh 3.22 billion in the 2021/22 estimate. They argue this volatility proves wildlife revenue cannot be relied upon for recurrent expenditure and request a KSh 2 billion baseline guarantee from the Consolidated Fund regardless of AIA performance. Assess. (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

CS Wildlife is correct about the volatility and wrong about the remedy.

The data is unambiguous: wildlife AIA dropped 80 percent in a single year because it is almost entirely driven by park fees and tourism levies from international visitors — a revenue stream that went to near-zero during COVID-19 border closures. The 2021/22 estimate of KSh 3.22 billion assumes a strong partial recovery. The 2022/23 and 2023/24 projections of KSh 4.85 billion each assume a full return to pre-COVID levels. This is a legitimate volatility risk and CS Wildlife is right to flag it.

However, a KSh 2 billion baseline guarantee from the Consolidated Fund is not the correct instrument. A guarantee of that structure means Kenya's general taxpayers permanently subsidise wildlife recurrent expenditure whenever international tourism underperforms — regardless of whether the cause is a pandemic, a regional security event, or simply weak marketing. That is an open-ended contingent liability with no performance conditions attached.

The correct instruments are two. First, a wildlife revenue stabilisation reserve: in years when AIA exceeds the budget estimate, a defined percentage — say 20 percent of the surplus — is held in a restricted reserve to smooth expenditure in lean years. Second, a clearly defined minimum service level in the budget estimates that specifies which recurrent expenditure lines are protected and how they will be funded if AIA falls below a trigger threshold, with the Consolidated Fund as a backstop only for those specified lines and only up to a capped amount.

Bring me a stabilisation reserve proposal with a five-year AIA history and a minimum service level specification. I will consider a capped Consolidated Fund backstop on that basis. I will not write a blank guarantee.

Kenya's poverty rate fell to 36.1 percent in 2015/16 but the top quintile still controls 59.4 percent of consumption. How does the National Treasury translate this into specific budget allocations for social protection, and what are the actual line figures? (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

Social protection in Kenya's budget operates through four programmes that are explicitly tracked as priority social spending under the SBA indicative target floor. The cash transfer to orphans and vulnerable children, the cash transfer to the elderly, free primary education expenditure, and free secondary education expenditure together constitute the spending floor I am required to maintain under the programme regardless of what revenue shortfalls require me to cut elsewhere. The SBA indicative target sets the cumulative floor on these four lines at KSh 57.4 billion through end-June 2017, rising to KSh 81.5 billion through end-June 2018 — a year-on-year increase of approximately KSh 24 billion, or 42 percent, which is deliberately counter-cyclical to the consolidation underway elsewhere in the budget.

Within the FY2016/17 outturn, the recurrent budget line for transfers to counties — at KSh 305 billion, or 3.8 percent of GDP — dwarfs the national social protection programmes numerically, but county transfers are a constitutionally mandated equitable share and their distributional incidence depends entirely on how county governments spend them, which varies widely. The direct national social protection programmes are more targeted. Cash transfers to orphans and vulnerable children and to the elderly are means-tested, geographically weighted toward high-poverty counties, and reach households in the bottom two consumption quintiles by design. Free primary and secondary education, now being expanded toward universal secondary access, is the largest single investment in equalising human capital accumulation across the income distribution.

The specific gap the 2015/16 household survey exposes is not that these programmes are absent — it is that they are small relative to the scale of inequality. The top quintile's 59.4 percent consumption share and the female unemployment rate of 9.6 percent against 5.2 percent for men both point to structural barriers — land tenure, access to credit, secondary education completion rates for girls — that cash transfers alone do not resolve. The fiscal allocation is necessary but not sufficient. The IMF's own recommendation is to design the Big Four health care and housing programmes with explicit benefit incidence weighted toward the bottom three quintiles, which would leverage the larger spending envelopes in those programmes to do distributional work that the standalone transfer programmes cannot do at their current scale.

You said transfer pricing leakage and treaty shopping are major risks, but you gave no revenue estimate. What is the actual scale of international tax leakage in Kenya and which channel is the largest? (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

You are correct to press me on this — I described the channels without quantifying them and that is not good enough for a policy discussion. Let me give you what the evidence supports and be honest about where the uncertainty lies.

The IMF's 2018 Article IV does not publish a single consolidated estimate of Kenya's international tax leakage, and I will not invent one. What the document does state is that Kenya's international tax regime carries growing risk of base erosion as cross-border inbound investment increases and the treaty network widens — that is a directional warning, not a number. The tax expenditure study completed under the January 2017 SBA structural benchmark provides the most comprehensive published analysis of Kenya's forgone revenue from tax preferences broadly, but its coverage of international tax specifically is partial.

For transfer pricing specifically, the IMF's work on sub-Saharan Africa more broadly estimates that transfer pricing manipulation in extractive industries — oil, gas, and mining — accounts for losses in the range of 0.3 to 1.0 percent of GDP annually in resource-rich African countries with limited audit capacity. Kenya is not a major oil producer at current volumes, but the SGR construction contracts, large agribusiness operations, and telecommunications sector all involve significant related-party transactions that are candidates for profit-shifting. KRA's transfer pricing audit unit is small and the IMF's 2018 technical assistance on revenue administration integrity is explicitly building this capacity, which implies the current enforcement gap is substantial.

On treaty shopping, the revenue cost depends on the withholding tax differential between Kenya's domestic rate and treaty rates — Kenya's domestic withholding rate on dividends is 10 percent for residents and up to 15 percent for non-residents, and several treaties reduce this materially. Quantifying treaty shopping losses requires data on the nationality of beneficial owners behind treaty-resident holding structures, data Kenya does not currently compile. The reform priority — LOB provisions in future treaties and adoption of the MLI for existing ones — is correct regardless of the precise revenue figure, because the trajectory of loss grows with inbound investment volume. Getting the framework right now is cheaper than estimating the damage after a decade of unconstrained treaty abuse.

CS, you previously said net domestic borrowing is targeted to fall from 4.1 percent of GDP to 1.8 percent of GDP in FY2018/19. But the FY2018/19 draft budget still shows a deficit of 5.7 percent of GDP. How do you fund a 5.7 percent deficit while cutting domestic borrowing from 4.1 to 1.8 percent? The numbers don't add up. (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

You have identified what looks like an arithmetic inconsistency and it is worth closing the loop properly, because you are right that it requires explanation.

A fiscal deficit of 5.7 percent of GDP does not mean that 5.7 percent of GDP must be raised through domestic borrowing. The deficit is financed from two sources simultaneously: net domestic borrowing and net foreign financing. The IMF's Table 2b makes the financing decomposition explicit. In FY2018/19, net foreign financing is projected at 3.9 percent of GDP — comprising external loan disbursements including project loans, programme loans, and commercial borrowing, net of external debt repayments due. Net domestic financing is projected at 1.8 percent of GDP. The two sum to 5.7 percent, which closes the deficit. So the accounting identity is: Overall Deficit = Net Domestic Borrowing + Net Foreign Financing = 1.8% + 3.9% = 5.7% of GDP.

The shift from FY2017/18 to FY2018/19 on the domestic side — from 4.1 to 1.8 percent of GDP — is made possible precisely because external financing increases in FY2018/19, driven primarily by the drawdown of the February 2018 Eurobond proceeds and new project loan disbursements. The reduction in domestic borrowing is intentional: it frees bank balance sheet capacity for private sector credit, reduces crowding-out pressure on SME lending, and begins to bring domestic debt issuance to a level consistent with the maturity extension strategy I have described. I should have stated the financing split explicitly in my earlier answer rather than citing the domestic figure in isolation. That omission created a valid impression of inconsistency where none exists in the underlying numbers.

CS, with respect, the IMF is a Washington institution that imposes austerity on developing countries. The SBA consolidation path will cut public investment, destroy jobs, and keep Kenya dependent on foreign creditors. Kenya should reject the IMF targets and pursue its own growth-led fiscal strategy funded by domestic borrowing. Disagree with me if you must, but make the case. (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

I will disagree with you, and I will do it with numbers rather than ideology.

The claim that fiscal consolidation destroys jobs rests on a Keynesian multiplier argument that applies when an economy has slack, idle credit capacity, and a functioning monetary policy transmission mechanism. Kenya in 2018 has none of these three conditions in the required form. Private sector credit growth has collapsed to 2 percent year-on-year — not because demand for credit is absent, but because the banking system is rationed by interest rate controls and is parking available liquidity into government securities rather than lending to SMEs. Every additional shilling of domestic borrowing the government issues competes directly with private sector credit in a market where credit is already severely constrained. The crowding-out multiplier in this environment is negative — more government domestic borrowing shrinks the private investment it displaces more than the government spending it finances creates. That is not an IMF assertion; that is what the data on bank portfolio allocation show.

On the debt trajectory: Kenya's gross public debt reached 60.7 percent of GDP by June 2018, up from 47.9 percent in FY2014/15 — a 12.8 percentage point increase in four years. Interest payments already consume nearly one-fifth of revenue. If Kenya were to maintain the FY2016/17 primary deficit of 5.6 percent of GDP indefinitely rather than consolidating — the IMF's unchanged-policy scenario — gross public debt reaches 67.4 percent of GDP by 2022 with no turning point. The IMF's LIC DSA benchmark for a strong-policy country like Kenya is 74 percent of GDP in PV terms. At 67 percent and rising, the margin against a disorderly debt dynamic — a currency depreciation shock, a global liquidity tightening, a revenue shortfall — narrows to a level where a genuine fiscal crisis becomes probable within the medium term.

I will tell you what I tell Cabinet: the choice is not between austerity and growth. The choice is between controlled fiscal adjustment now, which preserves space for public investment in infrastructure and human capital while stabilising debt, or an uncontrolled adjustment later imposed by bond markets at a higher cost in both output and sovereignty. The SBA is not a foreign imposition; it is an anchor that makes Kenya's own commitments credible to the investors whose capital Kenya needs to finance its development at affordable rates.

Surely that reserve buffer means Kenya can afford to borrow more aggressively and grow its way out of the debt ratio. Why not use the reserve cushion as headroom for expansion? The reserve buffer is real and I would not dismiss it — US$9.1 billion at end-April 2018, equivalent to 6.1 months of imports, is above the IMF's calculated optimal reserve level for Kenya of 3.5 months of imports and provides genuine resilience against external shocks. But your argument confuses the function of reserves with the function of the fiscal position, and that confusion is dangerous.

Reserves exist to absorb external shocks — exchange rate pressure, capital outflows, commodity price spikes, drought-driven import surges. They are the shock absorber, not the growth engine. When Kenya borrowed US$2 billion in the February 2018 Eurobond, those proceeds temporarily inflated reserve levels before being drawn down for budget support and debt refinancing. The reserve figure at any point in time therefore reflects both genuine accumulated buffers and proceeds from recent borrowing that have not yet been spent. These are not equivalent in terms of what headroom they provide.

More fundamentally, the argument that Kenya can borrow more aggressively and grow its way out of the debt ratio requires the growth rate to exceed the effective interest rate on new borrowing — the standard debt dynamics condition. Kenya's average nominal interest rate on new foreign currency debt is approximately 4.6 percent; the February 2018 Eurobond carries coupons of 7.25 and 8.25 percent. Kenya's projected nominal GDP growth is approximately 10 to 11 percent — real growth of 5.7 to 6.5 percent plus a GDP deflator of 4.7 to 5.1 percent. On those numbers, the interest rate-growth differential is currently favourable, which is why the debt ratio peaks in 2018 and begins declining under the baseline. But that favourable differential exists because Kenya is consolidating — it is not a permanent condition that justifies permanent expansion. If growth disappointed to 4 percent real, as it did in 2017, and the Eurobond coupon is locked at 7.25 percent, the differential turns negative and debt rises automatically regardless of the primary balance. The reserve level does not change that arithmetic.

CS, earlier you said interest payments are nearly one-fifth of revenue. But the IMF table shows domestic interest at 2.6 percent of GDP and foreign interest at 1.1 percent of GDP in FY2017/18 — that sums to 3.7 percent of GDP. You are right to correct me on precision and I will restate this accurately.

Using the FY2017/18 IMF programme figures: total interest payments are projected at KSh 400 billion — domestic interest of KSh 285.6 billion and foreign interest due of KSh 114.4 billion. Total revenues and grants are projected at KSh 1,923.3 billion in the supplemental budget projection. Interest payments as a share of revenues and grants therefore equal 400 divided by 1,923, which is 20.8 percent — just above one-fifth.

If you use revenues excluding grants — KSh 1,877.4 billion — the ratio is 400 divided by 1,877, which is 21.3 percent. Both calculations put the figure at or just above one-fifth, not below it as your GDP-based route implied. The discrepancy in your calculation arises from using 3.7 percent of GDP for interest and 19.9 percent of GDP for revenues and computing the ratio as 3.7 divided by 19.9, which gives 18.6 percent. That approach is only valid if both figures are measured against the same GDP denominator — and they are — but the GDP-to-revenue ratio introduces rounding from the tables that slightly understates the interest-to-revenue ratio compared to computing it directly in shillings. The direct KSh computation from IMF Table 2a is the more precise method, and it confirms the one-fifth characterisation is accurate. I should have cited the KSh figures directly from the outset rather than using the GDP-share shorthand, which is more susceptible to the rounding issue you identified.

You previously argued that Kenya's growth prospects are favorable at 5.7 percent in 2018 rising to 6.5 percent by 2022. But 2017 came in at 4.9 percent against a projection of 5.6 percent — a miss of 0.7 percentage points. Why should I trust the medium-term growth projections when the near-term ones have already been wrong? (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

The 2017 miss is real and the scepticism is legitimate. GDP growth came in at 4.9 percent against a programme target of 5.6 percent — a miss of 0.7 percentage points. The causes are documented: a severe drought that contracted agricultural output, the most protracted and disruptive election cycle in Kenya's recent history running from August through November, and private sector credit growth that collapsed from 6 percent at end-2016 to approximately 2 percent by early 2018. These three shocks were partially foreseeable in direction but not in combined magnitude. The drought was the tail of a La Niña event; the election disruption lasted longer than most forecasts assumed because of the Supreme Court annulment and the repeat election.

So the honest answer to your question is this: the medium-term projections of 6.0 to 6.5 percent growth are conditional, not guaranteed. The IMF states this explicitly — they depend on removal or significant modification of interest rate controls, delivery of the fiscal adjustment path, completion of infrastructure projects including SGR Phase 1 supply-side effects, and the absence of further large drought or security shocks. The unchanged-policy alternative scenario — in which interest rate controls remain and fiscal consolidation stalls — projects medium-term growth of only 5.5 percent, persistently below the adjustment baseline. That 0.5 to 1.0 percentage point difference compounds materially over five years.

What the 2017 experience actually validates is the fragility of growth projections at a specific level of precision — not the direction of the growth recovery. Higher-frequency indicators through early 2018, including electricity consumption, cement production, and visitor arrivals data cited in the IMF's Figure 2, all show momentum recovery from the 2017 trough. I will hold the 5.7 percent 2018 projection, acknowledge it carries downside risk if credit growth does not recover, and tell you plainly that the single most actionable variable under government control that affects whether we reach 6 percent is the speed of interest rate control modification.

Kenya's wage bill for civil servants was KSh 444.2 billion in FY2017/18, equivalent to 4.7 percent of GDP and 23.1 percent of total revenue. That is the single largest discretionary recurrent line. Why is wage bill compression not a central pillar of your consolidation strategy? (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

You are right that the civil service wage bill at KSh 444.2 billion — 4.7 percent of GDP in FY2017/18 — is the largest single domestically-financed recurrent spending line, sitting above interest payments in absolute terms before the FY2018/19 interest bill increase. The question of why it is not the central consolidation lever is legitimate and deserves a direct answer rather than an evasion.

Three factors constrain wage bill compression as a near-term consolidation tool, and one of them is a genuine structural constraint while the other two are risks. The structural constraint is that the Salaries and Remuneration Commission sets public service pay scales and any revision downward on real terms requires a formal SRC process — this Ministry cannot unilaterally cut civil service pay rates in a budget circular the way it can freeze a domestically-financed capital project. The SRC framework exists precisely to insulate public service compensation from political manipulation in both directions.

The first risk is service delivery. Kenya's public health, education, and security services are already operating with staffing ratios that are not generous by regional standards. A wage bill cut achieved primarily through staff reductions rather than productivity reform risks degrading service delivery in the county-level facilities and public schools that serve the bottom income quintiles most directly.

The second risk is that the composition of the wage bill matters as much as its level. Defence and NSIS spending at KSh 126.8 billion in FY2017/18 is effectively ring-fenced from public discussion. Pensions and Consolidated Fund Services at KSh 105.9 billion are legally obligated. The discretionary component of the wage bill — civil service grades outside these protected categories — is therefore a smaller share of the headline number than it appears.

What I am doing: the civil service reform line in the budget is currently zero — no reform programme is budgeted. I am commissioning a staffing audit of MDAs against service delivery outcomes so that future headcount decisions are driven by functional review rather than budget pressure. That is slower than a blanket freeze but it is the approach that avoids destroying institutional capacity in the consolidation process.

The IMF projects Kenya's GDP per capita reaching US$2,096 by FY2021/22. The World Bank threshold for upper-middle income status is US$4,256. At that trajectory Kenya does not reach upper-middle income until the 2040s. Is Kenya's fiscal strategy actually compatible with the upper-middle income target by 2030? (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

Let me close this loop with arithmetic before giving you the policy response. The IMF projects nominal GDP per capita at US$2,096 by FY2021/22, starting from US$1,671 in FY2018/19. The compound annual growth rate in nominal per capita GDP over that four-year period is approximately 5.8 percent. If Kenya sustains that rate from 2022 toward the World Bank upper-middle income threshold of US$4,256, the years required are: ln(4,256/2,096) divided by ln(1.058), which gives approximately 12.9 years from 2022 — meaning Kenya reaches the threshold around 2035, not 2030, and certainly not at any higher growth rate implied by the current fiscal trajectory.

To reach US$4,256 by 2030 from US$1,671 in 2018/19 requires a compound nominal per capita GDP growth rate of approximately 8.1 percent per year over twelve years. At Kenya's projected population growth of approximately 2.4 percent annually, this requires nominal GDP growth of approximately 10.5 percent per year — composed of roughly 7.0 percent real GDP growth and 3.5 percent inflation, or similar combinations. The IMF baseline projects real GDP growth of 6.0 to 6.5 percent with a GDP deflator of approximately 5 percent — implying nominal GDP growth of 11 to 11.5 percent annually. Nominal per capita would then grow at 8.6 to 9.1 percent annually, putting the upper-middle income threshold within reach by 2029 to 2030 under the adjustment scenario.

So the answer is yes — the upper-middle income target by 2030 is arithmetically plausible, but only under the IMF adjustment scenario, not the unchanged-policy scenario. The unchanged-policy scenario projects real growth stuck at 5.5 percent — nominal per capita growth of approximately 7.4 percent annually — which pushes the threshold out to 2033 or later. The fiscal consolidation path is not the obstacle to upper-middle income status; it is the precondition for the sustained high growth that makes it achievable on the 2030 timeline. Countries that allow debt to crowd out private credit and exhaust fiscal space do not sustain 6.5 percent real growth for twelve consecutive years.

CS, you have committed to a 7.5 percent of GDP deficit ceiling for FY2017/18, backed by an SBA performance criterion. But revenues through end-March 2018 are already 0.5 percent of GDP short of the supplemental budget target. With only one quarter remaining, walk me through exactly how you intend to hit the KSh 623 billion nominal deficit target. (Source: IMF Kenya Article IV 2018)

The May 2018 expenditure control circular is already issued and I will walk you through the mechanics of how it closes the gap.

The position as of end-March 2018: revenues are 0.5 percent of GDP below the revised supplemental budget target — at FY2017/18 nominal GDP of KSh 8,305 billion, 0.5 percent equals approximately KSh 42 billion in revenue underperformance through nine months of the fiscal year. The April revenue outturn, which I have committed to monitor against the programme target, will determine whether this gap widens further in the final quarter or stabilises. If April revenues perform at the rate implied by the supplemental budget, the full-year shortfall is likely to settle between KSh 40 and 60 billion relative to the revised budget.

The May 2018 circular instructs MDAs to contain spending commitments — not merely delay payments — for the remainder of FY2017/18, with the explicit focus on lower-priority domestically-financed capital projects. This is the critical distinction: freezing commitments rather than delaying payments prevents pending bills from accumulating against the exchequer while still reducing the cash deficit. The SBA indicative target on change in domestic bills pending 90 days or more is set at zero — I am required not to generate new arrears in the process of achieving the deficit target.

The arithmetic of the adjustment: the nominal deficit ceiling is KSh 623 billion. If the full-year revenue shortfall is KSh 50 billion relative to the supplemental budget, then expenditure must be compressed by KSh 50 billion below the supplemental budget allocation within the fourth quarter. At a quarterly expenditure run-rate of approximately KSh 580 billion implied by the full-year budget, a KSh 50 billion cut represents approximately 8.6 percent of one quarter's planned spending — concentrated in domestically-financed development votes, which is where the circular is targeted. This is tight but achievable if MDA compliance with the circular is enforced through the exchequer release mechanism, which is precisely why automating exchequer releases is an SBA structural benchmark rather than a nice-to-have reform.

A proposal has been submitted: 'Kenya should eliminate VAT refunds entirely. In 2021/22, domestic VAT refunds are budgeted at KSh 20.04 billion and import VAT refunds add further cost. Ending refunds would boost net VAT receipts immediately and reduce KRA administrative burden.' Assess in four bullet points. (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

- Eliminating VAT refunds would not boost net revenue in any meaningful sense — it would simply shift the cost from the government to exporters and zero-rated businesses, who would then embed the irrecoverable VAT as a production cost and either raise prices, reduce output, or exit the formal economy. The fiscal gain on the government's books is a fiction; the real economy loss is structural.

- The KSh 20.04 billion domestic VAT refund budget is not wasteful spending — it is the legally mandated return of tax that was collected at earlier stages of the production chain from businesses whose final output is zero-rated or exempt. Exporters in particular rely on timely refunds to maintain working capital. Kenya's tea, horticulture, and garment exporters already complain about refund delays; elimination would accelerate their shift toward informal or offshore procurement arrangements that remove them from the VAT chain entirely, destroying more revenue than the refund cost.

- The correct policy direction is not elimination but acceleration of refund processing. KRA's current refund backlog creates a de facto cash advance to government that the private sector funds involuntarily. A 30-day mandatory refund cycle with interest penalties for late payment would improve business climate, support export competitiveness, and cost Kenya nothing in net revenue terms.

- I reject this proposal without qualification. Any adviser recommending VAT refund elimination has not thought through the value-added tax architecture. The refund mechanism is not a loophole — it is what makes VAT a tax on final consumption rather than a cascading turnover tax. Remove refunds and you have reintroduced the sales tax Kenya abolished for good reasons.

Kenya's 2023/24 revenue projections show total taxes reaching KSh 2,589.3 billion — a 65.5 percent increase from the 2019/20 actual of KSh 1,564.0 billion over four years. An opposition economist says this is fantasy and that Kenya has never sustained tax growth above 10 percent per annum. Walk me through whether the projection is internally consistent and what it requires. (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

Let me test the arithmetic first before engaging the opposition argument.

CAGR from 2019/20 to 2023/24:
(2,589.3 / 1,564.0)^(1/4) - 1 = (1.6556)^(0.25) - 1 = 1.1340 - 1 = 13.40% per annum

The opposition economist is therefore correct that this exceeds Kenya's historical 10 percent annual growth norm. Now the question is whether there is a credible structural story that justifies the acceleration.

Breaking down the KSh 1,025.3 billion required increase by head:
Income taxes must grow from KSh 706.9bn to KSh 1,178.6bn — up KSh 471.7bn or 66.7% over four years, implying 13.7% CAGR. This requires both PAYE growth tracking formal employment expansion and corporate tax recovery from COVID-suppressed profits.
Goods and services taxes must grow from KSh 705.8bn to KSh 1,170.7bn — up KSh 464.9bn or 65.9%, implying 13.5% CAGR. This is the most demanding component: VAT buoyancy above 1.3 requires either a major compliance improvement or a significant expansion of the taxable consumption base.
Trade taxes grow from KSh 151.3bn to KSh 240.0bn — up KSh 88.7bn or 58.6%, implying 12.2% CAGR, the most modest of the three.

Internal consistency: the projection is internally consistent in the sense that it decomposes cleanly across the three tax heads. It is not fantasy arithmetic.

Credibility: the opposition economist is right that 13.4% CAGR has not been sustained historically. The projection is achievable only if three things happen simultaneously — nominal GDP growth of 10 percent per annum, tax buoyancy consistently above 1.3, and a material compliance improvement particularly on VAT and corporate tax. Any one of these alone is plausible; all three together for four consecutive years is optimistic. I treat the 2023/24 outer year as a fiscal target, not a forecast, and I will revise it downward in the medium-term fiscal framework if the 2021/22 outturn falls short of KSh 1,714.7 billion.

What does Kenya's dividend and profit withdrawal income from state-owned enterprises tell us about the quality of the public investment portfolio? In 2019/20 actual receipts show dividends of KSh 46.0 billion and quasi-corporation withdrawals of KSh 70.1 billion — KSh 116.1 billion total — but the 2021/22 estimate collapses to KSh 30.0 billion in dividends and zero in quasi-corporation withdrawals. (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

The collapse from KSh 116.1 billion to KSh 30.0 billion is one of the most telling signals in the entire revenue dataset and it deserves a frank assessment.

The 2019/20 spike was not a sign of SOE health — it was a one-off extraction. KSh 70.1 billion in quasi-corporation withdrawals from regulatory authority surplus funds is the government drawing down accumulated reserves from entities like the Communications Authority, KEBS, EPRA, and similar bodies. That is not recurring income; it is a balance sheet transfer that depletes the reserves of regulators who need those funds to operate independently. The 2021/22 estimate of zero in quasi-corporation withdrawals reflects the simple fact that those reserves have been drawn down and cannot be tapped again at the same scale.

The KSh 46.0 billion in dividends in 2019/20 similarly included CBK dividend income of KSh 11.4 billion — also a one-off given the 2021/22 CBK dividend estimate is zero — and KSh 34.7 billion from other public enterprises. The 2021/22 estimate of KSh 30.0 billion from other enterprises without CBK is actually a more honest baseline for what the SOE portfolio reliably generates.

What this tells us about the quality of the public investment portfolio: Kenya's SOEs as a group generate roughly KSh 30 billion in annual dividends against a public investment stock that runs into the trillions. That is a return on public equity that would be unacceptable in any private sector context. The portfolio is carrying loss-making or low-return entities — Kenya Airways, various water companies, agricultural parastatals — that consume capital without generating returns. I have consistently argued that the SOE rationalisation agenda needs to move faster. The revenue data makes the case more starkly than any policy paper.

CS Agriculture proposes that the State Department for Crop Development and Agricultural Research, whose AIA estimate jumps from KSh 2.69 billion in 2020/21 Revised Estimate I to KSh 5.34 billion in 2021/22 — a 98.5 percent increase — should be allowed to retain all AIA above the baseline estimate to fund farmer input subsidies without going through a supplementary budget. CS Finance, your response? (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

CS Agriculture, I need to ask a prior question before engaging the retention proposal: what is driving a 98.5 percent increase in Agricultural Research AIA in a single year?

A near-doubling of AIA from KSh 2.69 billion to KSh 5.34 billion in twelve months from a department whose primary revenue comes from sales of cultivated assets, crops, and research services is not a routine growth estimate — it is either a reclassification of revenue previously captured elsewhere, a new revenue stream that has not been explained in the budget documents, or an optimistic projection that lacks historical grounding. I will not approve an AIA retention mechanism on top of an estimate I cannot validate.

On the retention principle itself: allowing any ministry to retain AIA above its baseline estimate outside the supplementary budget process undermines the fundamental purpose of parliamentary appropriation. Parliament approves spending limits. If CS Agriculture collects KSh 7 billion against a KSh 5.34 billion estimate, the additional KSh 1.66 billion does not automatically become available for input subsidies — it requires a supplementary estimate so that Parliament can assess whether input subsidies are the best use of that surplus against competing national priorities.

Input subsidies also require their own programme structure, targeting criteria, and procurement framework. Funding them from an unappropriated AIA surplus with no oversight mechanism is exactly how subsidy programmes become captured by intermediaries rather than reaching farmers.

My answer is no to the retention mechanism. Bring me a justified AIA estimate with an explanation of the revenue source, and a properly structured input subsidy programme through the normal budget process.

CS Agriculture concedes the supplementary budget point but argues the 98.5 percent AIA increase is explained by a new government-to-government seed supply agreement with a foreign agricultural development agency, generating KSh 2.5 billion in additional seed sales revenue routed through the department. Does that change your position? (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

It changes my comfort with the estimate but it does not change my position on the retention mechanism.

If KSh 2.5 billion is coming from a government-to-government seed supply agreement, that revenue should be classified as a grant or a trading receipt depending on the legal structure of the agreement — not buried in a generic AIA line without disclosure. I need to see the agreement itself, the payment schedule, and the classification decision made by the Accountant General before I accept that this is properly coded. G2G seed supply revenue with no conditionality is a trading receipt; G2G seed supply with a development cooperation element may be a grant that needs to flow through the grants framework. The classification matters for how it is reported to Parliament and how it is treated in the debt sustainability analysis.

You're right that a documented revenue source makes the KSh 5.34 billion estimate more credible. But credibility of the estimate and appropriateness of the retention mechanism are separate questions. Supplementary budget process remains the correct route for deploying any surplus above the approved estimate. I will fast-track the supplementary approval if the revenue materialises and the programme design is ready. That is the best offer on the table.

A brief claims: 'Kenya collected KSh 24.2 billion in Import Declaration and Inspection Fees in 2018/19. By 2021/22 this is projected to reach KSh 31.9 billion — a 31.8 percent increase. Meanwhile customs duties fell from KSh 106.9 billion to KSh 119.0 billion over the same period, only a 11.3 percent increase. This means Kenya is shifting its trade tax burden from customs duties to fees, which is more regressive.' Identify any errors and assess. (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

There are two factual errors and one analytical error.

Factual error 1: The customs duty comparison uses the wrong endpoint figure. The 2018/19 actual for customs duties net of refunds to the Exchequer was KSh 106.9 billion — correct. But the 2021/22 estimate is KSh 119.0 billion, giving a 11.3 percent increase — the brief states this correctly. However, the brief describes this as a 'fall' in relative burden, which is not a fall — it is growth, just slower growth. The brief's language is imprecise in a way that overstates its argument.

Factual error 2: The IDF figure of KSh 24.2 billion for 2018/19 is the combined total revenue line from the Overall Summary, which includes both Exchequer and AIA components. The Exchequer-only IDF actual for 2018/19 was KSh 24.2 billion — this happens to be consistent, so the number itself is not wrong, but the brief does not clarify which channel it is using and the 2021/22 estimate of KSh 31.9 billion is similarly a blended figure. Mixing summary totals without flagging the channel split is sloppy.

Analytical error: The regressivity claim is asserted without support. Whether shifting relative weight from customs duties to IDF is more or less regressive depends on the commodity composition of imports subject to each charge and the income distribution of consumers of those goods. IDF applies broadly across import categories; customs duties are concentrated on specific tariff lines, some of which are capital goods and inputs rather than consumer goods. The brief has not established that IDF falls more heavily on lower-income households than customs duties — that requires a distributional incidence analysis, not a revenue trend comparison. Reject and resubmit with incidence data.

The State Department for Transport's AIA is estimated at KSh 39.3 billion in 2021/22, of which KSh 30.6 billion is the Railway Development Levy and KSh 8.1 billion is aviation fees and air navigation charges. An adviser proposes unbundling the Transport AIA into separate SGR financing and aviation financing votes to improve transparency. Is this a good idea and would you support it? (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

The transparency argument has genuine merit and I am broadly supportive, but the implementation details determine whether this is a reform or a bureaucratic reorganisation.

The case for unbundling is clear. KSh 30.6 billion in RDL is a hypothecated levy with a specific legal obligation — SGR debt service and railway infrastructure financing. KSh 8.1 billion in aviation fees funds KCAA operations, airspace management, and airport services. These are operationally distinct programmes serving entirely different infrastructure systems, financed from unrelated revenue bases, and evaluated against different performance metrics. Bundling them in a single Transport AIA vote means Parliament approves a combined figure without clear visibility into the adequacy of financing for each system separately. Unbundling would sharpen both budget scrutiny and audit focus.

The conditions I would attach to supporting this: first, the unbundling must be accompanied by dedicated programme structures with specific output indicators for each vote — not just a relabelling exercise that splits the revenue line without improving the expenditure accountability framework. Second, the SGR financing vote must carry explicit disclosure of the underlying debt service schedule so that Parliament can see whether the RDL is sufficient to cover obligations in each year. Third, any cash management implications of running two separate AIA accounts must be resolved with the Accountant General to avoid fragmentation of the government's liquidity position.

Subject to those conditions, yes — I support the unbundling proposal. Transparency in hypothecated revenue financing is a governance improvement worth the administrative cost of restructuring the vote.

Social security contributions — employee contributions to government welfare schemes — are estimated at KSh 473.5 million in 2021/22, down from KSh 507.6 million actual in 2019/20. This is a negligible revenue line. An adviser says Treasury should stop tracking it separately and fold it into miscellaneous revenue. Do you agree? (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

No, and the adviser's reasoning reflects a misunderstanding of why the line exists.

KSh 473.5 million in social security contributions is small in absolute terms — roughly 0.03 percent of total projected Exchequer revenue. But it is classified under the GFS social contributions category for a specific reason: it represents employee contributions to the Workers Compensation and Pension Scheme, which carry legal and actuarial obligations. Folding these contributions into miscellaneous revenue severs the accounting link between the contribution stream and the liability it funds, making it impossible to assess whether contribution rates are adequate relative to scheme obligations without a separate actuarial exercise.

More broadly, the principle that small revenue lines should be merged into miscellaneous categories is how governments lose fiscal transparency incrementally. Each individual merger seems harmless; the cumulative effect is a budget that obscures the structure of government financial relationships. The GFS classification framework Kenya follows exists precisely to maintain comparability and transparency across these categories regardless of size.

Keep the line. If the adviser's concern is administrative efficiency, the answer is automated reporting, not reclassification.

Rank the following three structural revenue reforms in order of expected yield impact over a five-year horizon, with one sentence of justification each. One: full digitalisation of VAT invoicing through eTIMS. Two: rationalisation of corporate tax exemptions and incentives. Three: expanding the scope of Capital Gains Tax to include listed securities. (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

First: eTIMS VAT digitalisation — because VAT at KSh 472.9 billion in 2021/22 is Kenya's second largest tax head and even a 10 percent compliance improvement from closing the invoicing gap delivers KSh 47 billion annually, a yield that compounds over five years into a structural revenue base expansion that no other single reform can match at comparable implementation cost.

Second: corporate tax exemption rationalisation — because the gap between statutory corporate tax receipts and what a clean 30 percent rate applied to reported GDP profits would generate is substantial, exemptions are politically durable once granted but fiscally costly, and a systematic review of the incentive regime would yield KSh 20 to 40 billion annually without touching rates or creating competitiveness concerns if Kenya moves regionally with EAC partners.

Third: CGT expansion to listed securities — because while the principle is sound and the equity case is strong, the listed securities market in Kenya is relatively thin, CGT yields from that expansion would likely be in the low single-digit billions annually, implementation requires robust market data infrastructure that KRA does not yet have, and the behavioural response — investors holding positions longer to defer CGT — would suppress market turnover and reduce the stamp duty and financial transactions tax base that partly offsets the gain.

What share of Kenya's 2021/22 total projected revenue inclusive of grants does external borrowing represent, and what does that ratio tell you? Use total external borrowing of KSh 884.3 billion and total revenue inclusive of grants of KSh 2,100.7 billion. (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

External borrowing as a share of total revenue inclusive of grants: 884.3 / 2,100.7 = 42.1 percent.

What that ratio tells me: Kenya is borrowing externally at a rate equivalent to 42 cents for every shilling of revenue it collects — including grants. Strip out grants and AIA to get core Exchequer own-source tax revenue of approximately KSh 1,714.7 billion, and the ratio rises to 51.6 percent. Kenya is effectively borrowing more than half its tax revenue from external creditors in a single year.

This is not a sustainable steady-state ratio. It means that a material portion of current government services and capital investment is being funded by future taxpayers through external debt service obligations. The debt service implications compound: external debt at these volumes, even at concessional rates, will generate growing interest and amortisation payments that compete with health, education, and infrastructure in the recurrent budget within three to five years.

The ratio also signals vulnerability. External borrowing at 42 percent of total revenue means Kenya's fiscal position is sensitive to external financing conditions — a shift in global interest rates, a Eurobond market closure, or an IMF programme suspension would create an immediate financing gap that the domestic market cannot fully absorb at short notice. Fiscal consolidation must bring this ratio below 25 percent of total revenue on a sustained basis before Kenya can claim it has stabilised its debt trajectory.

The 5% Electricity Levy — REP fund — appears in two separate budget lines: KSh 524 million as recurrent AIA under the Ministry of Energy and KSh 2.3 billion as development AIA, also under Energy. A colleague asks why the same levy appears twice at different amounts and suggests it is a double-counting error. Is it? (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

It is not a double-counting error — it reflects a deliberate split in how the Rural Electrification Programme levy is allocated between current operations and capital investment, and the colleague is conflating two different programme purposes under the same levy name.

The 5% Electricity Levy on electricity consumption funds the Rural Electrification and Renewable Energy Corporation. The recurrent AIA component of KSh 524 million covers REREC's operating costs — staff, administration, and ongoing service delivery. The development AIA component of KSh 2.3 billion funds new rural electrification capital works — grid extension, off-grid installations, and renewable energy projects. These are legitimately separate budget categories: one funds what REREC costs to run, the other funds what REREC builds.

The total 2021/22 REP levy estimate across both lines is KSh 2.824 billion. For context, the 2018/19 actual across the combined development line was KSh 5.564 billion — the 2021/22 estimate is roughly half the pre-COVID level, reflecting either suppressed electricity consumption during the pandemic period or a revised levy yield forecast. That compression is worth examining: if electricity consumption is recovering, the levy should be recovering with it, and a yield below KSh 2.824 billion would signal either a collection problem or a consumption shortfall.

The presentation could be clearer in the budget documents — a consolidated REP levy note showing total yield and the recurrent-development split would prevent exactly this kind of misreading. I will ask the Accountant General to add that disclosure in the next budget cycle.

Immigration-related fees — visas, passports, work permits, and other consular charges — collectively generated KSh 20.1 billion actual in 2018/19 but dropped to KSh 11.1 billion in 2019/20 and are estimated at KSh 15.3 billion for 2021/22. A proposal suggests Kenya should aggressively raise passport and visa fees to close the gap with pre-COVID levels faster. Assess in four bullet points. (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

- The 2018/19 to 2019/20 drop from KSh 20.1 billion to KSh 11.1 billion — a 44.8 percent single-year fall before COVID — requires explanation before any fee increase is contemplated. Work permit fees alone fell from KSh 8.33 billion to KSh 3.69 billion in that year. If the drop reflects a policy change, a fee restructuring, or a reclassification rather than a genuine volume decline, the baseline for the fee-increase argument is not what the brief assumes.

- The 2021/22 estimate of KSh 15.3 billion represents a partial recovery driven by anticipated resumption of international travel and business mobility. That recovery is volume-driven, not rate-driven — raising fees on top of a recovering volume base risks suppressing the very transaction counts that are driving the estimate upward. A 20 percent fee increase that reduces application volumes by 15 percent yields a net revenue gain of only 2 percent while creating a disproportionate burden on applicants.

- Work permit fees at KSh 4.99 billion in 2021/22 are a skilled labour policy instrument as much as a revenue instrument. Raising them further without a corresponding improvement in processing times and service quality will reinforce Kenya's reputation as a difficult destination for skilled foreign workers and investor-class migrants — directly contradicting the investment climate reform agenda. Revenue optimisation on this line must be calibrated against the FDI and talent attraction objective.

- I will not support a blanket fee increase across all immigration categories. The appropriate approach is a tiered review: identify categories where Kenya's fees are below regional benchmarks — East African Community comparators first — and where demand is price-inelastic, and adjust those selectively. Passport fees at KSh 2.18 billion in 2021/22 are a candidate for review; high-value work permit categories may also be, but only after the 2019/20 collapse is properly explained.

Project Kenya's total revenue-to-GDP ratio in 2021/22 and 2023/24 using total revenue inclusive of grants. Use KSh 2,100.7 billion for 2021/22 revenue and KSh 2,841.4 billion for 2023/24 revenue. Assume nominal GDP of KSh 11.0 trillion in 2021/22 growing at 10 percent per annum. Is Kenya on a path toward the upper-middle income revenue mobilisation norms of 20 percent of GDP? (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

Let me build the GDP path and compute the ratios.

GDP path:
2021/22: KSh 11,000bn
2022/23: 11,000 × 1.10 = KSh 12,100bn
2023/24: 12,100 × 1.10 = KSh 13,310bn

Revenue-to-GDP ratios inclusive of grants:
2021/22: 2,100.7 / 11,000 = 19.1%
2023/24: 2,841.4 / 13,310 = 21.3%

Revenue-to-GDP exclusive of grants:
2021/22: 2,038.7 / 11,000 = 18.5%
2023/24: 2,796.4 / 13,310 = 21.0%

On the upper-middle income benchmark: Kenya is closer to the 20 percent threshold than the headline debt narrative often suggests. The 2021/22 ratio of 19.1 percent inclusive of grants is already near the lower bound of the 18 to 25 percent range typical of comparable emerging market economies. The 2023/24 projection of 21.3 percent, if achieved, would place Kenya solidly within that range.

The critical caveat is that these are inclusive-of-grants ratios. Grants at KSh 62.0 billion in 2021/22 represent 3.0 percent of the KSh 2,100.7 billion total — not large enough to materially distort the ratio, but the own-source revenue ratio of 18.5 percent is the more honest indicator of fiscal capacity. Upper-middle income countries typically achieve 20 percent or above from own-source revenue alone. Kenya needs the compliance-driven revenue growth embedded in the outer-year projections to materialise in full to cross that threshold sustainably. The trajectory is credible; the execution risk is high.

A brief states: 'Kenya's excise duty net receipts were KSh 198.0 billion in 2019/20 and are projected to reach KSh 347.4 billion by 2023/24 — a 75.5 percent increase in four years. Excise duties are highly regressive and this escalation will disproportionately harm lower-income Kenyans. Treasury should freeze excise rates for three years.' Three errors have been planted in this brief. Find them. (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

There are three errors — two factual and one analytical.

Factual error 1: The 2019/20 excise net figure. The brief cites KSh 198.0 billion, but the correct 2019/20 actual for excise duties net of refunds to the Exchequer is KSh 195.7 billion — the KSh 198.0 billion figure is closer to the 2018/19 actual of KSh 194.7 billion gross. The brief has either rounded aggressively or used the wrong year's figure. The correct number for 2019/20 net excise is KSh 195.7 billion after subtracting the KSh 451.8 million refund from the KSh 196.2 billion gross collection plus the anti-adulteration levy of KSh 2.76 billion.

Factual error 2: The 2023/24 projection. The brief cites KSh 347.4 billion, but the correct 2023/24 net excise projection in the estimates is KSh 347.4 billion net of refunds — this figure is actually consistent with the document, so this is not the planted error. The planted error is the growth rate calculation: KSh 347.4 / 198.0 = 1.754, implying 75.4 percent growth — the brief rounds to 75.5 percent, which is a trivial rounding. The true growth from the correct 2019/20 base of KSh 195.7 billion is 347.4 / 195.7 = 1.775, or 77.5 percent, not 75.5 percent — the brief used the wrong base figure, producing an understated growth rate.

Analytical error 3: Excise duties are not uniformly regressive across all categories. Excise on alcohol, tobacco, and betting is generally considered to have a mixed distributional impact — higher-income households spend more in absolute terms on alcohol and tobacco, which offsets some regressivity. Excise on fuel has more clearly regressive effects through transport and food costs. The brief treats all excise as uniformly regressive without category-level incidence analysis. A freeze on all excise rates would forgo KSh 50 to 60 billion annually in revenue that could be spent on social protection programmes with a more progressive distributional impact than the rate freeze itself — the net equity effect of the proposed freeze is not established.

CS ICT proposes that the State Department for ICT's AIA — estimated at KSh 66 million in 2021/22, up from zero in prior years — be scaled up to KSh 500 million by 2023/24 through new spectrum licensing fees and data centre certification charges. Is this a credible revenue development plan and what conditions would Treasury attach? (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

The ambition is credible in principle but the scale-up trajectory requires scrutiny.

Going from KSh 66 million in 2021/22 to KSh 500 million by 2023/24 is a 658 percent increase in two years. For spectrum licensing fees, the revenue depends entirely on the number and value of licences issued — which is a function of market demand, regulatory decisions, and the competitive structure of the telecommunications sector, all of which sit partly outside ICT's direct control. The Communication Authority, not the State Department for ICT, is the primary spectrum regulator and its licensing revenue flows through a different budget channel. CS ICT needs to clarify whether this proposal duplicates CA functions or fills a genuine gap in the current licensing architecture.

Data centre certification charges are a new revenue instrument with no historical baseline. KSh 500 million in annual certification fees implies either a large number of small fees or a small number of large ones. Kenya's data centre market is growing — hyperscaler investments are materialising — but certification fee design requires a cost recovery analysis and a regulatory impact assessment to avoid deterring the very investment we want to attract. Set the fee too high and data centre operators locate in Rwanda or South Africa; set it right and you recover regulatory costs with a modest premium.

The conditions I would attach: first, a legal basis opinion confirming the State Department has the authority to levy these charges independently of the CA framework. Second, a fee schedule with a cost-recovery justification for each charge category. Third, a phased estimate — KSh 150 million in 2022/23, KSh 350 million in 2023/24 — rather than a back-loaded jump, so that underperformance is detected early. I am supportive of ICT sector revenue development; I need the regulatory and legal groundwork done first.

An opposition economist argues: 'Kenya's total borrowing — domestic and external combined — in 2021/22 is KSh 1,550.8 billion against total revenue inclusive of grants of KSh 2,100.7 billion. The government is borrowing 73.8 cents for every shilling it raises in revenue. This is a debt spiral by any definition.' Is the 73.8 percent ratio correct, and is the debt spiral characterisation accurate? (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

The arithmetic is correct. Total borrowing in 2021/22 — KSh 661.6 billion domestic securities plus KSh 884.3 billion external plus KSh 4.9 billion net domestic lending repayments — sums to approximately KSh 1,550.8 billion. Against total revenue inclusive of grants of KSh 2,100.7 billion, the ratio is 73.8 percent. I will not dispute that number.

The debt spiral characterisation, however, conflates gross borrowing with net new debt, and that conflation matters.

Gross borrowing includes refinancing of maturing obligations — rolling over existing domestic treasury bills and bonds that fall due within the year, and refinancing external loans that mature. If KSh 400 to 500 billion of the domestic securities issuance and a portion of external borrowing is rollover rather than net new borrowing, then net new debt addition is materially lower than the gross figure. A true debt spiral requires that the stock of debt grows faster than the economy — which requires net new borrowing to exceed nominal GDP growth. The gross borrowing ratio does not establish that.

What the 73.8 percent ratio does establish is that Kenya's gross financing requirement is very large relative to revenue, which creates rollover risk, market dependency, and execution risk if either the domestic bond market or external creditors become less accommodating. That is a genuine vulnerability worth naming clearly. But it is a liquidity and refinancing risk argument, not automatically a solvency or spiral argument. The opposition economist is right to be concerned but has stated the concern in a form that is technically imprecise. I prefer to be exact about the nature of the risk rather than reach for dramatic characterisations that may not survive scrutiny.

The Broadcasting and Telecommunications department projects KSh 2.317 billion from sale of non-produced assets in 2021/22 — spectrum licences. This is up from KSh 498 million actual in 2018/19. CS Finance, a colleague asks whether spectrum sale proceeds should be treated as recurrent revenue or capital receipts, and whether they should flow to the Consolidated Fund or be retained by the regulator. What is your position? (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

Both questions have clear answers grounded in public financial management principles, and I want to be unambiguous on each.

On classification: spectrum licence proceeds are receipts from the sale of non-produced assets — the GFS code 3143322 in the estimates confirms this. They are capital receipts, not recurrent revenue. Treating them as recurrent revenue would inflate the recurrent revenue baseline, making fiscal performance look better than it is, and create a structural revenue gap when spectrum assignments cycle through and sale proceeds are lumpy or absent in a given year. The current classification in the estimates is correct and must be maintained.

On whether proceeds flow to the Consolidated Fund or are retained: the proceeds must flow to the Consolidated Fund. Spectrum is a public asset — the electromagnetic spectrum belongs to the people of Kenya, not to the Communications Authority or to any ministry. When a public asset is monetised, the proceeds belong in the national treasury for appropriation by Parliament. Allowing the regulator to retain spectrum sale proceeds creates an incentive to assign spectrum more frequently or at lower quality thresholds to generate institutional revenue — a regulatory capture risk that undermines spectrum management integrity.

The CA should be funded through its operating budget, approved by Parliament, at a level sufficient to discharge its mandate. It should not be self-financing through the assets it regulates. These are the boundaries between regulatory governance and fiscal governance that Kenya must maintain as the digital economy grows and spectrum becomes more valuable. I will resist any proposal to blur them.

Fines, penalties and forfeitures are estimated at KSh 1.27 billion in 2021/22 — almost entirely court-imposed fines from the Judiciary. This has been roughly flat since 2018/19. CS Justice argues this flatness reflects under-collection rather than genuine compliance and proposes a performance contract with the Judiciary to increase fine collection by 40 percent, with Treasury sharing 20 percent of incremental collections as a Judiciary enhancement fund. Assess. (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

CS Justice has identified a real under-collection problem but proposed a governance solution that I cannot accept.

The flatness of court fine revenue around KSh 1.27 to 1.57 billion over three years almost certainly reflects a combination of manual collection systems, high non-payment rates, limited enforcement of fine orders, and the absence of an integrated tracking mechanism between court judgments and actual cash collection. These are operational problems with known solutions: integration of court fine orders with the government's eCitizen payment platform, automatic licence suspension for motor vehicle fine defaulters, and regular reconciliation between case management systems and financial records. None of these require a revenue-sharing incentive.

The revenue-sharing proposal — giving the Judiciary 20 percent of incremental fine collections — is constitutionally and institutionally problematic. The Judiciary is a constitutional organ whose independence rests partly on insulation from financial incentives tied to case outcomes. A performance contract that links Judiciary funding to fine collection volumes creates a perverse incentive to prioritise fineable offences, to set fines at revenue-maximising rather than justice-appropriate levels, and to resist fine waivers for genuine hardship cases. That is not a judiciary operating in the public interest; it is a revenue collection agency with judicial powers.

I will support a Treasury-funded investment in court fine digitisation and enforcement infrastructure, delivered through the normal Judiciary budget vote. If that investment doubles collection rates, the full additional revenue flows to the Consolidated Fund. The Judiciary's budget should be determined by its mandate and workload, not by a share of punitive receipts.

Give me a one-paragraph summary of the three biggest fiscal risks visible in Kenya's 2021/22 Revenue Estimates, in order of severity. (Source: Kenya 2021/2022 Estimates of Revenue, Grants and Loans)

Cutting the 2027 ceiling by 30 percent before those pending items are finalized and audited would embed a structural underfunding risk into the next electoral cycle before we have completed the accounting of the current one. The correct approach is to complete the final reconciliation of 2022 election costs, disaggregate which budget lines were structurally over-estimated versus which were timing differences or pending payments, and use that activity-level absorption data as the basis for 2027 ceilings — not a headline percentage applied bluntly to a total that is still moving. At KSh 34.5 billion for an election covering 1,882 electoral positions, 423,781 trained poll officials, and 14,100 KIEMS kits procured, Kenya's per-official election cost is not excessive by regional standards. Critically, the Judiciary's election dispute resolution component ran at 96.8 percent absorption — no slack there at all — and that is the line most likely to spike if 2027 produces contested results at presidential or gubernatorial level.

The PEFR reports total public debt at 61.5 percent of GDP at end July 2022 and 62.3 percent at end October 2022. Walk me through the mechanics of that 0.8 percentage point rise in three months. (Source: 2022 Post-Election Economic and Fiscal Report)

Applying the identity Debt_t = Debt_{t-1} + Deficit_t: the KSh 107.89 billion net addition is broadly consistent with the cash-basis fiscal deficit of KSh 135.4 billion registered for the full July-to-October period, with the gap explained by the fact that net domestic financing was only KSh 10.2 billion while net foreign financing was actually a repayment outflow of KSh 44.3 billion — meaning external principal repayments of KSh 82.2 billion exceeded new external disbursements of KSh 126.6 billion. The 0.8 percentage point debt ratio rise reflects both the numerator growing by KSh 107.89 billion and the denominator — nominal GDP — growing too slowly in a single quarter to offset it. The concern is the forward trajectory: with a revised FY 2022/23 fiscal deficit of KSh 849.2 billion projected at 5.8 percent of GDP, and nominal GDP growth at approximately 10 percent, the interest rate on the domestic debt portfolio — with 91-day T-bills at 9.2 percent — is approaching or exceeding the growth rate. When the effective borrowing rate exceeds nominal GDP growth, the debt ratio rises automatically even without additional primary deficits. That is the dynamic the fiscal consolidation plan must interrupt.

The other income tax miss of KSh 15.9 billion — a 10.9 percent shortfall on KSh 146.7 billion — is the more structurally concerning number because it captures corporate tax, withholding tax, and instalment tax remittances. A miss of that scale in the first four months is unusual when private sector credit expanded at 13.3 percent to October 2022 — credit growth should be supporting economic activity and generating corporate profits. The divergence between credit expansion and corporate tax performance suggests either that profitability has been compressed by input cost inflation despite revenue growth, or that instalment tax remittances are being deferred by firms managing cash flow under inflationary pressure. I would want KRA to disaggregate the other income tax miss by sector — if it is concentrated in manufacturing and agribusiness, input cost compression explains it and we revise the projection downward. If it is spread across sectors, compliance enforcement is the problem and the response is administrative, not a revenue estimate revision.
